A snowmobiler was caught carried and fully buried in an avalanche on a northeast-facing slope in Leroux Creek on Thursday February 8 2024. The group discussed the High avalanche danger and decided to avoid avalanche terrain but visibility was very poor due to flat light while they were out and the individual drifted onto a slope steeper than they thought without knowing. After triggering the avalanche and being fully buried the party completed a very impressive companion rescue largely due to two members having completed avalanche rescue training with Matt Entz and the individual was found unconscious. A member of the group had Wilderness EMT training and cleared snow out of their airway after which they regained consciousness. The group wrapped her in a bivy bag and then lit a fire in nearby woods to warm her up. This was a very close call with a good outcome largely thanks to the heroic avalanche rescue.

The avalanche occurred on a small steep slope just southeast of Priest Mountain in the Grand Mesa National Forest. It was a soft slab avalanche that was unintentionally triggered by a snowmobiler. It was small relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to bury injure or kill a person. The avalanche broke on a layer of facets between the new snow and the old snow surface (SS-AMu-R2-D2-O). The avalanche broke on a steep slope about 75 feet tall running the full length of the slope and breaking around 100 feet wide. The crown face of the avalanche was about two feet thick.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) forecast for the area around Priest Mountain on the Grand Mesa for February 8 2024 rated the avalanche danger at High (Level 4 of 5) near and below treeline. The primary problem was Persistent Slab avalanches on west through north to southeast aspects near and below treeline. The likelihood was Likely and the expected size Small to Large (up to D2). The second problem was Storm Slab avalanches on all aspects near and below treeline. The likelihood was Very Likely and the size Small to Large (up to D2). The summary statement read: 

An Avalanche Warning is in effect for the Grand and Battlement Mesas. Heavy snow and strong winds are creating very dangerous avalanche conditions. Natural and human-triggered avalanches are very likely. Avalanches can break wide across terrain features they can occur in trees or on steep slope cuts above trails and you can trigger them from long distances away. Travel in avalanche terrain is not recommended Wednesday evening through Friday morning.

column20:
The avalanche occurred on Ski Hayden Peak at the headwaters of Sawyer Creek approximately 7 miles south of the town of Aspen. It was a soft-slab avalanche remotely triggered from the bottom of the slope by a pair of backcountry tourers. It was very small relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to bury injure or kill a person. The avalanche broke on a layer of facets near the bottom of the snowpack (SS-ASr-R1-D2-O). The avalanche broke on a rocky uneven slope where the snowpack was notably thinner than adjacent slopes. It broke about 200 feet wide and ran close to 300 vertical feet.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) forecast for the area around Ashcroft for February 7 2024 rated the avalanche danger at Considerable (Level 3 of 5) at all elevations. The primary problem was Persistent Slab avalanches on west through north to southeast aspects at all elevations and south and southwest aspects above treeline. The likelihood was Likely and the expected size Large to Very Large (D2-D3). The summary statement read: 

Dangerous avalanche conditions exist throughout the Elk and West Elk Mountains. You can easily trigger a large and deadly avalanche you can trigger them from a distance and they will likely break wider and run farther than you expect. The most dangerous slopes face west through north to southeast where an unusually weak layer of snow was buried by one to two feet of snow during the last storm. Additional snowfall Tuesday night throughout the day Wednesday will increase the danger. You can find safer travel options on slopes that got less than about a foot of snow during the last storm or by simply avoiding travel on or underneath steep slopes on aspects of concern.

column20: A party of six (4 skiers 2 boarders) skinned up to approximately 11300' and proceeded to ski down a face that was predominately west facing. The party stopped around 11000' when a significant roll into a steep section was noticed. Boarder 1 proceeded to the top of the roll advised the party to take lines to the skiers' right of the steep section and maintained the position as spotter.   Skier 1 skied the line to a safe position below and radioed the team advising them to stay left to avoid a ridge and steep section. Boarder 2 took a line more to the left of Skier 1's. Skier 2 started down the same line and then trended further left after clearing a section of trees.   Skier 3 took a similar line crossing over Skier 2's line through a concave section below a northwest face. The face broke free the moment when Skier 3 crossed Skier 2's line.   Boarder 1 observed the event and alerted Skier 3 who was able to ski to a safe position beyond the slide.

column20: 11600' approximately on a North West Face skiers right of the normal Hollywood line below Red Mountain No.3 - Skier 1 was on skis and skier 2 was on a splitboard. As Skier 1 prepared his line and as we discussed our stopping points Skier 2 positioned her splitboard so she could ride near that same line which cause her to move out onto the slope a little farther from the protection of the rockband with small trees above them. Skier 2 then sat down and positioned herself in a comfortable position to keep eyes on Skier 1. We both discussed if anything were to go it would probably be no bigger than a D1 given all the shallow rock outcroppings that would discontinue any chance of a full propagation across the slope. Skier 1 dropped onto the slope doing a ski cut with a couple hops to see if he would get any results or information from the snowpack. As Skier 1 headed down the slope he took 1 turn toward the gully which remote triggered the slope above skier 2. The slope that propagated avalanched down the gully away from Skier 2 which then caused a sympathetic avalanche to propagate right where Skier 2 was sitting. Given she was on a snowboard and sitting she was unable to take a step up the hill where she would have missed taking a ride. The avalanche continued to propagate more which looked like another sympathetic avalanche. This avalanche went to the ground and in some places the crown appeared to be at least 7 feet and a small as 1 foot. The crown was about 600 feet across and ran about 700 feet. Skier 2 took the ride for about 150-200'. When the avalanche came to a stop on the shelf Skier 2 was buried up to her hip and had to dig herself out. . Skier 1 had stopped before the discussed point due to Skier 2 yelling on the radio about the avalanche and about her then being in the avalanche. column20: One skier traveling in a party of three was caught and carried in a large avalanche on a northwest-facing slope below treeline off Mount Justice. Within the first few turns of the descent the skier noticed the slope fracture around them and tried to keep up their speed and ski out of it. The avalanche knocked the skier over and began dragging them down the slope. The avalanche immediately knocked one ski off their feet and after dragging them around 50-100 feet down the slope their other ski was ripped off by the debris. With their skis off their feet they were able to self-arrest on the bed surface and managed to escape the moving debris. The avalanche broke on deeply buried weak layers and slid on the ground taking the entire season's snowpack down the slope with it. The skier was able to find one of their skis and strapped branches to their other foot while they ascended to the ridge and skied with one ski back down to the trailhead with no serious injuries.

column20: Two groups traveling on these low angle south facing meadows potentially simultaneously remote-triggered this avalanche. One group found themselves below this gully and one group found themselves above this gully. The group traveling below the gully recognized the overhead hazard and traveled one at time across the slidepath. As the second skier began skinning across the path they felt a collapse and looked up and observed the avalanche release. The debris swept down piling up around 6' deep on the road and continued down the slope for another 200'. The group above the gully also felt the collapse but was standing on 25* terrain and observed the avalanche release about 100' below them. No one was caught carried or injured but a spooky close call.

Group of 5 skied from Opus Hut at 11:55am. Skier 1 skied a short pitch down into a treed area (150ft vert). After communicating with Skier 1 about conditions skier 2 told the rest of group that they would ski the slope and play it through. Skier 2 proceed to ski the entirety of the run top to bottom (700ft vert) they stopped on the second road cut which is the ascent track to Opus from the Silverton side. Skiers 1 3 4 and 5 regrouped just below where Skier 1 had initially stopped and proceed to pitch the rest of the run out due to poor visibility and a decision to maintain group continuity. After a few pitched out sections the rest the group skied the final 250ft of vert down to the road one at a time. When Skier 5 approached the road they made a hard turn and slowed down at a convexity in doing so the slope released 10ft below them. The rest of the group had stationed themselves in a safe area on the road with no overhead and when the avalanche released no one was in harms way. The avalanche propagated on a micro-feature that was a convexity. It was a wind-loaded east facing pocket that had a 3.5ft deep crown. When the initial mass of the avalanche crossed the road snow below the road began to fracture and another slab released a and more snow was carried into the micro gully below the road.

column20: Submitting this observation on behalf of the party who triggered and was caught and carried in this avalanche. I was able to investigate the crown of this avalanche on my descent and got decent pictures. Farther down on my group's descent one of my partners also triggered a small persistent slab avalanche on a small steep slope that sees sun exposure and willow facet-farm effects. Three avalanches were observed in all but the biggest one was unintentionally triggered and resulted in the skier taking a short ride on top of the debris. They were not buried or injured and were able to ski out on their own. That said I believe this is the first avalanche of this nature to occur in this area this season. There was around 4 feet of debris piled on the uphill side of several trees. It's possible this triggered another sympathetic slide out of view behind a tree island as the terrain wrapped aspect to the south as more debris was observed in the flats below.

On Saturday January 14 2024 at approximately 11:30 AM a skier unintentionally triggered an avalanche on a mid-elevation (~8500’) northwest-facing sparsely treed slope above an indistinct gully on the Northwest Face of Little Poudre Mountain. This large soft slab avalanche filled a relatively narrow path (SS-AS(u)-R3-D2). The area was too dangerous for a crown profile. Still it is assumed that the avalanche broke on a layer of near-surface facets and surface hoar responsible for a widespread avalanche cycle in the region. The weak snow layer formed during a prolonged dry period in December that was buried by approximately 30” of snow falling during a series of storms that began on January 4th. The avalanche broke approximately 50’ wide and 1-3’ deep and entrained more snow along the flanks of a shallow gully. The avalanche fell approximately 600 vertical feet. The slide path is one of several sparsely wooded avalanche paths on the northwest face of Little Poudre Mountain that run the full 1200’ length of the face. (Figure 1) This avalanche was one of the dozens reported in the region during a particularly active avalanche cycle. (Figure 2)

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Bridger-Teton Avalanche Center forecast on January 14 2024 rated the avalanche danger in the Greys River zone at High in elevation bands above 7500’ and Considerable below. Persistent slab avalanches were the primary avalanche problem on all aspects above 7500’. The expected size of the persistent slabs was projected to be large to very large (D2-3) and very likely to be human-triggered. Deep persistent slab avalanches were also listed as possible ranging from large to very large or D2 to D3.5. The Bottom Line section of the day’s forecast stated:

Very dangerous avalanche conditions exist today. Triggering an avalanche large enough to bury injure or kill a person is likely in avalanche terrain at all elevations. In addition destructive natural avalanches are likely in the middle and upper elevations. Traveling in near or under avalanche terrain is not recommended today.

SS-ASr-R1-D2-O.  Skied slope and looked back to see debris pile to the skiers right of my tracks.  I had not noticed the avalanche until this point and felt no collapse or heard anything while skiing down.  The descent is on a very small and lower angle ridge just to the lookers right of where the avalanche occurred and around 30°.  I investigated the avalanche and found the crown to be 56cm high with HS of 179cm.  Elevation was ~12100' and a 38° NE aspect. Slope angle at the crown was 37° and 30° at the toe. It appeared the avalanche slid on buried surface hoar that were noted to be around 8+mm in size.  The avalanche was estimated to have been approx. 150' across and 200' long.  There was also another avalanche approximately 100 yards across the slope that was presumed to have sympathetically released at the same time.  This was estimated at 200' across and 400' long.

Near and below treeline slopes produced a widespread cycle of soft slab avalanches breaking on the January weak layer; these all appeared to run last night and this morning. We had limited visibility of alpine terrain. Slides were generally D1 to D1.5 with a few D2s in larger terrain; slabs were typically 30 to 50 cm; larger with elevation up valley. Avalanches occurred on nearly all aspects; the most extensive activity was on E and NE slopes (mostly due to terrain biases) with a significant amount of activity on SE SW and W aspects. We remotely triggered a handful of avalanches on near treeline slopes as well. Remotely triggered an avalanche cycle in South Baldy Bowl from ~1500 feet away to the nearest avalanche. ~2500ft to the furthest avalanche. Measured on Google Earth. Basically one avalanche ran and that likely sympathetically triggered 3 others. Up to D2 . Poor visibility and I couldn't see the whole production as it was happening. Those crowns spanned from 11800ft to 12200ft on SE to S aspects.

I made several trips between CB South and Mount CB today (I did not have a good camera hence no pics however I did have binoculars just before sunset to see some things in the distance (noted in individual avalanche obs). Timing is uncertain due to periodic visibility. Lower elevation northerly slopes along HWY 135 lower flanks of Whetstone Gibson Ridge and Sunlight Ridge had avalanche activity before noon (I suspect most of this ran in the early AM during peak precipitation). Just before sunset I was able to spot with binos a pile of avalanches on westerly terrain NTL on Double Top (mostly D1.5s maybe 1 D2) a D2 on SE start zone of Whetstone's X Chute a D2 with drifted-over crown on a south aspect of Red Ridge NTL and a D2 on drifted south-facing Teocalli. I could see many other suspect-looking textures in the snow at upper elevations but poor vis prevents confirmation However I did get great vis of southerly terrain in Twin Lakes drainage Pearl Mountains area along Elk Crest and White Mountain without seeing any avalanche activity. Additionally there are countless other tiny-small avalanches on north half of compass in sheltered terrain.

column20:
The avalanche occurred on a northeast-facing slope above Current Creek in an area locally known as “Moonlight Basin.” It was a hard slab avalanche remotely triggered by two backcountry tourers from about 1000 feet away. It was medium-sized relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to bury injure or kill a person. The avalanche broke two to four feet deep in a layer of old faceted snow (HS-ASr-R3-D2.5-O). It was around 400 feet wide and ran 600 vertical feet.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) forecast for the area around Berthoud Pass for December 5 2023 rated the avalanche danger at Considerable (Level 3 of 5) near and above treeline and Moderate (Level 2 of 5) below the treeline. The primary problem was Persistent Slab avalanches on northwest through north to east-facing slopes at all elevations and southeast-facing slopes near and above the treeline. The likelihood was Likely and the expected size Small to Large (up to D2). The second problem was Wind Slab avalanches on northeast through east-to-south-facing slopes near and above treeline. The likelihood was Likely and the expected size was Small to Large (up to D2). The summary statement read: 

You can find dangerous slabs on northerly and easterly-facing slopes and trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you. The avalanche occurred on Marble Peak near treeline in a north-facing bowl locally known as “The Fridge.” It was a soft-slab avalanche unintentionally triggered by a group of backcountry tourers. It was small relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to bury injure or kill a person. The avalanche broke on a layer of facets at the bottom of the snowpack (SS-ASu-R2-D2.5-O/G). The avalanche broke one to three feet deep over 1000 feet wide and ran almost 700 vertical feet.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) forecast for the area around Marble Peak for November 25 2023 rated the avalanche danger at Considerable (Level 3 of 5) near and above the treeline and Moderate (Level 2 of 5) below the treeline. Persistent Slab avalanches with a likelihood of Likely and a size of Small to Large (up to D2) were highlighted on northwest through north to east-facing slopes at all elevations and southeast-facing slopes near and above the treeline. The summary statement read: 

You can trigger an avalanche where you find more than about 10 inches of drifted snow resting over old weak snow. The most dangerous slopes face north to northeast through east near and above treeline. Avalanches may break deeper and wider than you anticipate. Shooting cracks and audible collapses are warning signs and you should move to lower-angle or wind-sheltered terrain. Getting caught in even a small avalanche at this time of year could end badly if it carries you into rocks or other shallowly buried hazards.

This was a naturally triggered wet loose avalanche. The avalanche was small relative to the path with a destructive size of 1.5. The avalanche was likely triggered by a mass of melting snow falling from a rocky convexity onto the slope below. (WL-N-R1-D1.5-O). It started on a north-northeast-facing slope at around 11940 feet and entrained wet snow in the start zone and track. 400’ lower the avalanche struck a party of two ski mountaineers carrying them downslope. Both skiers were partially buried and injured; one died due to injuries sustained during the avalanche. The debris was made up of round masses of wet snow up to 40 cm in diameter. The debris was 20 cm to 50 cm deep and covered an area that extended downhill 150 m and was 50 m wide.

Avalanche Forecast

The avalanche occurred within the forecast area of the Eastern Sierra Avalanche Center which issued daily avalanche forecasts during the 2022-23 season from December 4th to April 29th. ESAC’s final forecast product a General Avalanche Information advisory expired on June 1st – two weeks prior to the accident.

This avalanche occurred on the east face of Bald Mountain about 6.5 miles southeast of Breckenridge. It was triggered by a skier on a broad above-treeline slope and then ran through two steep east-facing chutes. The slide was small relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to bury injure or kill a person. It started in steep terrain below the summit of Bald Mountain. As the debris ran downhill it entrained a few inches of wet snow from the chutes and slope below. The debris continued to gouge into the wet snow lower in the avalanche path. Eventually it flowed into a narrow gully in the runout zone. It ran about 1700 vertical feet (SS-ASu-R1-D2-I).

This avalanche occurred on the northeast face of the northernmost peak of King Solomon Mountain (point 13045) about 3.5 miles east of Silverton. It was a soft-slab avalanche unintentionally triggered by a backcountry skier. The slide was small relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to injure a person in the very steep rocky terrain. It released at the interface between wind-drifted snow and the old hard snow surface (SS-ASu-R1-D1.5-I). The fracture line was six to eight inches deep and about 70 feet wide. It started above treeline in steep terrain below the summit and then ran through a steep northeast-facing chute.  

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) forecast for the area around King Solomon Mountain for Friday April 28 2023 rated the avalanche danger at MODERATE (Level 2 of 5) above treeline and LOW (Level 1 of 5) near and below treeline. Wind Slab avalanches with a likelihood of Possible were highlighted above treeline on northeast through southeast to south-facing aspects. The expected avalanche size was Small to Large (up to D2). Loose Wet avalanches with a likelihood of Possible were also highlighted near and above treeline on east through south to west-facing slopes. The expected avalanche size of these avalanches was Small (up to D1.5). The summary stated:

The most problematic areas are high-elevation slopes where the wind drifts the new snow into thicker slabs. Re-route your travels to wind-sheltered slopes and those below treeline if you see cracking in the snow surface or fresh avalanches where you plan to recreate. Avalanches may be easier to trigger on slopes with wind-drifted snow deeper than about 6 inches. Smooth lens-shaped surfaces below ridgelines are an indicator of recent drifting and areas of heightened danger. Even small avalanches in complex or extreme terrain can knock you off your feet and send you on a dangerous ride like very steep couloirs hanging snow fields or steep faces with cliffs.

With fresh snow a strong sun and warming temperatures watch for wet snow avalanches from steep sunny slopes. Retreat to shady slopes if you see rollerballs or find around 6 inches of wet sticky snow.

I was walking on the rock ridgeline with the cornice to my left and lee slope to my right. While stepping on large rocks one of my left pole plants remote triggered a large and loud cornice break/crack. The initial break occurred about 15 feet away from me and then cracked toward me and away from me. I was in a safe stance and did not have to make any movements to avoid the cracking and cornice fall but the sensitivity of the crack/break and the fact that I was very very far from the edge took me by surprise. Good reminder to always give cornices no matter the weather or conditions an incredibly and sometimes stupidly wide berth. The avalanche was a HS-ACr-R1-D2-I that ran approx 2800'.

Pole Canyon is located on the southernmost end of the Oquirrh Mountains with Flat Top South Peak (10420 feet) at the head of the canyon. Pole Canyon mainly runs north and south. It has many steep avalanche-prone slopes that funnel into terrain traps and gullies formed by snowmelt and summertime water runoff. The base of the drainage is Cedar Valley and there is a small town just east of the canyon in the foothills called Cedar Fort. Most of Pole Canyon is private land with no public access.

This avalanche fractured over parts of a bowl facing east southeast and south on Flat Top South Peak. This large open bowl has very few trees or vegetation on the steep slopes. The avalanche fracture line (crown face) was 4250 feet wide based on measurements in Google Earth and CalTopo. The avalanche ran 2360 vertical feet downhill. The avalanche traveled a horizontal distance of 1.26 miles (6635 feet) from the crown face to the toe of the debris. The runout (or alpha) angle was approximately 20 degrees.

The avalanche was a hard slab that piled debris deeply on specific terrain features like the steep gullies and flat benches where we found debris greater than 20 feet deep. In areas where the debris fanned out it was generally less than 5 feet deep. While there is little historical data for this area conversations with one resident helped us classify this avalanche as HS-AM-D4-R4-O. This large avalanche fractured over an extensive area and broke relatively deep creating a massive volume of snow that funneled into the deep gully below.

The avalanche occurred in Maroon Bowl on a near treeline northwest-facing slope on Highland Peak in an area adjacent to but outside the Aspen Highlands ski area boundary. It was a very large avalanche unintentionally triggered by a group of sidecountry skiers. It was small relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to bury and destroy a car damage a truck destroy a wood frame house or break a few trees. The avalanche broke on a layer of well-developed depth hoar that formed the bottom 50cm of the snowpack (HS-ASu-R2-D3-O). The avalanche broke up to six feet deep 1000 feet wide and ran 1500 vertical feet towards Maroon Creek.

column20: Triggered a wind slab avalanche in the elevator shaft couloir on the S face of Hallets peak. We noticed some signs of a small slab in the 6-7 hand pits we were digging on the way up but no cracking or wumphing and decided that the conditions were not alarming. As we continued up the couloir we started to notice more signs of instability in the hand pits so we decided to bail and head down. As we were digging out our transition area where we bailed from we heard a wumph. A few hundred feet down from our high point we triggered a shallow wind slab avalanche. The crown was 2-5 inches and propagated about 25-30 feet across most of the face.  I was carried roughly 5 feet before self-arresting while the avalanche continued for about 500-600 feet to the bottom of the apron.

I remotely triggered a large avalanche from a 20-degree slope above the path. I felt a small collapse that seemed like it was just the snow around me collapsing and then looked over to see a small northeast-facing slope sliding. I looked over to the bigger east-facing path and saw a large powder cloud low in the path. The avalanche had propagated from a small northeast-facing slope for about 500 feet to the south and around an east-facing slope. The avalanche broke on facets on a melt-freeze crust below the storm snow from March 10th. The crown of the avalanche was 30 to 45 cm deep. As the avalanche ran it stepped down and gouged to the ground. Debris piles were over 10 feet deep and small trees about 8 inches in diameter were broken. The entrainment of older snow in this avalanche was impressive. If someone was caught in this avalanche the chance of surviving would be slim.

column20: On March 14 a roof avalanche at a construction site caught and buried two workers. The roof was unfinished and covered only in roofing membrane. The north-facing roof avalanched in the early afternoon. Two construction workers were on the ground below. The avalanche buried them between the structure and a dirt berm about 10 feet away. Other workers saw the avalanche bury the two called 911 and rushed to help. Workers and sheriff's deputies rescued the two workers seven to ten minutes after the avalanche from under several feet of debris. One worker lost consciousness and both were taken to the hospital for care.  March 14 was the warmest day of the winter so far. The avalanche involved most of the roof surface and most of the season's snow accumulation. Avalanche debris included blocks four to five feet across but no ice.

The avalanche failed on a north-facing slope at 8800’ near the summit of Observation Peak (9151’) in the Sawtooth Mountains of central Idaho (Fig. 2). The slope is short and sparsely treed with a convex rollover at the top. Members of the party estimated the maximum slope angle at the crown was around 35 degrees; this aligns with estimates of the slope angle from digital mapping tools.

The avalanche crown was about 500 feet wide and 3-4 feet tall (Fig. 3). The avalanche ran a maximum of 150 vertical feet. Much of the debris stopped a short distance down the bed surface where the slope angle decreased. Large blocks of the slab remained intact. All evidence indicates this was a hard slab avalanche. Sparse tree cover appeared to arrest or inhibit the flowing debris downslope of the trees and the avalanche entrained snow where the slope was free of trees. The victim appeared to be buried in one of the deeper fingers of the debris (Fig. 4).The bed surface of the avalanche was described as slick and icy by the members of the party

A housekeeper reported witnessing an avalanche at 17:10 on March 4 2023 to CAIC staff while performing snow removal for a house. The individual reported hearing ""a loud rumble"" followed by a large powder cloud quickly moving down the slope. They ran into their vehicle for additional shelter and waited until the powder cloud settled. The worker reported ""about one to two inches of snow being deposited with pine needles."" CAIC staff confirmed the event happened just prior to 17:10 with webcams from Aspen Mountain and visited the site for additional information and pictures on March 7. Best estimates are that the cornice at the top of Marty's Chute failed during a rapid uptick in southwest winds which sympathetically triggered a second avalanche in Marta's Chute. The crowns do not appear to connect across the shoulder separating the two chutes. The avalanche in Marty's was large (R4) relative to the path and the avalanche in Marta's was small (R2) relative to the path. Both avalanches were very large (D3) in destructive force ""Could bury and destroy a car damage a truck destroy a wood frame house or break a few trees.""

column20: 2 groups were present in the area ours and another. We started our tours at similar times talked about each others plans and shared radio channels. Group A (their group) was a group of 4. Group B (our group) was also a group of 4. Group A and B both arrived at the top of the intended slope at the same time. We decided Group A would ski the slope first while Group B would ski a different slope tour back up and then ski the originally intended slope. Group A skied the skier's right side of the slope to the right side of small ribbon of trees with no incident. Group B skied our alternative first slope with no incident and toured back up to the top of the main intended slope. Group B discussed our approach to the slope and decided to ski the upper slope one at a time and move slightly left of Group A's tracks. Skier 1 dropped and skied until encountering a convex roll where he pulled off to a safe spot on the right side of the slope the remaining 3 skiers met and regrouped there. The group decided to continue skiing the slope. Skier 1 went first again and skied the slope without incident pulling off at another safe spot below. Skier 2 skied about 10-15 feet skier's left of skier 1's track and made about 5 turns before triggering a large persistent slab avalanche. Skier 2 saw the avalanche crack quickly before it gained too much momentum and was able to ski out of the path skier's right. After the debris settled skiers 23 and 4 all regrouped at the bottom of the slope and debriefed the event. We took another HS recording took some pictures aspect elevation estimated slope angle then skied the remainder of the slope and used group A's skin track to ascend back to the top. Group A radio'd Group B with some beta about the skin track at which time Group B informed Group A of the avalanche. While skinning up Group B was informed that Group A had also triggered a smaller avalanche on the slope that Group B had skied first. The second avalanche that Group A triggered appeared to be a wind slab with new snow on top of it that slid on a melt-freeze crust.

Black Crater is a shield volcano in the Cascade Range in Deschutes county Oregon. The mountain is approximately 8 miles west from the town of Sisters OR. The mountain tops out at just over 7200’ and the vertical relief is approximately 2500’. The mountain has experienced at least one wildfire in recent years leaving many standing dead trees. Black Crater is within the Central Cascades zone covered by the Central Oregon Avalanche Center (COAC) and has become an increasingly popular backcountry touring destination in recent years.

The wind slab avalanche was unintentionally triggered by a skier at an elevation just under 6500 ft. at the top of a feature known as the ‘Lake Bowl’ on the east side of the mountain. The avalanche released on a major convexity where the slope went from low angle to 40+ degrees. The slope below is steep with many standing dead trees. 

The skiers had been to Black Crater several times before but had never skied the slope where the avalanche was triggered on March 2.

Avalanche Forecast

The avalanche Danger was rated moderate on the day of the avalanche with the only problem listed being wind slabs.

Problem description for March 2:     

“Most of the wind slabs formed during the last storm are trending toward stubborn to non reactive to triggering. There could be a few lingering pockets of wind slab on isolated terrain features that could still go but I suggest paying more attention to new wind loading as the snow begins falling on Thursday. West winds will be moving snow as soon as it hits the ground. The incoming storm could drop 2-4"" of snow by the afternoon and wind slabs will build on north through east and south aspects near and above treeline. 

Look for wind slabs building below ridge tops peaks and around features that catch blowing snow from cross slope winds. Most wind slab avalanches will be on the small side however monitor the depth of wind deposited snow. As wind slabs become deeper resulting avalanches can become larger.”

Link to archived forecast for March 2: https://www.coavalanche.org/forecasts/#/forecast/central_cascade/120918

Three snowmobilers were riding in the West Mancos area and climbed the adjacent ridge line to where the incident occurred. We gained the ridge above a north facing open slope in the trees. Rider 1 descended the open slope to the right near the trim line rider 2 followed. As rider 3 descended they entered the slope about 10m to the riders left of the previous tracks. Rider 3 triggered an avalanche that propagated across the entire slope and caught and buried rider 3. The slide completely buried Rider 3. Riders 1 and 2 had eyes on and quickly initiated a beacon search and located rider 3. The probe struck him at about 160cm. They quickly dug down and excavated the snow from his face after striking his helmet with the shovel. Rider 3 was unconscious but quickly regained consciousness when the airway was cleared. Rider 2 estimates they cleared his airway within 5-7 minutes. The crown was about 3 feet deep in the deepest spot. It seemed to have been a wind slab that failed on the interface from 2 storms ago as there was a prominent dust layer in the middle.

column20: Ashcroft Mountain has numerous avalanche paths that threaten the Express Creek road a popular route for backcountry travelers going to the Markley Opa's Taylor and Goodwin-Greene huts. The first three avalanche paths you cross as you ascend the road are known as Express 1 2 and 3 respectively (north to south). Express 2 and 3 share a similar runout as the paths join right around the road. At some point between February 23-25 2023 Express 2 had a D2.5 natural avalanche cross the road and reach the creek. The avalanche in Express 2 was divided by a large terrain feature halfway up the avalanche path and the debris split into two different flow paths. Express 3 had a D3 natural avalanche cross the road cross the creek and break/bend trees on the opposite side of the drainage burying the creek in around 20 feet of avalanche debris. These avalanches failed during an unusually strong wind event that occurred during a snowstorm. The Upper Tayler SNOTEL at 10717 ft. about 4 mile south of Ashcroft Mountain gained 1.3 inches of SWE from February 20-25 increasing from 13.5 to 14.8 inches of SWE on the season. From February 23 at 17:00 to February 25 at 17:00 Aspen Highland Peak weather station about 8 miles northwest of Ashcroft Mountain recorded consistent wind speeds between 15-30mph with gusts reaching over 60mph around noon on the 24 consistently from a south-southwest to a southwest direction.

On Thursday February 23 2023 at approximately 12:15 a snowmobiler unintentionally triggered an avalanche on a mid-elevation (8020’) west-northwest facing slope below tree-line one half mile north of the Poker Flats Safety Shelter (42.5236 -110.7626). It was a small avalanche and medium-sized relative to the path. The avalanche broke on a layer of faceted snow crystals above a thin crust buried on January 26th. This avalanche was triggered at a thin spot in the snowpack created by wind scouring due to variable wind directions over the course of the season. The slope above the trigger-point was loaded with drifted snow primarily from a southerly wind direction in the days prior to the accident. The avalanche broke 75 feet wide with a maximum crown height of 30 inches and average height of 20” with a vertical fall of just 50 feet (HS-AM(u)-R3-D1.5). The slope where the avalanche occurred terminated into a streambed located at its base. This avalanche was one of only two avalanches on a northwest aspect of the 81 avalanches observed or reported across all forecast zones in the 30 days prior to this incident.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Bridger-Teton Avalanche Center forecast on February 23 2023 rated the avalanche danger in the Greys River zone at Considerable above 9000’ and Moderate below 9000’ where the incident occurred. Wind slab avalanches were highlighted as the primary avalanche problem on all aspects above 7500’ with persistent slabs highlighted on all elevations and aspects except SE S and SW lower elevation slopes. The expected size of wind slabs was small to large (D1-2.5) and likely. Persistent slab avalanches were listed as possible ranging from small to very large or D1.5 to D3. The Bottom Line section of the day’s forecast stated:

At elevations above 9000′ triggering a large avalanche remains likely on steep wind loaded slopes. Many lower elevation areas also contain wind drifted slopes as well as 1′ to 2′ thick slabs of storm snow that sit on top of weak snow. It is possible to trigger an avalanche large enough to bury a person on steep slopes even near valley bottoms. Evaluate the snowpack and terrain carefully for wind drifts shooting cracks in the snow surface or sounds like whoompfing that indicate weak layers in the snowpack.

On February 19th a group of six climbers attempted the Northeast Couloir route on Colchuck Peak. At approximately 1:15pm while ascending the lead climber triggered a slab avalanche that caught and carried four members of the team approximately 1000 vertical feet. All four climbers suffered traumatic injuries during the event three perished. The remaining teammates attempted to evacuate all individuals but were unsuccessful. The Chelan County Sheriff’s Office was notified of the accident Monday morning February 20th. Mountain rescue teams met the remaining survivors at Colchuck Lake and assisted the injured party member to the trailhead.

On Friday February 24th a helicopter rescue team located and removed one of the deceased individuals. Ongoing avalanche hazard and inclement weather continued to delay recovery efforts. As of late March 2023 the two remaining deceased climbers are assumed to be buried by additional snowfall and subsequent avalanches near the base of the couloir.

Avalanche

Due to the high consequence nature of the terrain ensuing stormy weather limited visibility and ongoing avalanche danger very few specifics are known about the avalanche. However GPX tracks and interviews with the survivors provide some insights.

The avalanche occurred high within the NE Couloir at around 8200ft. This N to E facing terrain often contains slope angles near or above 45 degrees. Given the confined nature of the chute it would typically only be capable of producing relatively small avalanches (D1-2 in size). This corresponds with the description given by the group and the lack of initial burials. Based on this information and statements by the party the avalanche was likely a D1.5 in size.

Given the extremely steep sustained nature of the terrain debris from the slide descended at least 1000 vertical feet to near the base of the couloir where slope steepness eases. 

NWAC Forecast Zone: East Central Zone 

Avalanche Danger Rating (Above Near or Below Tree-line): 

The forecasted avalanche danger was Moderate near and above tree-line and Low below-treeline at the time of the accident with increasing danger during the day.

column20: In Upper Hunter Creek and Brush Creek. All three recent avalanches below have seen recent wind-loading and they all have massive fetches.  The first wind-loaded test slope I put a track on produced a result that slightly displaced a small wind slab. This slab didn’t push over the stauchwall. The crown was 4 inches to 2 feet thick and failed on a non-persistent density chance.  The next test slope was slightly steeper and connected to a much bigger wind-loaded slope. South 11800ft. A wind slab released in the upper snowpack before stepping down into a couple of different more deeply buried weak layers. The resulting avalanche was large in size. The crown height ranged from 1 foot to an estimated 4 or 5 feet. In the section of the crown I could access the avalanche released on a thin layer of small facets that were atop what looked like an old wind-board. This was about 10cm below the only crust in the upper snowpack. In another area this avalanche stepped down to the lower half of the snowpack before further gouging to the ground.  Got a closer look at the previously reported natural avalanche near the top of Hunter Creek. South 12000ft. This avalanche appeared to fail similarly to the avalanche described above. The upper crown failed between P-hard snow above K-hard snow. The knife-hard snow had dust blown in on it from the ridge. Like the avalanche above there appeared to be a thin layer of small faceted grains at this interface. There was 80 to 90cm of snow below the bed surface in the upper crown. Lower down on the slope there were two areas where the avalanche stepped down to near the ground. The upper crown height ranged from 2 feet to around 5 feet.  East 12000ft near Timbered Hill. I couldn’t see this avalanche well. It looked like a wind slab that released in the upper snowpack. D1.5. However it could have been a deeper crown that has been refilling in the last couple of days. I’d estimate it ran around a similar time as the other natural avalanche in upper Hunter Creek.

A large avalanche was triggered by a group of skiers around 12:45 PM on February 8 2023 on an east-southeast-facing slope above the treeline in the backcountry terrain adjacent to Aspen Snowmass. The skiers ""made three hard ski cuts on the way to the line"" and the first two skiers descended the slope one at a time and waited for skier 3 out from underneath the slope they just skied. Skier 3 reports seeing shooting cracks cross the whole face instantly on his second turn and he skied as fast as he could toward ""my plan A exit to the left."" All 3 skiers were unharmed in the avalanche.  Skier 3 stated in hindsight that the line they skied was ""generally not worth it and a bad decision"" since it was a shallow southeasterly-facing slope and to get back into the resort they had to cross numerous avalanche paths of similar aspects that had not slid yet. Skier 3 reports seeing dozens of ski tracks descending similar aspects above where they had just traversed with none of them triggering an avalanche. Skier 3 also reports having ""a bad gut feeling and decided to ski it as fast as possible and get out of the path asap. Always trust your gut if it says things are bad.""  Although there has been very little avalanche activity in the Elks recently this avalanche highlights the current Persistent Slab avalanche problem. You could be the third or maybe even the 50th person to ski a slope before you find the trigger point and cause a large avalanche that can break near the ground and take the whole season's snowpack down on top of you.

The line we skied was a gladed run varying between 100-115cm deep for 3 of 4 pitches until last pitch (crown height measured 40cm). 3 snowboarders entered the top of the crooked K from the lower angle ridge between the K and Y. We discussed our plan at the top of the tree line / snow line around 11700'. Rider 1 entered the slope and made a few turns and then stopped before the trees got dense still in an open area between the K and Y. Rider 1 pulled out their phone to take video at 1:52PM. Rider 2 planned to leap frog and ski past Rider 1 and then off to the skiers right into the steeper NW trees near the top of the crooked K eventually to a stopping point still in the trees but before entering the gut of the main K slide path.  Rider 2 descended making big turns and going past Rider 1. Rider 3 was still above near the snow line / treeline in a safe spot. As Rider 2 skied past Rider 1 and into the steeper trees both the top of the crooked K and lookers left Y remotely triggered and released. Rider 1 felt a large whumpf and loud noise saying they thought it was an avalanche bomb from Copper Mountain. Rider 2 was unaware of the avalanche and did not have any snow fracture around their line through the trees. Rider 1 did not hear anything either. Riders 1 and 3 saw snow moving on both sides and a large powder cloud from the Y as well as multiple fracture lines and the crown for the Y.  Rider 2 reached the end of the trees before the entrance to the K chute and saw moving snow in the path. After making contact with both riders above and ensuring nobody was caught in the slide Riders 1 and 3 followed Riders 2 tracks into the chute and skied down through the debris to exit the path.

column20: Porphry Basin Red Mountain Pass North facing trees. Approximately 75-100 feet from the ridgeline. Slide occurred below tree line. Approximately 11300 feet. As I was climbing a section of the trees maybe approximately 30-35 degrees my right skin began to lose adhesion to my ski and was coming off. I could no longer skin so I put my skis on my back and began to climb. At this point I was about 75-100 feet from my objective the ridgeline. After a few steps (snow was very deep and unmanageable) I heard a collapse and felt the surface begin to slide. There was nothing I could do to avoid being caught in the slide. The best I could do was try to keep snow away from my face. After maybe 10 seconds I came to a stop. My whole body except my head and right arm was locked in the snow immoveable. I began to process my situation. I couldn't really tell how much snow was above me. I used my right hand/arm to clear my face neck and chest. At this point I could breathe easily and rest. I slowly began to dig my self out. Fortunately my ski pole had landed near me and I was able to use it to push snow away from my body. I was also able to use it to probe and release my legs. After about 45min to an hour I was able to release myself from my backpack then dig out my legs and fully escape from the snow. I only lost my left ski pole. I transitioned my board and rode out of the trees as quickly as I could doing my best to avoid any steep terrain.

On December 31 2022 a snowmobiler was killed in a very large avalanche north of Cooke City MT near Daisy Pass on a southeast facing slope of Crown Butte at 9800’. Two brothers (ages 17 and 21) from Washington state were snowmobiling uphill on adjacent slopes. The older brother was climbing a steeper slope and triggered the avalanche 200’ below the top. He was carried and buried 5 feet deep near the toe of the debris which measured 10-15 feet deep. He was wearing an airbag pack that he did not deploy. Both riders had shovels and probes but no avalanche beacons. A nearby group was gathered at the bottom of the slope when the slide happened. They noticed the powder cloud turned around and saw a buried snowmobile and began to search. One rider went into Cooke City to alert Search and Rescue. Searchers located the buried rider with a probe line. He was extricated an hour after the avalanche happened but resuscitation efforts were unsuccessful. The avalanche was 500 feet wide 1.5-2 feet deep on average 4 feet at the deepest and ran 600 vertical feet with a runout angle of 25 degrees. The avalanche is classified HS-AMu-R4-D3-O.

The avalanche forecast on December 31 2022 stated:

Triggering large avalanches is a serious possibility today. You could trigger an avalanche within the snow that’s fallen over the last week on a weak layer buried just beneath that or deep in the snowpack… Continued loading every day this last week by new snow and wind drifting has kept stressing the weak layers and building thicker and more cohesive slabs of fresh snow. In general the snowpack has been able to keep up and accommodate the loading. Triggering slides has become slightly less likely but by no means does that mean conditions are safe. While the likelihood has gone down a little bit the potential size and destructive power has not decreased.

As Alex identified in yesterday’s video from Cooke City wind loaded slopes are where you’re most likely to trigger a slide today (Cooke City video). Steering clear of wind drifts altogether would be a wise call. Watch for signs of instability in the new snow such as shooting cracks collapses or recent avalanches. Assessing the deeper weak layers will be harder. Snowpack tests aren’t necessarily going to give you actionable information. For now simply don’t trust those deeper weak layers. Tone down your objectives appropriately for the possibility of triggering large deep slides. 

If you’re considering riding steep slopes today ponder this analogy: as we’ve gotten a few days out from the last rapid loading event (which hit particularly hard in the southern areas) we’ve removed a couple bullets from the gun you’re playing Russian roulette with. But the gun’s still got at least one bullet left. Is that really a game you want to play today? As an alternative mellow slopes (less than 30 degrees steep) will hold good riding conditions without the risk. 

Human triggered avalanches remain possible and the avalanche danger is MODERATE.

Two backcountry skiers were skiing in Waterfall Canyon west of the town of Ophir. From the ridge they descended a slope locally known as “Mustang”. Approximately a third of the way down this slope they traversed west from Mustang to another slope locally known as “Centerline”.  Skier 1 descended the upper portion of Centerline first and stopped in the trees to the skiers right of Centerline to film Skier 2’s decent. Skier 2 triggered the avalanche on his second or third turn. It “quickly swept him off his feet”. The avalanche carried him about 600 vertical feet down a gully and trhough sparse trees. When the avalanche stopped it fully buried Skier 2 about five feet deep.   Skier 1 provided the following account: “Skier 1 joined Skier 2 at the Waterfall Canyon Trailhead in Ophir at approximately 8:30 AM and they left the trailhead together around 8:40 AM. Their plan was to skin to the top of a locally know run called “Mustang” where they could discuss conditions along the way and assess a descent plan from there. It was discussed that they definitely wanted to avoid “Centerline” before they left the trailhead. The pair ascended the well-used up track on the western side of Waterfall Canyon. On the way up they crossed paths with several other local parties that they knew and discussed what everyone’s plans were. They reached the top of Mustang and decided to stick with the plan of skiing Mustang proper. As they dropped over the knoll from the transition point they approached Mustang proper to find many ski tracks through it. The group decided to ski a NE facing tree shot from the top of Mustang towards Centerline with the notion of contouring back around to the bottom of Mustang. They skied this pitch with no visible signs of avalanche hazards and reached the bottom of the trees at the opening to the top of Centerline. Skier 2 skied the first pitch hugging the tree line and safely tucked into the trees and radioed up to Skier 1 that he was in a safe zone. It should also be noted that there were 3 existing tracks in Centerline that overlapped the slide path.”  Rescue summary:Skier 1 watched the avalanche run into the gully. He radioed Skier 2 with no response. Another gorup of backcountry tourers watched the avalanche occur and called on a common radio channel l asking if everyone was okay. A third group heard the radio traffic and one of the party (Skier 3) headed toward the accident site. Ophir residents also heard the radio traffic and called 911 before heading towards Waterfall Canyon with a rescue sled.  Skier 1 began a transceiver search as he descened the avalanhe path. He followed the signal to a lowest reading of 1.6m and probed striking Skier 2. Skier 1 began to dig. Skier 3 arrived and began to help. They reached Skier 2 in about 10 minutes. Skier 2 was unresonsive but taking “deep labored breaths”. More rescuers arrived on scene. The group excavated Skier 2 and provided first aid. Skier 2 was eventually able to exit the backcountry under his own power.  Aditional Comments: Skier 2 provided a detailed writeup of the rescue to the CAIC. He said that “the fast actions taken by other groups in the area their medical skill and experience and the availability of two-way radios likely saved Skier 2’s life.” The Telluride Mountain Club estabilshed common 2-way radio channels and protocols for the Bear Creek and Ophir areas in 2020. The protocols were instrumental for a fast resuce in this instance and have been intrumental in other avalanche rescues (3/31/2020 3/24/2020).

This avalanche occurred in the backcountry outside of the Breckenridge ski area south of Peak 10 in an area locally known as the Numbers. Individual avalanche paths are numbered in ascending order from west to east along the ridge. Number 5 the location of the accident is the path closest to the ski area boundary and Number 1 is the farthest away. Number 5 is a steep southeast-facing avalanche path with a start zone that is near treeline. It was a soft slab avalanche unintentionally triggered by a skier. It was medium-sized relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to bury injure or kill a person. It started in a layer of faceted crystals 1 to 2 millimeters in size above a fragile melt-freeze crust. The avalanche stepped down to the ground in many places. The avalanche broke 1 to 3 feet deep and about 150 feet wide. It ran about 200 vertical feet (SS-ASu-R3-D2-O/G).

column20: Triggered multiple R1D1 avalanches on steep north and northeast facing roadcuts around 10000-10600' with snowmobiles from below. Crowns were generally 1-3' deep and ran to the ground.

Descending the gully we were staying high skiers left and trying to avoid being pulled into the bottom of the gully. This was manageable but with the gutless base conditions of purely faceted snow it was not easy to maintain speed and stay as high as we wanted to near the end. Exiting the gully there is a small opening with steeper walls on either side that can be managed with maintaining speed and moving quickly from one point to the next. I was barely able to quickly clear the area but my partners skis sunk into the facets in the center of this feature. As that happened she tried to shuffle out but unbeknownst to her due to the small size of the avalanche the fact that it propagated behind her and the structure of a very soft slab over a non-planar PWL the avalanche piled around her legs up to her waist before she could get out of the way. The avalanche released simultaneously from both the ESE and NNW aspects on either side of the gully. We had to shovel out her feet and unbury her skis.

This avalanche occurred in an area locally known as Nitro Chute about three-quarters of a mile north of the summit of Berthoud Pass. Nitro Chute is a steep east-facing chute in the near treeline elevation band. It was a soft slab avalanche unintentionally triggered by a snowboarder. It was small-size relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to bury injure or kill a person. It broke into old snow layers and stepped down to the ground in places. From Grand County SAR: Yesterday (Dec 23 2022) GCSAR was paged out for a cliffed out skier on the west side of Berthoud Pass. The party was uninjured but unable to move as the snow was deep and avalanche risk was considerable. The skier also triggered a small slide and deployed his avalanche air bag. The team page went out at 9:24am while several GCSAR members were training with @fflco on their Rescue Deployment skills at our base in Fraser. In conjunction with @grand_county_sheriff and Grand County EMS they were able to utilize the help of FFL to transport two members to a landing zone above and near the subject. Other members responded to the staging area at the top of Berthoud Pass.  Using a rope system one rescuer was able to reach the subject and attach them to our system. The subject and rescuer then climbed back up the slope and away from potential avalanche danger. Flight For Life refueled and stood by at the top of Berthoud Pass in case further assistance was needed. Another GCSAR and MMRT team snowshoed in below the subject and first team to act as backup. The subject and rescuers were able to ski back to the parking lot after ascending the dangerous cliff section.

column20: Skier 1 triggered a small avalanche at 9750 feet on a northwest aspect on a 39-degree slope (SS-ASu-R2-D1.5-O). Skier 1 was traveling with his partner and dog and was very familiar with the area including around a dozen visits to that area earlier in the season but he had never skied on that particular slope before. He knew of the avalanche danger and attempted to trigger an avalanche at the top of the slope. After not triggering an avalanche on his first few turns he committed to skiing the slope and after a few more turns he triggered an avalanche and was swept off his feet. The avalanche debris accumulated in a terrain trap and buried Skier 1 about chest deep. He dug himself out of the avalanche debris and joined his partner and dog below the slope where they were waiting for him.   Skier 1 initially expected to trigger an avalanche but he thought the slope was safe after he did not trigger an avalanche at the top after his first few turns. Persistent Slabs are a complex problem that is difficult to assess predict and manage. Skier 1 stated ""The avalanche did what I expected it to do just not where I expected it."" The best way to avoid being caught in a Persistent Slab avalanche is to have large margins for error when you are traveling near steep slopes on aspects where the Persistent Slab avalanche problem is known to exist. Luckily in this case everyone in the party was uninjured and Skier 1 only lost one ski pole.

column20: A party of three snowmobilers were riding in the Spring Creek area on Saturday. They did not observe any signs of unstable snow such as shooting cracks or collapsing sounds. The party noticed one small avalanche near a cornice that was a few days old. No other recent avalanches were observed. One rider was riding up a lower angle depression and wound up riding further right on to a steeper slope. The rider said ""he got over confident"" in the avalanche conditions. The rider was sidehilling when the avalanche broke above him. He tried to accelerate and out run the avalanche but he could not. He jumped off of his sled and was carried in the avalanche. He successfully deployed his avalanche airbag pack. The rider came to rest buried with just his head and one shoulder exposed. The other members of his party did not know where he was. He was able to free his arm and shoulder and dig himself out. The rider was uninjured and the party of three returned to the trailhead.

column20: The plan was to ski the South facing aspect down to the valley floor.  Obvious wind loading on the more SE-E facing terrain so the plan was to stay away from those slopes.  Skier #1 dropped in and stuck to the south facing terrain for the first 2/3 of the ski line and stopped just above the apron of the slope.  Snow was slightly wind effected but minimal slab present.  Skier #2 dropped and skied along the tracks of skier #1 and made several turns past skier #1 before stopping.  Skier #1 started skiing again and made their first turn slightly into the SE side of the line and immediately triggered the slide.  The avalanche propagated below above and adjacent to skier #1.  Skier #2 skied off to the south side of the slope and out of the avalanche's path. The avalanche took out the majority of the SE-E side of the ski line.  Crown averaged around 18"" deep and ran on basal facets.  The majority of the season's snow avalanched on the SE-E side of the ski line.  Skier #1 was carried by the avalanche just above the apron of the ski line and was partially buried approximately 30 yards uphill from the toe of the debris.  Skier #1 was able to self extricate and was not injured.    This is an example of how dangerous connected terrain is right now.  The south facing terrain we were skiing and ascending during the morning was a night and day difference from the adjacent SE facing slopes which were heavily wind loaded with a very reactive slab.  We let our guard down at the bottom of the ski line and skied slightly into the SE facing terrain which resulted in the avalanche.

Starting at 0800 we ascended a mining road out of the town of Ophir traveling from Waterfall Canyon to Swamp Canyon. We began to break trail above a mining road on a west aspect at approximately 10800'. The snowpack was touchy and very communicative: We heard many rumbling collapses and observed shooting cracks. We were sure to travel only on and beneath low angle slopes and spaced out to avoid exposure to micro terrain features that appeared wind loaded. We had anticipated after observing previous cracking collapsing and wind loading that the steeper north slopes off the ridge would be easy to trigger and kept our distance accordingly. We remote triggered the avalanche from about 10' away atop very low angle terrain on the ridgeline. No other parties were observed in the area.

column21: Approached wind-loaded ridge to see how much of the crown had filled in from the 11/29 avalanche. The crown and debris were completely covered. While skinning up the ridge near treeline the the hard slab on the steep rollover triggered and failed uphill into less than 30 degree terrain. The fracture propagated up the ridge approximately 600m to a steep wind-loaded slope which ran through the bench at the bottom. The hard slab that occurred on the rollover had limited slope to run and stopped on a bench 20m down. Closer to treeline debris ran into small trees. The average crown size was 1m. Though the main part of the avalanche only ran a short distance the upper portion ran the majority of the track. The bed surface was a mix of old snow and ground.

column20: Skier triggered a couple of small slides. The first was while descending small but steep terrain. The 2nd was while bouncing for a collapse resulting in a remotely triggered avalanche from about 25 feet away.

Vis was poor on the sled ride up but we had one window which I noticed a disturbance in the snow BTL on a NE aspect. I assumed it was debris from a long-running slide path off the uphill ridge. Without binoculars too hard to tell. On our ascent we (obviously) felt heard and saw many signs of an incredibly unstable snowpack. Again “touchy” is the word. Once on the ridge above a suspect slope which is barely 30 degrees one of my ski partners very easily kicked off a small slide which gouged to ground and funneled into the trees. Although not a large avalanche due to slope angle and terrain feature it would have been a scary ride. On the ascent for our the second lap we triggered another storm slab from about 100? vertical below. Slab moved about 1? at the apex and fractured most of the adjacent terrain (to ground) but low slope angle and small area meant that it didn’t quite have enough energy to fully rip.

This was a soft slab avalanche unintentionally triggered by a backcountry skier. It was small in size relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to bury injure or kill a person. The avalanche released at the ground (SS-ASu-R1-D2-G). The avalanche broke about 60 feet across the slope ran 1200 vertical feet and started on a 42-degree north-facing couloir above the treeline.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

This avalanche occurred before the Colorado Avalanche Information Center (CAIC) was issuing daily avalanche forecasts for the 2022-23 season. The CAIC updated the Statewide Avalanche information on October 27 2022. The Statewide read:

We received our first significant snowfall of the season between late Saturday and Thursday morning. Storm totals range from 6 to 14 inches in the San Juan Mountains 12 to 24+ inches over much of the Central Mountains and 5 to 12 inches across the Northern Mountains though portions of the Flat Top Mountains did even better than that. 

We now have over a foot of settled snow on the ground in many locations. This is enough snow to drift and obscure the ground cover. This means we need to start taking the threat from avalanches seriously. Once snow piles up or drifts deep enough to obscure the ground cover avalanches are possible. This doesn't take much on grassy slopes or steep rock slabs. 

It's very early season. The only slopes with enough coverage to slide on will also be the most dangerous. Look for and avoid steep slopes with stiffer wind-drifted snow. Even a ride in a small avalanche can end your season early or worse as you're likely to get dragged through rocks and other shallowly buried obstacles.

Nearly every fall avalanches catch eager riders and late-season hikers off-guard. Hunters traveling through the high country should exercise caution on steep snow-covered terrain. Please consider the threat of avalanches if you visit steep slopes in the high country. Below we describe some considerations for early-season fall avalanche concerns.

We will update the Statewide Avalanche Conditions as necessary. On November 1 2022 we will resume our daily weather forecasts. Our backcountry avalanche forecasts will begin in mid-November.

The avalanche occurred above treeline on the north face of Mount Meeker in a couloir and climbing route called Dreamweaver. It was a wet-loose avalanche triggered by rock fall. It was medium-sized relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to break trees or destroy a car. It gouged into old snow and talus (WL-NR-R3D3-O). At 8:26 AM the climbers heard a sound like thunder cracking above them and to their right. They saw an “RV sized” rock falling from the “top… middle” of the Flying Buttress. The immense rock broke as it fell. The large mass of rock triggered a wet-loose avalanche when it hit the snow-filled couloir. It left a crater about 50 feet wide. The large volume of rocks in the avalanche debris left deep ruts in the bed surface. The avalanche ran 800 vertical feet through the couloir and onto the talus fan below. There was little snow cover on the talus fan prior to the avalanche. Investigators measured the debris field as 112 feet wide and 450 linear feet from top to toe. They measured debris up to five feet deep. A large percentage of the avalanche debris contained dirt and rocks ranging from gravel to car-sized boulders.

First skier intentionally cut the top of the slope triggering a windslab beneath the cornice about 50 feet wide. Skier was able to get off the slab after about 3 seconds by skiing to a predetermined safe zone to the right away from the gut. He was not caught. That slab stepped down 3-4 feet to a deeper weak layer roughly 200 vertical feet below our entry. The gut of the chute ran fully from there but still was isolated to the gut. When it neared the bottom about 1000 feet below us the entire left side of the chute released - roughly 850 feet above where the debris from the first slide was at the time. Once that sympathetic slab had reached the flat bottom but was still moving we watched the much larger basin to our left rip wall to wall to ground starting at least 1000 feet above where the other debris was churning at the time. It sent a very large avalanche racing down the bowl. We estimated the crown to be as deep as 10 feet in places. Most of it appeared to be 4-8 feet deep. The debris pile from that avalanche overran much of the debris pile from the original chute. We estimated the distance from the first wind slab to the northern edge of the third sympathetic avalanche to be almost a half mile wide.   We very much underestimated the potential for deep slab avalanches today. We also underestimated the wind slab's potential to step down into deeper layers though we talked about it at length. Of note: After our first run while skinning back up we observed two small soft slab avalanches from either yesterday or the day before that ran about 800 feet but only entrained surface snow. Both released from a similar spot in the bowl that ultimately fractured 8-10 feet deep today (the skier's right side of the basin that you see in the photo of the fracture line). Also of note: there was no direct visible propagation connection between the chute and the bigger basin that slid last. They are separated by a rocky ridge for almost the length of the chute.   Our biggest takeaway was that this snowpack is nowhere near stable in a lot more places than one might expect. The chute that released had been exposed to sun for weeks; it was not a super high sheltered northerly slope. In fact it is probably in the sun from 8am to 5pm every day right now when the sun is out.

This was loose snow slough we intentionally triggered with a ski cut. Though this bowl feature is mainly North and Northwest facing there is a small and narrow piece of terrain near the top that faces more Northeast. We ski cut this terrain suspecting more wind-loading than the other aspects and a slough about 3-5 inches deep released. It entrained most of the storm snow in the chute below and this snow ran through the top half of the bowl feature. This was storm snow running on the prior dusty-crusty surface and did not propagate or otherwise trigger anything else. However it was still enough loose snow to knock someone off their feet in tight terrain. R1-D1 in our opinion but feel free to adjust that judgment as you see fit.

Triggered a sluff on a steep rollover (around 11000ft) that knocked me over and carried me 400ft down the slope. Only the new snow (20-25cm) slid on a very firm (and dirty) crust. D1 in size but entrained a decent amount of snow with the toe of the debris 100cm at the deepest; 40-50 feet wide at the widest point. Relatively slow moving but it feels quite fast when you are in it. Bumped into a couple of small trees but fortunately just some bruises on my right leg. Deployed my airbag (almost didn’t bring it) midway down and came to a rest on top of the debris. Feeling thankful to be (mostly) unharmed and processing the poor decisions that led up to the slide. After not seeing much movement in the uppermost turns (on more northerly aspect) let down my guard when entering the more easterly (and steeper) terrain. I could have anticipated the firmer bed surface and continued managing for sluff by skiing across the terrain. The more easterly snow while still dry and soft was a bit heavier than what we had initially encountered at the top of the ridge. Luckily it was just a good lesson learned and a pole and a ski lost today. I will carry the lesson with me and I will find the gear when the snow melts.

This was a soft slab avalanche unintentionally triggered by a backcountry skier. It broke on a layer of faceted snow buried 24 to 40 inches below the snow surface. It was medium in size relative to the path and produced enough destructive force to bury injure or kill a person (SS-ASu-R3-D2-O). The avalanche broke 70 feet across ran 300 vertical feet and released on a 43 degree north-facing slope below treeline.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) forecast for the Aspen zone on the day of the avalanche rated the avalanche danger as MODERATE (Level 2 of 5) in all three elevation bands. The forecast listed Persistent Slab avalanches as the primary problem on northwest through north to east-facing aspects at all elevations with a likelihood of Possible and a size Large to Very Large (up to D3). The forecast listed Wind Slab avalanches as the secondary problem on northeast to east through south-facing slopes near and above the treeline at Possible and Small (D1) and Loose Wet avalanches as the final problem on east to south through west-facing slopes at all elevation bands at Possible and Small (D1). The summary statement read:

You can trigger a dangerous avalanche on northerly and east-facing slopes. They can break surprisingly wide and be very destructive. You could trigger them from a distance away.

Winds have drifted recent snow near and above treeline. In some spots the drifted snow is sitting on a strong snowpack and avalanches will be confined to the fresh drifts. Other spots the drifted snow overlaps the issues on the buried weak layer. 

You will be able to trigger small avalanches as the snow surface becomes wet and soggy. This could happen rapidly with today's sun and warming temperatures. They will be easier to start and get bigger through the day.

The easiest solution to avoid avalanches is to give yourself a wide margin around northerly and easterly-facing slopes steeper than about 35 degrees. Avoid steep slopes with freshly drifted snow or more than about six inches of damp snow. You can reduce your chances of being caught in an avalanche by traveling on low-angle slopes with no steep slopes above.

column20: We started skiing down around 1:30pm on March 24 from the top of the north facing bowl directly south of the Markley Hut. The slope we were on was approximately 35 degrees with mostly dense trees with some narrow avalanche paths separating the trees. Our goal was to stay in the relatively dense trees but as we skied down we had to cross two avi paths. We crossed these carefully one at a time. After crossing the second avi path we reconvened in the trees about 25 feet away from the open avi path. Two of our party skied a few turns further and stopped as the last in our party was about to ski she heard a crack and saw the slope break a few feet above her. We suspect it quickly shot up into the avi path forming a crown 100 feet higher than our location. The crown was about 2-3 feet tall. The skier that triggered the slide was caught but was able to hold on to a tree about 20 feet below where she was standing and was uninjured. The avalanche moved past her mainly in the avi path and ended with a short run-out at the bottom. No other skiers were caught.

The avalanches were triggered from an east-southeast-facing slope around 11600 feet and propagated to 12400 feet in elevation and over 1000 feet wide. We traveled out to Mount Owen to inspect an avalanche that was reported to run at 11am off the east ridge of Mount Owen. We noted three other fresh human-triggered avalanches on east-facing slopes although the Mt. Ownen avalanche was the largest. Investigating the Mt. Owen slide it appeared that a group of sled-access snowboarders likely triggered this avalanche remotely from low angled terrain around 600 feet away. The avalanche broke in the February facet layer. The slab ranged from around 50cm to 110cm thick (estimated as we did not measure across the entire crown face). The slab thickness and overall snowpack depth were shallower than other nearby slopes. Previous avalanche activity on this slope removed some portion of the mid-pack. This avalanche was large in size (D2) and could have easily buried a person.
Late in the afternoon an avalanche was reported to hit Kebler Pass Road. This was a Wet Slab avalanche. It appeared to be remotely-triggered by a snowbike based on a nearby snowbike track. Visible cracks connected between the snowbike track and the flank of the avalanche. The avalanche covered a little more than half the width of the groomed road. This too was a repeat-performer avalanche having run on December 24. This avalanche released in the February facets below the prominent dust strip. About an hour after the slide occurred we found the dryspell facets were still wet from meltwater although the bed surface and snow surface were now shaded and refrozen.
En route to the Mt. Owen slide we observed two fresh snowboarder triggered slabs in the recent storm snow also on east-facing terrain near treeline. Both small avalanches broke just below the crust formed on Wednesday only a few inches thick.
