column20: A skier-triggered avalanche occurred on a SE facing roughly 32 degree corniced developed slope at 11049ft; at approx. 1334 MST. Slope was attached to a large steep gully overhead. The lower gully wall feature propagated and released when skier made first turn near concave slope. The avalanche consisted of a hard packed slab with a 6-15 inch crown. It ran for roughly 60 feet in width and 25 feet in length. The slab likely failed on the weak foundation from the near-surface crust. The propagation occurred within the small terrain feature but did not extend uphill into the SE facing gully. Skier was not caught and was able to ski out of debris path and self rescue from avalanche terrain.   A second avalanche occurred directly after the skier-triggered avalanche. It was considered a remote-triggered avalanche. This slide occurred directly after the skier-triggered avalanche on a SE facing roughly 30 degree wind-loaded slope at 11040ft. Remote-triggered avalanche occurred in a small gully wall directly adjacent to the skier-triggered avalanche likely from the groups weight and cautious movement above slope when exiting area. The avalanche propagated along a similar path/route as the skier-triggered avalanche and the crown varied between 3-10 inches in height. This avalanche ran roughly 40 feet in width and 20 feet in length. Both avalanches shared similar releases with minimal energy needed to produce failures in the near-surface snowpack layers.

The skiers that triggered it said they would submit an obs and they grabbed some hopefully better pictures during a break in the weather.   We skied the south gully east of pt 12414 at around 9:30. I had remembered the line seeming quite mellow in the past and it felt mellow this time. I wouldn't have thought anything of it if the other party hadn't had their slide. It goes through a 3 or 4 turns of low-mid 30s terrain. Anyhow  6 of us skied it without incident. We then skied around closer to no name for a few hours. As the weather closed in we headed back to hippie trees around 12:30 and a partner noted the slide(s) that had covered our earlier tracks from the side. We ended up catching up with the party that triggered it the next lap.   A direct report from them might be clearer  but this is my interpretation. They seemed pretty green to backcountry skiing  so I prompted them a bit on some of the terminology to try and understand. They said they skied near our tracks (a few meters here could make a difference...) down to a safe zone (no one was caught) . The triggering skiers partner said the slide broke 40' or so above the skier  propagating across the initial SE face. Probably r2 d1.5 from the looks of it. That slide sympathetically triggered another r1d1 adjacent.  Finally that triggered a larger r3 d2.5 ish slide that went into the terrain trap gully below. Elevation is 12k. We exited the zone adjacent to the slide  but it was too socked in go a great view.   I've noted the slide on the attached map. To me  this slide is indicative of pretty darn touchy conditions. Certainly has me reevaluating our day...

Avalanches: Unintentionally triggered a small wind slab at the entrance to the exit slope of purple palace which propagated and entrained most of the season’s snowpack running with energy through small trees about 300 vertical feet to the creek. Didn’t get an exact read on the depth of the debris pile but may be close to 6 feet. I believe I caught the bottom edge of the slab the crown is maybe 15 feet above my entrance track. I saw the slab breaking around me and immediately skied traversing to the right to exit the slide. Extreme moment of complacency not identifying the obviously windloaded pocket and high consequence of the relatively small avalanche problem due to the terrain trap. Low danger rating minimal feedback earlier in the tour and being so close to the end of the tour added to the recipe for complacency. In retrospect the entrance was obviously windloaded and should have been quickly identified as a hazard.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The summary in the backcountry avalanche forecast for the Vail and Summit County zone on December 20 2020 read:

Strong westerly winds continue to transport snow to easterly-facing slopes. Steep wind-drifted terrain below ridges or the sides of cross-loaded gullies are the most likely places to trigger an avalanche. Look for clear warning signs of unstable snow like shooting cracks and audible collapses. Wind-drifted snow will often appear smooth or rounded and feel denser than the snow in protected terrain. With growing slabs and weak snow below any avalanche you trigger may break wider and deeper than you would expect.

In deeper snowpack areas you may also be able to trigger an avalanche below treeline on buried weak layers. The recent storm snow is gaining cohesion and is becoming more reactive on steeper slopes. Sticking to slopes less than around 30 degrees will greatly reduce your chances of getting caught in an avalanche.

Two people were reported missing on Saturday evening after planning to ski in an area north of Silverton locally known as the Battleship. In the dark from a helicopter search and rescue members could see a large avalanche and ski tracks on the north side of the Battleship (point 12442'). The skiers are still missing and search and rescue operations continue this morning.

On December 18 2020 a snowmobiler triggered a soft slab avalanche on a steep slope that frequently slides.  The rider was caught and did not survive.  It was triggered around 4 pm near the bottom of a steep east facing slope.  There are very few trees at this location.  The limbs of the few small trees that do exist at this site had been stripped from those trees by previous avalanche activity.  

Self-rescue efforts were conducted near the end of the day.  Those involved did not provide information regarding the size of the avalanche the depth of the avalanche crown or the extent of the avalanche flanks.  An organized rescue occurred that evening.  Avalanche forecasters from the Bridger-Teton National Forest Avalanche Center (BTAC) visited the site on December 20 with search and rescue personnel who had conducted the organized rescue.  On December 20 the visibility was limited and wind drifted snow had buried the crown and flanks of the avalanche.  Search and Rescue volunteers were able to delineate the extent and boundaries of the avalanche debris even through it was partially buried.  Excavations in the debris where the partially buried rider and his sled were found were still visible.  

Based on the extent of the debris the topography of the terrain and the structure of the snowpack it is believed that this soft slab avalanche was small relative to the size of the path and destructive enough to injure bury or kill a person.  It failed on a persistent weak layer (SS-AMu-R2-D2-O).  The slab is believed to have been about two feet deep.  The debris from the slide did not run very far past a slope transition at the base of the slide path.  Avalanche debris appeared to be 3 to 5 feet deep.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The BTAC avalanche danger scale rating for the Southwest Trails/Greys River Area was Moderate (Level 2) at all elevations on December 18.  The avalanche advisory listed Persistent Slabs as the day’s avalanche problem on all aspects between an elevation of 7500 to 10500 feet and on west through north to east aspects between an elevation of 6000 feet and 7500 feet.  The likelihood of triggering a small to large avalanche was possible. The general avalanche advisory read:

Yesterday’s storm brought 5 to 10 inches of new snow to the Greys River area. Up to two feet of snow has fallen since December 11. Persistent weak layers exist at the interface beneath this new snow and old snow surfaces that formed during a long dry period. On avalanche prone slopes the weight of a single person could trigger a slab avalanche on this interface. At the higher elevations these slabs could be large enough to seriously injure or fully bury a person. This persistent weak layer was especially active yesterday between an elevation of 7300 and 7800 feet. The slides that occurred in this elevation zone were smaller than what you might trigger up higher where new snow depths are greater. This type of hazard is best managed by terrain assessment skills and conservative terrain choices. Evaluate steep slopes carefully and anticipate the potential consequences of triggering a slab avalanche of any size above terrain traps or on slopes with low snow hazards that can cause serious trauma.

The persistent slab avalanche problem description read:

At the higher elevations large slab avalanches formed by southwest to west winds could be human triggered on steep avalanche prone slopes. These slabs could be two to three feet deep. Slab avalanches triggered below an elevation of 7500 feet are likely to be a foot deep.

The avalanche was small relative to the avalanche path and large enough to bury injure or kill a person. The avalanche broke on a layer of faceted snow capped by a thin layer of surface hoar (SS-ARu-R2D2-O). The avalanche released broadly about 300 feet across the full width of this small avalanche path. The extent of propagation for such a soft slab hints at the very weak nature of the weak snow below the slab. The slab broke around 14 to 16 inches deep and was relatively soft (4-Finger on the hand-harness scale). As the avalanche ran it scoured most of the weak snow down to a buried sun crust that became the bed surface. Debris piled up to three feet deep. The avalanche occurred on a very steep (42 to 49 degree) northeast facing slope below treeline.

column20: Skier triggered an avalanche in a very small localized gully atop a convexity adjacent to a small group of trees. The trigger point was the most thin area of the crown of the avalanche.   Our group's travels were masked by complacency as we traversed low angle slopes on the return to the car after having noted major instabilities at higher elevations. The terrain immediately preceding the had such a gentle slope angle and a significant enough amount of snow that it was not possible to maintain one's momentum across it. We neglected to note and actively avoid steeper slopes particularly areas of locally increased slope angles in small contours of the drainage.   We took a moment to regroup next to the small grouping of trees  and plan our path towards the approach route in the trees farther to our left. We did not think much of the consequences of the shorter but maybe 15 degree steeper slope below us that we would traverse across briefly; as my partner began to edge across the slope it released and he was carried in a small avalanche that propagated roughly 100 feet wide and ran approximately 200'.  My partner was carried and briefly submerged in the moving snow before coming to rest atop the snowpack 100 or so feet above the toe of the slide. The event took place in a small contour to the drainage that became a terrain trap and could have potentially resulted in an unnervingly deep burial.   This slide was a sharp reminder of the potential consequences of any backcountry terrain even in the relatively benign areas that we traverse on approaches to and exits from the main ski runs. We noted that we were in the place at the particular time as a result of having to conceded to the avalanche danger the possibility of skiing anymore that day. The decision to bail and cross very low angle terrain (up until the avalanche's path) in some ways made us un-perceptive to the hazards posed by the smaller undulations in the terrain that was below us. This served as a good reminder to ensure that my companion rescue skills are practiced and efficient and to carefully assess all terrain that we pass through throughout the season.

Widespread natural cycle yesterday and last night: extensive soft slab naturals that broke 1 to 2 feet deep on the storm interface (12/10 facet layer). Slides ranged from small to large (D1 to D2.5); most propagated across much or all of their start zones and ran to mid track. I estimate that 90% of the north or east facing paths or features in Happy Chutes Climax Chutes and Schuylkill Ridge ran (roughly 60 slides) as well as the west facing near treeline terrain below Baldy and Gothic (about 5 slides). Last night’s winds obscured the evidence of avalanche activity in the alpine. There were some fresh crowns triggered by wind transport last night (about 5) but more commonly evidence of activity during the storm was subtle and harder to characterize. The most notable was the east face of Mineral Point which ran to valley bottom.  In contrast the southerly aspects that we could see showed minimal signs of avalanche activity. Today we or other parties near us appeared to remotely trigger a handful of soft slabs up to 2? thick. These were on small pockets or features so generally harmless in size.

Natural avalanche activity spiked mid-day during a period of heavy snowfall. Soft slabs of new snow failing on the very weak faceted old snow. Many D1’s near treeline and a few D1’s below treeline. About five D2’s and one D2.5 near treeline. For the most part these were very soft slabs that just slumped into the weak facets below started moving then stopped 50 to 100ft downhill. Others initiated the same way but continued to gain momentum and entrain the full snowpack.  Not all these slabs propagated widely but there were some standouts. Runaway Ski propagated across most of its start zone and continued all the way across Thanksgiving. Runaway Ski mostly just slumped and was D1.5 in size. While Thanksgiving ran nearly wall to wall and hit the bench. Even the skiers left shoulder in Runaway pulled 90% of that terrain feature.  Yogy’s had a soft slab propagate across 80% of its start zone. The skier’s right side mostly slummed and continued to run about 1/2 way to the bench as a D1.5. While the skier’s left side quickly entrained the full snowpack and was estimated to be D2 in size I couldn’t see how far the skier’s left side ran given poor vis.  The crown lines on these avalanches were already getting hard to see from a distance given their soft slumpy character and the 15-30cm crowns were filling back in.

column20: 3 Skiers 1 dog.  Left Winter trailhead below Kite lake around 0845. CAIC avalanche forecast discussed amongst the skiers for the day at the trailhead and during the hike with an objective to ski the SW chute of Mt. Democrat. Hiking boots required till around 12300' where skiers transitioned to skis and skins along with beacon check. Was able to skin over a very thin snowpack to lake Emma (12630'). Skiers transitioned to boot packing at the lake. First snow observations were made at this point and discussion amongst the group regarding best approach to get above the knoll above Lake Emma. Followed previous bootpack from 12/5/2020 up right side of chute making several quick pit observations and measurements of slope angle. Skier # 1 dropped at exactly 1230 while skier #2 and 3 remained on the ridge. Skier #1 made several slow turns at the entrance of the chute due to thin snowpack. Around 13550' skier #1 was able to link a few consecutive turns when wind slab triggered sweeping skier #1 off of their feet and losing left ski. Skier #1 yelled ""Avalanche"" and was also able to use radio device to skiers #2&3 during the slide. The dog was ahead of skier #1 and was within the slide initially but able to exit the debris at the bottom of the chute unassisted/uninjured. Skier #1 was carried approximately 100-150' and remained on the surface and was not buried and no injury. Skier #1 stopped approximately 2/3 down the chute and left ski was carried to bottom of debris. Radio Communication was made between all skiers and were able to to ski/hike out.

This was a wet loose-snow avalanche unintentionally triggered by a climber while glissading down a snowfield. It was small relative to the avalanche path and large enough to bury or injure a person. The avalanche entrained 12 to 24 inches of wet snow including old snow (WL-AFu-R1-D2-O). The wet avalanche was about 40 feet at the widest point and ran over 1000 vertical feet. 

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

A Special Avalanche Advisory was in effect for the Northern Central and Southern Mountains of Colorado from 4 PM May 1 until 8 PM May 3. 

The regional backcountry avalanche forecast for the Southern Mountains issued on the afternoon of May 1 rated the avalanche danger on May 2 as Considerable (Level 3). The Highlights section read:

Dangerous wet avalanche conditions continue through the weekend. The potential to trigger a large Loose Wet or Wet Slab avalanche increases as the day heats up. Wet snow problems are not isolated anymore to sunny slopes and we’re seeing an increase in size and distribution of wet avalanches on all aspects and elevations. Avalanches that start near the top of the snowpack can gouge deeply into the snowpack and entrain a lot of heavy wet debris. Smaller avalanches are triggering deep and long-running wet slabs in some instances taking out the entire snowpack depth. 

Plan to start very early and be out of avalanche terrain before supportable crusts break down. Choose your terrain to avoid traveling across or below any slopes steeper than about 35 degrees with wet cohesionless snow. Signs that the conditions are deteriorating include a slushy snow surface a punchy snowpack that no longer supports your weight pinwheels and rollerballs and wet avalanches running from steep rocky terrain.

The avalanche began as a wet-loose avalanche triggered by a backcountry skier. The wet-loose avalanche was only a few inches deep and spread to 150 feet wide at the widest point. It was small relative to the avalanche path and large enough to bury or injure a person (WL-AS-R1-D2-O). The skier triggered the slide on a northeast-facing slope about 42 degrees in steepness with scattered trees.

The wet-loose avalanche ran over a cliff band and triggered a wet-slab avalanche on the slope below. This avalanche broke down to the ground. This slope had avalanched in early March so the depth of the snowpack was much shallower than in surrounding areas (two to four feet deep). The wet-slab avalanche was 190 feet wide at the widest point and ran 500 vertical feet. It was small relative to the avalanche path and large enough to bury or injure a person (WS-AS-R1-D2-G). The slab ran on a densely treed slope about 45 degrees in steepness. The bulk of the slab was composed of clustered rounded snow grains. Meltwater only recently percolated below a melt-freeze crust to reach the rounded grains.

Skiers climbed a NNE facing couloir that topped out around 13700’ located east of Pacific Peak in the Tenmile Range. Other slide paths nearby were looking heavily loaded and skiers chose to climb a couloir with less obvious loading. Skiers climbed the majority of the couloir with axes and crampons identifying and avoiding wind loads on the ascent. Skier 1 attempted to ski cut above the start zone of the couloir with no results. Skier 1 proceeded to ski cut lower in the start zone this second cut produced a D1.5 soft slab avalanche that broke under his feet about 1’ thick and propagated ~15’ in front of him. After a short discussion with skier 2 skier 1 then proceeded to ski cut the rest of the start zone. Shortly after skier 1 cut onto the hangfire that had not released with the second ski cut cracks propagated across the rest of the start zone and a few feet above skier 1. The rest of the slope slid with crown depths up to 3’. This second avalanche broke deeper in the snowpack and propagated through the layer that had after as the bedding surface for the first avalanche. Skier 1 was caught. Skier 2 remained above the start zone and prepared for rescue. Thankfully skier 1 was able to stay on his feet and stop by digging the edges of his skis into the bedding surface after being carried ~100’ downslope. No injuries occurred.

I spotted four skiier-triggered avalanches between 11800' and 12200' on NNE aspects. All avalanches ran between 11am and 2pm on Friday 4/24 and appeared to only break at the interface between the new storm snow and the underlying crust. Overnight wind drifting appears to have played a role as the snow had a rippled pillowy texture and all slides broke on the lee-side of prominent terrain features. All slides also fractured in thinner areas adjacent to rocks.  While three of the four avalanches were small enough as to not pose much threat to backcountry travelers one avalanche caught and carried a skier for approx. 300.' My partner ski cut the upper entrance to the slope and stopped below the large rock skier's right visible in the photos. This portion of the slope is approximately 36 degrees and commonly rocky. There were no obvious signs of instability and up to 8"" of new snow. I ski cut the upper slope as well and stopped adjacent to the large rock. We then decided that I would ski down the rest of the slope initially a slope angle 35 degrees or less decreasing to 30 degrees or less until there was an obvious stopping point approximately 600' below on 25 degree or less terrain. We would then send the other skiers in our party one at a time down to me. As soon as I started skiing the snow was deeper than up top approximately 12-18"". After three turns I noticed cracking on both sides of me and a slab approximately 150' accross released and my partner yelled avalanche. I turned slightly to my right since I knew the slope angle was less then since I was staying on my feet decided to ski straighter down hill to try and ski out of the slab. Fortunately I was able to ski out of the slab which ran approximately 300'. Our entire party had avalanche safety equipment and I was wearing an avalanche airbag packpack. Since I was able to stay on my feet and quickly skied out of the avalanche I did not deploy it. In hindsight I should have.  We were able to communicate and decided that I should ski down the lesser steep terrain away from the bowl above then skin up the standard route up an E aspect slope and back to the ridge that connects with Bald Mountain. The rest of our party skied the ridge down to eventually meet me.  We've skied this slope dozens of times withought mishap and felt as though it's a reasonable choice during a moderate hazard due to the slope angle terrain shape and configuration and moderate length of the run. Neither my partner nor I have seen this slope slide in over 15 years of actively skiing here. Upon reflection today we were caught off guard by the absence of any activity when we ski cut the top portion the amount of new snow and the obvious week layer reported in CAIC Forecast for the Northern Mountains. Since the top of the slope is steep enough to slide it did under these tender conditions.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) regional backcountry avalanche forecast for the Central Mountains on Friday April 17 (issued the afternoon of April 16) rated the avalanche danger as Considerable (level 3 of 5). The CAIC forecast read:

A spring storm has created dangerous avalanche conditions which will linger through Friday. The danger is greatest in areas which picked up more than about 8"" of new snow. Strong southwest to west winds have built fresh easy-to-trigger slabs on north through east to southeast-facing slopes near and above treeline. The drifted snow rests on slippery old-snow surfaces. A slab avalanche may break wide or wrap around terrain features. Choose terrain cautiously and avoid steep wind-loaded slopes. Wednesday a skier was killed in an avalanche in a north-facing alpine couloir in the Gore Range.

As the sun comes out on Friday sun-exposed slopes at lower elevations may see a ""shed cycle"" of small loose avalanches. This concern will increase as snow surfaces wet throughout the day.

This was a hard slab avalanche unintentionally triggered by a backcountry snowmobiler. The avalanche was small relative to the path but large enough to bury injure or kill a person. The slide broke on a layer of faceted snow about 6 inches (13cm) above the ground (HS-AMu-R2D2-G). This was a persistent slab avalanche. 

The avalanche released near treeline on a sparsely-treed north northwest-facing slope around 35 degrees in steepness. The slide ran around 700 vertical feet down a sparsely treed slope and to the open gully below. Avalanche debris piled approximately 5 to 8 feet at the deepest places. 

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) backcountry avalanche forecast for the Sawatch zone on April 8 rated the avalanche danger as Moderate (level 2 of 5) at all elevations. Loose Wet avalanches were listed as the primary avalanche problem type highlighted on all aspects and elevations except above treeline on northeast and east-facing slopes. The likelihood of triggering was possible and the potential size was small to large. The CAIC summary for the Sawatch zone read:

“You will find a variety of avalanche issues related to wet loose snow today. Like shave ice snow cones and Slurpees wet loose avalanches are about the snow texture and amount of water. Different texture many flavors possible but the same ingredients. Avalanches will become more likely and easier to trigger as the day warms and sunshine pounds on slopes. Wind and clouds will slow the warming. Reassess the snowpack frequently throughout the day or as you change slopes. The boot test is a great indication of dangerous snow. Stand on the snow surface in your boots. Avoid steep slopes and seek shadier terrain before the snowpack fails either of the tests.

Standing in ankle-deep snow is an indication you can trigger wet loose avalanches in the surface snow. They usually start on slopes steeper than about 35 degrees. They can be surprisingly powerful and even small sluffs can take you for a nasty ride into trees rocks or gullies. You will find this shallow wet snow at higher elevations and on shadier slopes.

If you punch through to the ground when you stand on the snow wet avalanches could become large. They may gouge deeply in the snow or to the ground and entrain a destructively large amount of snow. You can find the unconsolidated snow on shady low elevation slopes or on sunny southerly facing slopes near and below treeline. This could be a particular issue in the afternoon or on your return to the trailhead.”

The avalanche occurred on a steep southeast facing slope at the head of Austin Canyon.This area is remote high alpine terrain comprised of numerous glacial cirques that are situated among some of the highest peaks in the Snake River Range.  It is complex avalanche terrain whose access requires expert riding skills.  

A saddle in a ridge at the top of the slope is the divide between Austin Canyon and Dry Canyon which was the group’s intended route back to the trailhead.  The slope to the right of the route up was sparsely treed.  Cornices were present along the ridge line above the more open area that the rider was attempting to ascend.  The avalanche released below that cornice.  The summit of Peak 9630 is about 400 feet west and 230 feet above the crown of the avalanche.  This summit is surrounded by steep cirque walls in Austin Dry and Waterfall Canyons.  The slope where the slide occurred is wind loaded by southwest to westerly winds.  

This wind slab avalanche is classified as SS-ASu-D2-O. It released at an elevation of 9400 feet and ran approximately 1700 feet to an ending elevation of about 8800 feet.  The crown was reported to have been 18 to 24 inches deep.  The slope was open and concave.  The rider was completely buried in the run-out zone of the avalanche. He was found 30 to 50 feet uphill of his sled which was partially buried.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) backcountry avalanche forecast for the North San Juan zone on March 31 rated the avalanche danger as Moderate (level 2 of 5) at all elevations. Persistent Slab avalanches were listed as the primary avalanche problem type and highlighted on west northwest north northeast and east aspects. The likelihood of triggering was possible and the potential size was large to very large. Loose Wet avalanches were listed as the secondary avalanche problem type and highlighted on east southeast south southwest and west aspects. The likelihood of triggering was likely and the potential size was small to large. The CAIC summary for the North San Juan Zone read:

When the sun hits the fresh low-density snow we’ll see a round of loose-wet slides on slopes steeper than 35 degrees. They’ll start first on east-facing slopes then move south around the compass. By late in the day warmer temps could help west facing slopes produce larger slides. New snow rests on crusts in some places providing a slick sliding surface and slides may travel farther than normal.

Weak layers buried two to three feet deep on northwest through northeast to east-facing slopes have also been stressed by the additional load keeping heightened concerns on the north side of the compass. These slides may be stubborn but if you manage to find the “not so sweet” spot avalanches could break two to three feet deep leading to a dangerous ride. Avoid likely trigger spots like thinner areas on the margins of the slab and near shallow exposed rocks. Practice safe protocol and only expose one person at a time and get well out of the way at the bottom of each run. Cornices have also been given a new load so be diligent about staying well away from the edge as these things have a nasty tendency to break farther back than you expect. Safer riding can be found on lower-angle slopes out of the sun not connected to steeper terrain.

This was a hard slab avalanche triggered by a snowboarder. The avalanche was medium-sized relative to the path and large enough to bury and destroy a car damage a truck destroy a wood frame house or break a few trees. The avalanche was triggered by a snowboarder riding through wind-drifted snow on a steep cross-loaded terrain feature. The initial avalanche was relatively small. As it ran down the slope it stepped down to deeper weak layers and eventually gouged down to the ground. (HS-AR-R3D3-O).The avalanche damaged a remote avalanche control unit used to manage the hazard to the Loop Road and covered over 400 feet of the roadway with debris up to 20 feet deep. The Loop Road is a service road that is open to the public but mostly used by highway maintenance workers. It connects the eastbound and westbound portions of Interstate 70 and runs over the top of the west portal of the Eisenhower Johnson Memorial Tunnels.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Backcountry Avalanche Forecast for the Vail-Summit County zone on March 25 rated the avalanche danger as Moderate (Level 2) at above and near treeline elevations. The forecast listed Wind Slab avalanches as the only problem on north to east to southeast-facing slopes. The likelihood of triggering was possible and potential size small to large. The Vail-Summit County Summary for March 25 read:

You can trigger avalanches that break at the interface between recently drifted slabs and the older harder snow below. You are most likely to find dangerous conditions on higher elevation wind-prone easterly-facing slopes were the prevailing winds thickened these slabs. If you trigger an avalanche at the interface between the recent and old snow it can break 2 feet deep and propagate wider than you might think. Look for recent cornice formation or smooth rounded pillows of snow to identify possibly dangerous areas. You can find safer riding options in wind-sheltered areas and below treeline.

column20:
The avalanche was a soft-slab unintentionally triggered by a backcountry snowboarder. The avalanche was medium relative to path and large enough to bury injure or kill a person. It failed in a layer of depth hoar and gouged to the ground in many places (SS-ARu-R3D2-O). The height of the crown face ranged from 18 to 36 inches. This was a persistent slab avalanche. 

The avalanche released below treeline on a sparsely-treed west-northwest-facing slope around 40 degrees in steepness. The party involved described the avalanche as large moving blocks of snow. The debris ran through a densely treed slope a gully and then over a bench approximately 600 vertical feet below. The debris was over 2 meters deep in places. 

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) backcountry avalanche forecast for the North San Juan zone on March 24 2020 rated the avalanche danger as MODERATE (level 2 of 5) at all elevations. Persistent Slab avalanches were listed as the primary avalanche problem type and highlighted on west northwest north northeast and east aspects. The likelihood of triggering was possible and the potential size was large. The CAIC summary for the North San Juan Zone read: 

Two to four inches of new snowfall yesterday and overnight and moderate west to southwest wind has amounted to a small refresh to the surface without increasing the hazard much.  Triggering an avalanche however on west through north to east-facing slopes remains possible. A layer of weak faceted snow that formed at the surface in Late-February is now buried two to four feet deep at all elevations on these aspects. Many recent rider-triggered slides occurred in the last few days (Obs1 Obs2 Obs3).

The further away from the main loading event last week the more stubborn avalanches have gotten. Obvious signs of instability like cracking and collapsing may not be present until it’s too late but if you manage to find that “not-so-sweet” spot slides will be large enough to bury injure or kill you. Avoid likely trigger spots like smooth rounded pillows below ridges or thinner zones near small rocky outcrops. Minimize exposure by riding one at a time and get well out of the way at the bottom. As is normal this time of year when the sun peeks out between breaks in the clouds watch for another round of small wet avalanches on southerlies. Safer riding can be found on wind sheltered slopes less than 35 degrees out of the sun.

R2/D2 rider triggered slide in the new/old interface at 11500ft on NW aspect 40deg steepness. Crown was 2-3ft broke 150ft wide and ran 800ft. Witnessed from the Around the World Ridgeline. Two riders approached the banker choke from the Around the World Ridgeline through the trees. Rider 1 turned into the NW facing slope to his right releasing the avalanche. Rider 1 was caught and carried 200ft coming to rest on top of the snow after hitting an unknown number of trees.   Rider 2 descended to Rider 1. Rider 2 found Rider 1 conscious sustaining multiple skeletal fractures and chest injuries. Our group (3) established contact with Rider 2 via shouting. Skied down to Banker Bench and met another party of two we skinned up debris to Rider 1 and 2. Communication established with SAR via radio. Pt stabilized vitals obtained splinted with available gear and extricated to the Banker Bench to rendezvous with SAR/Helitrax for evac to hospital.   Both were experienced riders and carrying avalanche equipment. Signs of recent avalanches were apparent on northern aspects in the surrounding area.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Backcountry Avalanche Forecast for the North San Juan zone rated the avalanche danger as Considerable (Level 3) near and above treeline and Moderate (Level 2) below treeline. The forecast listed Storm Slab avalanches as the primary problem on all aspects and elevations all elevations. The likelihood of triggering was Likely and the potential size Small to Large. Persistent Slab avalanches were listed as the second problem on northwest north northeast east and southeast aspects near and above treeline. The likelihood of triggering was Possible and the potential size Large. The summary read:

Dangerous avalanche conditions continue. 15 to 20 inches of new snow over the last 48 hours is a quick shock load to the snowpack and it got pushed near its breaking point. Natural avalanches are still possible today but are becoming less likely now that the main loading period is over. Human-triggered slides remain likely and even where confined to the recent storm snow will most likely be large enough to bury or injure you. South-southwest winds built stiffer slabs at higher elevations and some drifts may exceed several feet thick – expect wind-drifted slabs to be touchier than fresh slabs in wind-sheltered terrain.

The new load also added a lot of weight and stress to weak faceted snow now buried 2 to 4 feet deep. Slides failing in the storm snow have potential to break deeper creating a larger more deadly slide. Stick to slopes less than about 35 degrees and give big open and steeper terrain an extra wide buffer if you have to travel below. Heed the warning signs of surface cracking and deep rumbling collapses indicating unstable snow below your feet. Make conservative terrain choices and avoid avalanche start zones to help reduce your avalanche risk.
No sign of natural avalanches on tour.

column20: On slopes steeper than about 35 degrees it was easy to trigger Storm Slab avalanches underfoot and remotely down-slope and on adjacent features 200-300 feet away. Slabs were slow and pushy generally between 1-2 feet deep but gather a pretty good head of steam given the dense new snow. Given the terrain we were testing most avalanche remained on the large side of D1 but where small slides ran into steeper connected terrain below the slides easily grew to D2's. Where the old snow surface was crusted triggering was easy failing on small facets above the crust. These facets were difficult to isolate on a card and identify given the sticky snow but no question the sunny slopes had facets failing below the storm snow. It was difficult to trigger slabs on steep northeasterly-facing slopes with soft old-snow surfaces but once avalanches initiated on crusted slopes impacted the shady slopes they would break too.

The avalanche occurred in an avalanche path known as ‘First Scary Monster’ a corniced slope entering ‘Canal Street’ on the north side of a prominent sub-ridge in the upper part of the Green Canyon drainage (Figure 1). With a large fetch consisting of a broad open slope to the south and sustained southerly winds in the previous 36 hours deep wind drifts formed on the concave slope on the northern side of the sub-ridge. 

The wind slab avalanche is classified as SS-ASu-D2-O. It released on a north-northwest facing slope at 8070 feet in elevation fractured 1 to 3 feet deep and approximately 180 feet wide and ran approximately 400 vertical feet through a moderately forested slope. The slope angle was 39 to 40 degrees at the crown (Figures 2 and 3). The slope angle gradually decreased below the start zone. The debris averaged 2-4 feet deep but piled up deeper on the uphill side of trees (Figure 5). The victim was buried about 130 vertical feet below the crown on the uphill side of a tree with his arm wrapped around it (Figure 4). The surviving skier was partially buried about 50 feet below and in the same fall line as the victim. According to Pebble Creek Ski Area staff this avalanche was larger than any slide in that avalanche path in many years.

The original objective of Atlantic Peak was shut down once near treeline as the extreme wind gusts had not diminished throughout our tour. We altered our plan to an East facing 25* wind loaded gully. The upper pitch of the line was firm wind pressed snow and once over the roll was pleasant spring powder conditions. We then opted for another line that was South facing and guessed to be slightly steeper than the first line. While skinning up the line The snow began to show signs of warming quickly and we began to witness shooting cracks. There was a talk of whether or not the line was steep enough to slide and once the slope was measured it was realized that the slope was 35* and had a steeper roll at the upper pitch. It was decided That we would not continue up and we would ski down a short pitch that had a clean runout. we did not skin up this line and it was through a narrow chute. The 1st snowboarder dropped in and once below the tightest part of the line noticed the snow around him cracking. Boarder 1 continued to ski to a more mellow slope to his right and was not caught in the slide.

The avalanche occurred as we made what would have been likely one of our last switchbacks before we were going to traverse to the north across scoured slopes.  Both skiers felt the whoompf and the slope begin to move shortly after.  Skier 1 was pulled down into the gulley and skier 2 was pulled through the trees.  Skier 1 was buried up to his waist and skier 2 ended up on top of the snow.   Skier 1 deployed an airbag and removed a ski after not being able to ski out of the avalanche.  Skier 1 rode the avalanche in a vertical sitting and standing position.  Skier 1 lost a ski and a pole.  Skier 2 was on a split board and ended up with his head downhill during the avalanche.  Skier 2 was able to locate all gear.  This was a hard slab avalanche with up to refrigerator sized blocks observed in the debris.

At approximately 10:45 am we watched from the east ridge as another party of two skiers dropped Yellow Mountain’s northernmost summit down the looker’s right above a rocky choke with large cliffs on either side (N/NE aspect from ~12800’). Skier One skied to a safety to the lookers left of the choke less than 100’ down the face. Skier Two began descending and within two turns triggered a large pocket of windslab which then propagated and entrained a fairly large amount of snow. The crown appeared to be 6-10” deep and about 20’ wide but ran the length of the steep terrain about 600’. We attempted to make radio and vocal contact but got no response. We watched as they carefully made their way down to the basin and skied our without further consequence. Neither skier was caught or carried by the avalanche.  The party will likely submit a report themselves but I just wanted to make the slide common knowledge for other backcountry users traveling in similar high-consequence terrain. I did not take photos.

column20: As we were nearing the bottom of the apron we were heading towards a gully with a steeper convexity at the entrance that we didn’t like so we went right in to some trees which put us above/on the trigger which wasn’t as obvious from a distance. My partner entered first and I skied down to meet him. It was clear as I got to him that just below us was bad news but with the new snow it was not obvious that we were already in such a thin an touchy spot.  My partner had gone just past the trigger point to a flat spot and when I came through to meet him there it went. He was completely out of harms way and was telling me that he could see me throughout the event. We observed three types of avalanches indicative of the complexity of the snowpack. On our skin up to the summit of outpost we observed a SS avalanche across the valley on a Western aspect. On a shallower snowpack this SS appears to have broken on old and rotten snow.   On outpost peak we observed a relatively deep snowpack at around 2 meters. Hazards still exist as there are definitive windward and leeward slopes where the ladder holds significant wind loaded layers. We observed evidence of a stiff wind slab that was releasing 4-6in slabs.   On our exit we found plenty of evidence of the rapid warming that our snowpack experienced earlier in the week as we dipped under 11k. Sun crusts and point release wet loose slides scoured the landscape on sun exposed aspects. It appears as if most of these wet-loose events happened on thursday or friday.

This was our first settle of the day and we had not witnessed any other avalanches. Small trees were broken in the slide.

Two snowmobilers unintentionally triggered three avalanches. The first and the one that caught the snowmobiler was medium-sized relative to the avalanche path and produced enough force to injure bury or kill a person. It broke initially on a layer of faceted snow in the middle of the snowpack and then stepped down to the ground (SS-AMu-R2-D2-O/G). The second and third avalanches were triggered sympathetically by the first. The third avalanche was the largest and broke at the ground (SS-AMy-R3-D2-O/G). Neither of the riders were caught in the sympathetic avalanches.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Backcountry Avalanche Forecast for the Sawatch zone rated the avalanche danger as Moderate (Level 2) at all elevations. The forecast listed Persistent Slab avalanches as the primary problem on north through east to south-facing slopes at all elevations. The likelihood of triggering was Possible and the potential size Large to Very Large. The Sawatch Summary on February 11 read:

You can trigger an avalanche that is large enough to bury you today. The most dangerous slopes face east and south where the wind built thick slabs on weaker snow layers and crusts. Observers reported cracking and collapsing in this type of terrain yesterday east of Leadville. Don’t let your guard down on other aspects. Most slopes harbor weak layers in the upper snowpack. Even below-treeline terrain has thinner softer slabs. The avalanches here may be smaller but they can be more easily triggered.

Consider the consequences of even a small avalanche. Slopes above trees rock or gully features are more risky.

Small slab (r1 d1) released between snowmobile tracks 2&3 of a 3 part slope test. Slab was roughly 8” thick with a bottom layer of snow/dirt mix from a wind/snow event on February 3rd. Since that date snow has fallen on 3 different occasions adding up to about 8” in this area. That snow/dirt mix is not binding well with the interface below. Slope is east facing at 10500 feet and measured 42 degrees. What is interesting about this series of tests and result is that cross-cutting the slope showed no signs of instability even with 2 separate tracks trenching into the snowpack up to 6’ deep. The 3rd track was a slow descent from the side and top of the slope down towards the 2 previous tracks cutting with the snowmobile on edge. Once sled was within about 10 feet of cross track small slab broke.

Skier 1 2 and 3 made 2 descents of 12380 from around 12000 feet or appr. 350 feet from the summit.  We started on the N side of the W slope where we measured a slope angle of 27 degrees.  Skiing one at a time after 300-400 feet we stopped where the slope pitched over to have eyes on each other as we skied the last problematic pitch down to the bowl.  Some crusty wind affected snow led us to very soft fun powder.  Everyone agreed it was good but didn't love the last pitch where it was likely just over 30 to 35 degrees.  Our second decent took us a little further S into the face.  Here we found rather large wind slab had formed to make a small head wall above a nice gully down to the basin.  Skier 1 and 2 skied this line in leap frog fashion with an amazing run that was under 30 degrees the entire run.  Skier 3 took a line near the first run down and skied out.  Skier 1 and 2 went back to the hut for lunch and to talk to other partners there about going back out in the afternoon.  Skier 3 left the hut.  Skier 1 2 were joined by 4 and 5 to go back and find more turns like the second run they had experienced.  We all went to the same top out as the first runs but decided to go even further S on what looked like the same type of skiing we had in the morning.  4 and 5 went first going down that same gully which 1 and 2 had skied early.  1 and 2 both went to the next two gullies skiing them without indecent but both coming away with a feeling that it was steeper than the gully.    We had now skied a total of 10 lines on this face and as the sun was getting low skier 1 and 2 decided to take it to the summit and come back down to ski the S most line on the face which appeared to be less steep than their previous run.  4 and 5 would only go back to the same high point as before and decide on a line themselves.  After the summit and taking photos 1 and 2 skied half way down on very low angle decent snow to about the half way point.    Looking down now we saw a slide path almost directly below us.  It was a frantic few moments when we distinctly saw a single skier in the middle of the pile.  We couldn't see if they were partially buried or digging for the other skier.  After a bit of yelling and we realized skier 5 was standing on a small rise near some trees.  Both skiers were accounted for but now we needed to get down. We chose to go even further skiers left (S) and try to come back to the slope from that angle but this proved to be a poor choice.  it was now clearly much steeper and we were going to need to get into the slide path and ski down the old snow. We re-grouped at the toe of the path discussed what happened and made plans to get back to the hut as the sun was setting.  The slide was triggered by skier 5 skiing directly after skier 4 on almost exactly the same line between rocks and trees on a slope of 35-40 degrees at treeline at 5:00 pm just a few moments before sunset.  It is likely 35+ degrees for only 50-100 vertical feet and it quickly drops down to less than 20 degrees.  He was carried by the snow down 200-300 feet ending buried up to mid waist in snow that wasn't too hard as he was able to dig himself out.  It was a large fracture line of 3 to 3.5 feet running between the rocks and the trees approximately 100 feet wide.    It is my guess that the slide was TL W SS AS /u R2 D1  A long day with many good decisions led to being complacent and sloppy at the end of the day.  It was warmer later in the day we were skiing on steeper slopes than we had intended and our guard was down.

This was a hard-slab avalanche unintentionally triggered by a backcountry skier. The avalanche was medium sized relative to the path and large enough to bury injure or kill a person. The avalanche broke on a layer of near-surface faceted crystals sandwiched between hard layers (Pencil on the Hand Hardness Index). The avalanche stepped to the ground in a few places near rocks and in wind-sheltered areas where the snowpack was less than 3 feet deep (HS-ASu-R3D2.5-O). The skier triggered the avalanche toward the bottom of a steep slope about 450 feet below the ridgeline. The avalanche broke above him in the rocks. The crown face was at the top of a heavily wind-loaded convex slope at a cliff band. The crown face was approximately ten feet deep in the heavily wind-drifted area and tapered off to about 4 feet toward the edges. The avalanche broke about 400 feet wide and ran about 540 vertical feet. The debris was composed of hard and soft snow and small to large blocks.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The avalanche danger was Considerable (Level 3) near and above treeline and Moderate (Level 2) below treeline on the day of the accident. Two avalanche problems were listed in the Front Range zone. A Wind Slab avalanche problem was listed as the first problem. They were listed as likely on northeast through east to south-facing slopes near and above treeline. A Persistent Slab avalanche problem was also listed as possible on north through east to southeast-facing slopes. Avalanches were expected to be small to large for both problems. The Backcountry Avalanche Summary for January 24 read:

Today the combination of recently drifted snow and old weak layers makes avalanche conditions dangerous. Give slopes with wind-drifted snow a wide buffer today. You can easily trigger an avalanche in wind-drifted snow. There is potential for the avalanche to break down to deeper weak layers. Avalanches on the older layers will be wider and deeper than you might expect or spread farther across terrain features. The most surprising spots may be near treeline or in open areas below treeline. There you can find ""soft"" feeling layers of drifted snow but it is sitting on a shallow and weak snowpack. 

Strong northwesterly winds formed layers of wind-drifted snow that are now one to three feet thick. On Wednesday a natural avalanche from a wind-drifted south facing slope caught partially buried and injured a skier in Rocky Mountain National Park. Look for sensitive drifts below ridgelines in cross-loaded terrain features like gullies and couloirs and around trees. Cracking in the new snow is an indication of fresh sensitive slab formation. 

On Thursday a skier triggered and was partially buried in an avalanche on a southeast-facing slope in Dry Gulch near Loveland Pass. The avalanche broke down to weak layers near the ground. Photos show layers of soft or gently drifted storm snow on an otherwise shallow and weak snowpack. Observers on other aspects near treeline reported whumping an indication that the recent snow is pushing those old layers closer to the breaking point. You could trigger these old weak layers from the middle or bottom of a slope. Caution route-finding to avoid traveling across or below steep slopes is in order.

There was quite the variety of avalanche activity in the last 24 hours in this area including Loose Dry Loose Wet Wind Slab Storm Slab and even a Glide avalanche. The 20-22 inches of recent storm snow released in widespread and long running sluffs up to D1.5 in size. Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) backcountry avalanche forecast for the Front Range zone on January 22 2020 rated the avalanche danger at Moderate near and above treeline and Low below treeline. Persistent Slab avalanches were listed as the only avalanche problem type highlighted on north northeast east and southeast aspects near and above treeline. The likelihood of triggering was Possible and the potential size was Small to Large. The summary from the backcountry avalanche forecast read:

New snow and strong northwesterly winds are forming small sensitive wind-drifted slabs today on east and south-facing slopes near ridgelines and in cross-loaded terrain features. Any avalanche in the storm snow will be small but it can trigger more dangerous avalanches breaking on weak layers deeper in the snowpack. The most suspect slopes now have fresh wind loading stacking on top of the these weak layers. You are most likely to trigger an avalanche on slopes steeper than around 35 degrees at higher elevations. Recent skier-triggered avalanches near Loveland Pass and near Frisco in the adjacent Vail-Summit zone provide good illustrations of the kind of avalanche you can trigger today. 

Avalanches can break wider and deeper than you might expect so give steep wind-loaded terrain a healthy buffer. In areas where the snowpack is less than about 4 feet deep you can still trigger avalanches that break near the ground. Lower-elevation sheltered slopes offer safer riding options.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) backcountry avalanche forecast for the Front Range zone on January 19 2020 rated the avalanche danger at Moderate near and above treeline and Low below treeline. Persistent Slab avalanches were listed as the only avalanche problem type highlighted on north northeast east and southeast aspects near and above treeline. The likelihood of triggering was Possible and the potential size was Small to Large. The summary from the backcountry avalanche forecast read:

You can trigger avalanches that break 1 to 3 feet deep on a layer of weak crystals below the recently wind-drifted snow. You are most likely to encounter this problem on east and southeast-facing slopes. If you trigger one of these avalanches in a previously wind-drifted area it can be large enough to bury you. These avalanches can break in surprising ways wider than you might expect and above you. In northerly and easterly-facing areas where the snowpack is less than about 4 feet deep you can still trigger avalanches that break at the ground. If you trigger one of these avalanches it will be large and dangerous.

Look for signs of previous wind-loading such as pillows of snow or freshly formed cornices. Use extra caution around previously windloaded east and southeast-facing slopes. Do not ride in steep meadows or on steep rollovers on these aspects without careful investigation. Seek out wind-sheltered areas for safer riding options or stick to lower angle terrain.

Two partners and I were approaching “Enter the Dragon”—a route I have done multiple times—that follows the main weakness up the Dragon’s Tail Spire on the south side of Flattop Mountain above Emerald Lake. We followed a diagonal snow bench towards the first pitch. I was in front and moving quickly across relatively good neve but as the slope steepened I began to punch through the top layer. Before I was able to assess the change properly a large portion of the slope broke above me with a crown of about 18” and I was swept off my feet past my partners and over the edge of the rock band below.  Luckily the trajectory of the fall allowed me to fall cleanly to the snow below. I landed on my right side and the fall which we estimated to be about 50 feet amazingly only resulted in a fractured clavicle. We were able to assess my injury and walk out to the trailhead. This is a good reminder for winter climbers that avalanche danger does not disappear when you take off your skis.

The Baker Creek drainage in central Idaho’s Smoky Mountains is a popular snowmobiling area accessed by riding 10 miles up a frequently groomed road (Fig. 1). The incident took place in a small draw just north of Baker Creek. This draw is often used to access Brodie Gulch and Apollo Creek both minor tributaries to the north of Baker Creek and the sites of avalanche fatalities. Since 2004 there have been five avalanche accidents in the Baker Creek drainage resulting in four fatalities and one serious injury that required a helicopter evacuation. Many of the avalanche paths in this area end in gullies and abrupt transitions or terrain traps increasing the likelihood of burials.  

The persistent slab avalanche was classified as SS-AMu-D2-O. It released on a south-facing slope at 9130 feet fractured 2-3 feet deep and approximately 200 feet wide and ran 650 vertical feet (Fig. 3). The slope angle of the start zone was 33-35 degrees. The slope angle increased below the crown to an estimated 35-37 degrees. The start zone is an open planar grass and sage-covered slope (Fig. 5). There are a few stands of trees along the margins of the track and in the runout zone. The slope becomes confined mid-track as it leads into a shallow gully. The south-facing and open nature of the terrain exposes it to winds blowing from a variety of directions. 

The debris averaged 3-5 feet deep but piled up to around 8 feet deep along a shallow gully near the bottom third of the slope. The victim was buried downhill of the deepest portion of the debris and the terrain trap is considered a contributing factor in this fatality (Fig. 4). The victim’s sled was completely buried and was recovered two days later approximately 20 feet directly downslope of the victim (Fig. 8).

The day after the incident USFS Sawtooth Avalanche Center staff visited the site. A summary of this initial visit can be viewed on YouTube.

The Rock Creek Drainage is located in the Elkhorn Mountains of Oregon. This is a location where advanced snowmobilers do ride but wouldn’t be considered popular. Traveling into the location of the accident you must cross under numerous avalanche paths. The group identified the slope where the accident occured as avalanche terrain and had seen it avalanche in the past.  

The avalanche was a storm slab classified as SS-AMu-D2-O. It occured on an east-facing slope at 7861 feet and ran 200 vertical feet. The crown was 2 feet deep and approximately 100 feet wide. The slope angle of the start zone was  35 degrees. The slope angle decreased below the crown to an estimated 30-34 degrees. The start zone is an open planar grass and sage-covered slope. There are a few stands of trees along the margins of the track and in the runout zone. The east-facing and open nature of the terrain exposes it to winds blowing from a variety of directions.

On January 7th 2020 seven skiers were caught in two back-to-back avalanches at Silver Mountain Resort outside of Kellogg Idaho. Two skiers were partially buried five were fully buried and three were killed. This accident occurred on an open ski run (Figure 1). 

Ski area avalanche accidents are complicated by the potential for multiple burials and many witnesses providing conflicting information.  Our goal in this report is to present the facts surrounding the accident and subsequent rescue. Excellent first hand accounts exist and can be accessed by contacting the National Avalanche Center at nac@avalanche.org. 

The avalanches occurred on '16 to 1' a northeast facing slope on Wardner Peak at ~6000 feet in elevation (Figure 2). We do not know much about the first avalanche because the second avalanche was much larger and overran the initial crown and debris (Figure 3). The second avalanche fractured on a weak layer of surface hoar buried near the ground. The first avalanche caught seven skiers and ran approximately 500 vertical feet. The larger second slide (AS-SS-R3-D3-O) ran ~900 vertical feet and overran the buried and partially buried skiers. The crown of this avalanche was approximately 30 inches deep and 500 feet wide with a slope angle of 35 degrees. The alpha angle was 21 degrees.

The '16 to 1' avalanches were connected  to another avalanche on the Morning Star ski run by cracks between avalanche crowns (Figure 2). We are not sure when the Morning Star avalanche released but the snowpack between these two ski runs did not avalanche. The Morning Star crown was on a 33 degree slope the face of the crown was 18-30 inches deep ~200 feet wide and ran ~250 vertical feet. To our knowledge the Morning Star avalanche did not involve any people. 

The Silver Mountain Ski Patrol conducted avalanche mitigation work with explosives  on the upper portion of Wardner Peak prior to opening '16 to 1' for the day. These efforts did not trigger avalanches on '16 to 1' Morning Star or other ski area terrain on Wardner Peak.  

BC Forecast

On the day of the accident backcountry avalanche danger was HIGH and the Idaho Panhandle Avalanche Center (IPAC) issued an Avalanche Warning for the surrounding area. Backcountry avalanche warnings and forecasts do not cover operating ski areas but because '16 to 1' had been previously closed to skiing for the season the forecast does provide a general sense of the day's conditions.

On the afternoon of December 31 2019 a group of four splitboarders accessed the Black Face area from the parking lot off of Lizard Head Pass. All riders were fully equipped with the necessary avalanche gear the plan was to have a mellow tour up to the Black Face and ski a line. The tour accessed the Black Face ridge line via the more gentle western approach up the ridge. Snow in the trees and open appeared affected by melt/freeze crusts sun and wind as the party gained elevation. Once on the ridge line the party traversed slightly to the east to find a more gentle slope with less of a convex rolling feature trees and safety zones to stop at while the riders descended.  On the traverse rider 1 weighted the slopes and noticed wind affected snow on the ridge on the traverse no signs of wumping or cracking were noticed the snowpack appeared scoured on the ridge line and thin. All four riders transitioned to downhill mode rider 1 ski cut the wind affected top slope of the ridge and noticed no instabilities and stopped at a safe zone. Rider 2 descended through the top wind affected slope and stopped at another safe zone below rider 1. Rider 1 then ski cut again across the slope to access better snow and skied 200-300 feet down to the trees and a relatively safe zone rider 2 skied down to rider 1 where they radioed to rider 3 to start descending. Rider 3 rode through the second ski cut that rider 1 put in and then yelled avalanche down to riders 1 and 2. Riders 1 and 2 both made verbal statements of an incoming avalanche and quickly decided to grab on to the trees in front of them and hold on and maintain eye contact with each other in case of a ride or burial. Rider 3 broke the avalanche at the crown and stopped immediately as it began propagating and running down the slope. Riders 1 and 2 were directly in the middle of the slide path and both were buried rider 1 was buried above his waist and rider 2 was buried to his neck both riders maintained verbal and eye contact and immediately after the slide stopped were able to dig themselves out and radio to riders 3 and 4 to assess the situation. At this point all riders were in contact accounted for no longer buried and agreed to have riders 3 and 4 ski the slide debris and regroup. All riders were uninjured and skied the slide debris out to the skin track to travel to the parking area. No other parties were observed in the area as it was late afternoon during the descent.  The avalanche was a dense wind slap that broke on the rolling slope of the ridge line the crown was approximately 2-4 feet deep average 3 foot the slide was approximately 75 feet wide and ran almost the length of the entire slope (500+ feet). The wind slab failed on weak layers at the surface and the avalanche broke all the way to the ground.

We came upon this recent skier triggered avalanche at about 3pm. It was on a NW aspect at 11600 feet. From the ridgeline we could see one track going into the slide near the apex of the crown. No tracks exited the slide back to the ridgeline and we could not see any other evidence in the chute below. After much deliberation amongst our group we decided not to search further. There was about 4 to 6 inches of new snow on the bed surface and the entrance track. We estimated it was triggered very early in the morning and a rescue effort more than seven hours later would not be worth the risk to our group. There was still more snow on the flanks of this slide that didn't slide and other steep suspect slopes to navigate once in the drainage. We truly hope this incident ended with a good outcome.

This short afternoon tour revealed plenty of recent avalanche carnage in the Slate River. These avalanches likely failed some time on 12/14. It is certainly possible that some avalanches ran on mid-pack persistent week layers but more investigation is necessary to make that determination. Avalanche size was mostly in the D2 range. Some smaller and some slightly larger.  Lots of interesting pocket avalanches and crown lines along Climax and Schuylkill Ridge that would be interesting to see why those crown lines failed the way they did. column20: Approaching the summit from the W we were skinning on an approximate 10-15 degree windslap intermixed with large talus. We heard a large wumpf and felt a collapse and continued to the summit. Below the typical cornice near the summit facing E we noticed sections of it had fallen and triggered an avalanche on the E facing slope. We were not able to look over the cornice until we dropped S off the summit and looked to the N as indicated in the photos. The crown was approximately 200' wide and the avalanche started on a 35 degree slope likely running 600' based on the legnth of the slope from personal experience and looking at CalTopo. The steepest part of the slope is up to 45 degrees. It appeared to be a size 3-4 and slid mostly to the depth of the talus field. This slide may have also triggered another slope approximately 600 to the S of this one in the bowl below the summit.  I've been skiing Craig Pk for over 10 years regularly and never triggered a remote avalanche like this one on the E facing slopes. We skied W facing slopes under 30 degrees down to Fulford Cave without mishap.

We skinned up the low angle terrain to the edge of treeline several hundred feet below the summit. The summit area is where the terrain becomes more connected and we both agreed that it was not a good idea to summit based on known avalanche problems. We transitioned and skied one lap down the low angle terrain approximately 800FT through the trees and saw no signs of instability. We transitioned and we went up for a second lap following the same skin track. At the top of the skin track around 11250 very close to our original transition point we felt a large collapse and saw a shooting crack go towards the east face. At that time a remotely triggered avalanche began on the east face and a large crown began to form across the entire east face beyond where we could see. A large avalanche ran the entire length of the east face. From our viewpoint we could not see how long the crown was. Both skiers transitioned at that point and skied down the low angle run to our second transition point. From there we found a good spot to get a better look on what slid. Based on our viewpoint the entire east face was remotely triggered and it ran down to the creek below. We could not see the end of the crown. There are other slide paths beyond on the east face that may have slid as well but we did not confirm this.  Based on what we could see our best guess was that the crown was approximately 3FT tall and was around 1500 feet long based on our measurements afterwards but we could not see the end of it. The slide also partially triggered a connected east facing bowl lower down known as ""Tea Cup Bowl.""  It appeared to break on the well known facet layer that exists on east faces across the zone but that is just an observation from our viewpoint as no analysis was done to confirm this. We skied back our intended route following the skin track on the low angle terrain back to the car. To the best of our knowledgeable there were no other skiers in the area and no one was on or below the slide path.

Small blocks composed the avalanche debris.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) backcountry avalanche forecast for the Gunnison zone on December 2 2019 rated the avalanche danger at Considerable near and above treeline and Moderate below treeline. Persistent Slab avalanches were listed as the only avalanche problem type highlighted on north northeast and east aspects near and above treeline. The likelihood of triggering was Likely and the potential size was small to large. The summary from the backcountry avalanche forecast:

Dangerous avalanche conditions exist. You can trigger large dangerous avalanches on north through northeast to east-facing slopes near and above treeline. Pay close attention to steep slopes in the near treeline elevation band especially if the slope ends in a terrain trap such as rocks or trees. Strong winds on Saturday deposited a lot of new snow in lower elevation areas. These areas were relatively safe before recent storms. Look for and avoid all areas where you see evidence of previous wind drifting such as smooth or hard pillows of snow. Steer clear of steep slopes below ridgelines if you see evidence of fresh cornices. You can trigger avalanches from below slopes or from a distance so give north through northeast to east-facing slopes a wide berth.

You can find safer riding options on slopes with a slope angle less than about 30 degrees with no steep terrain above you and in below treeline areas.

Snowshoers triggered and were caught in an avalanche on a north-facing slope above treeline. It was a soft slab avalanche medium sized relative to the avalanche path and large enough to bury injure or kill a person. It broke on old snow near the ground (SS-AIu-R3D2-O). The avalanche broke about three feet deep about 300 feet wide and ran about 300 vertical feet. The avalanche started in areas of wind-drifted snow on a north-facing slope. The starting zone averaged 38 degrees in steepness. A second avalanche triggered sympathetically to the first. The sympathetic avalanche was to the east closer to the weather station. It was a soft slab avalanche small sized relative to the avalanche path and large enough to bury injure or kill a person. It broke on old snow near the ground (SS-AIy-R2D2-O).

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) backcountry avalanche forecast for the North San Juan zone on November 30 2019 rated the avalanche danger at Considerable (Level 3) at all elevations. An Avalanche Warning had expired at 6:00 AM on November 30. Two avalanche problem types were listed. First were Persistent Slab avalanches highlighted on north northeast and east aspects near and above treeline. The likelihood of triggering was Likely and expected size was small to large. Storm Slab avalanches were the second problem type highlighted on all aspects and elevations. Triggering was Likely and expected size small to large. The summary from the backcountry avalanche forecast:

The howling Thanksgiving storm added a significant new load to our fragile early season snowpack and it will be easy to trigger dangerous avalanches on steep slopes today. Avalanches will be larger on north and east-facing slopes at higher elevations that received the most wind-drifted snow from sustained southwesterly winds. These are the same slopes with the weakest snow near the ground. Avalanches breaking in the new storm snow can break into these deeper weak layers and produce avalanches big enough to bury you.  

Shooting cracks or sounds of the snowpack collapsing are clear signs of unstable snow. You can trigger avalanches from a distance or from below so pay attention to locally connected steeper slopes even if you're travelling in low-angled terrain. Slopes less than 30 degrees with steeper terrain overhead offer safer riding options.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

The Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) backcountry avalanche forecast for the Vail and Summit County zone on November 28 2019 rated the avalanche danger at Moderate (Level 2) at above treeline and near treeline elevations and a Low (Level 1) danger below treeline. Persistent Slab avalanches were listed as the first problem. It was highlighted on north through east aspects near and above treeline. The likelihood of triggering was Possible and the potential size was small. 

 

Summary from the backcountry avalanche forecast on November 28 for the Vail and Summit County zone:

The avalanche danger remains elevated today ahead of another round of snow arriving tomorrow. Most lower elevation slopes where softer new snow overrides weaker snow from October are generally safe. The missing ingredient on these slopes is a stiffer slab of snow needed to produce an avalanche. On higher elevation slopes where the winds have drifted recent new snow into thicker slabs your chances of triggering an avalanche are higher. The most dangerous slopes are near and above treeline and face north and easterly. Use caution in steep areas below ridgelines and in steep gullies where recent winds may have built slabs over weak granular snow near the ground. If you trigger an avalanche in one of these areas it will most likely be small but could take you for a rough dangerous ride.

None of us could hear the other shouting even though we weren't very far apart so we needed to be in actual visual contact.

My partner and I climbed the route together to the top of the ridge leading to the summit. We navigated to the top of the ridge through the left flank of the cornice. From there I decided to descend into a wind-protected spot next to a rock just below where we separated. I utilized that vantage point on the northeast aspect to take pictures of my partner descending from the summit to skier's right of the cornices where others had previously dropped before him. After his descent my partner stopped further down the face and had eyes on me as I dropped down. I had intended to follow the fall line heading skier's left away from the cornices to manage any possible slabs. I slowly cut across the face a few times to see how the snow reacted before initiating my descent. On my second turn I had hit a pocket of firm snow which released and on my third turn my tail washed out to skier's right so I ended up in switch mode for a few seconds before recovering. As soon as I recovered I got swept from underneath by the slide. I attempted to move my board but it was locked into the heavy moving snow so I kept my hands free and after about 15 seconds the slide came to a stop and I was able to get up and ride out without injury.   A few things to note: the forecast discussion on Friday afternoon did not note any wind slab concerns. These concerns were added to Saturday afternoon's discussion. Above treeline the temperatures seemed very cold for the forecast and the wind was much stronger than forecasted. It was 24 degrees at the Ruby Gulch trailhead at 11 am (barely changed in 4 hours). The main takeaways from today's free lesson were to put much more consideration into the current weather observations and how they may lead to wind slab formation throughout the day.

We triggered a D1 windslab at the top of the east-northeast-facing gully just south of the summit of Coon Hill at approximately 12600 feet.  It ran approximately 500 vertical feet. One person was caught and taken for a ride for about 40 feet. One dog was caught and taken for a ride for about 100 feet.  There were no injuries or burials; we're not even sure the dog noticed.  Events leading up to the avalanche:  As a group of three we left the trailhead at about 7:30 am. We discussed our avalanche concerns for the morning tour which were primarily windslab. Once in the basin we made a plan to ski from the summit of Coon Hill. We ascended the ridge to the summit noting that the snowpack was mostly hardpack and unconcerning.  At the summit we planned to traverse under the cornice to the gully. We discussed that a small windslab might exist but that it was not large enough to be ""concerning."" We made a plan to ski cut the gully and ski one at a time.  Skier 1 traversed under the cornice and ski cut the gully without triggering anything. He stopped on the ridge just south of the gully in a safer zone.  Skier 2 traversed under the cornice and skied the gully without incident. Dog 1 entered and stopped partway down the gully confused whether she should follow Skier 1 or 2.  Skier 3 (a snowboarder) traversed under the cornice; Dog 1 started to run uphill towards Skier 3. At the top of the gully directly under the cornice Skier 3 triggered a small wind slab under his feet. He arrested on the bed surface as the slab slid by him. The slide was not large or fast-moving enough for him to feel the need to trigger his airbag. Dog 1 was caught by the slide and took a ride for approximately 100 feet before exiting the slide. The slide continued another ~500 feet toward the bottom of the gully. Skier 3 exited the debris and skied down the bed surface to confirm that Dog 1 and Skier 2 were ok.  The crown appeared to be 6-8 inches but slide debris contained hard windslab up to 24 inches thick. There was no cornice failure.
