Myself and 1 partner (splitboarder) switched over to crampons in a safe zone from both wind and the slop itself below a large rock face. From the start of the boot pack it was clear that the snow was deep but no weak layers were evident including wind slab. The new snow appeared to be well bonded and had come in entirely right side up. Once we got above 13000 feet and toward the top of the couloir we noticed a small slab but it seemed very well bonded and showed no signs of propagation when breaking through this. Towards the top out this wind slab became thicker but again manageable due to its structure or so we thought (heuristic in hindsight). A small but notable convexity right before the top-out was noted which would be key later. We transitioned and set up for the descent. I was dropping first. Upon gaining speed and making the first turn I noted the wind slab was a bit thicker where I was riding than where we had booted. As I turned by the small convexity the wind slab broke flowing skier's left and propagating a bit towards the skier's left eastern aspect of the apron below the sheltered choke. I was able to turn hard skier's right and drive my hands in the consolidated snow in the bed surface arresting myself and getting out of the slide path. I would say I was caught for 20-30 feet before exiting the slide (a GoPro video that I will submit later may be helpful here). The avalanche ran to the bottom of the couloir through the apron. The small debris pile and the wind slab portion that slid seemed to be isolated only to where we noted it upon inspection of the flanks. If we had booted up the climber's right more eastern-facing aspect I think we would have noted this as more of a weak layer much quicker and turned around. I would classify the avalanche as an R1-2 D1.5. If I had been taken by it I would have gotten taken over a few rocks but would not have been buried.  Heuristics certainly played a big part here. Both my partner and I consider ourselves conservative backcountry snowboarders with advanced snow science knowledge safe practices constant discussion continuing observations etc. We have safely navigated isolated pockets of wind slab before in isothermic spring snowpacks and managed them safely. We deemed what we found on the climb up ""safe"" due to its structure and noted resistance to propagation when punching through although it was still a wind slab. The classic ""I've been in these conditions before and we managed them safely"" was at play here. It only took one turn to find the shallow weak spot that propagated to a thicker slab to the skier's left to create a wind slab avalanche. Luckily I was able to exit it quickly. The spatial variability of the slab's thickness was also a factor as we were climbing in the thinner part on climber's left but the thicker and more dangerous part was to our climber's right and out of observation on the way up. This was a good wake-up up and will keep our heads on more of a swivel in the future. Upon reading the avalanche forecast again for 4/30/19 we deemed it spot on and exactly what we encountered. Great reporting and a user error on our end.

column20: After skiing a high alpine northwest aspect and climbing a southeast Skiers 1 and 2 transitioned around 13250 feet to ski a similar northwest aspect on the way to a third line. Skier one started the descent and Skier 2 was watching until Skier 1 reached the flats.  Skier 1 made approximately 4 turns center of the depression and slightly skiers left. Skier 1 felt the snow give and looked over their right shoulder to see a 6-inch crown 15 feet above terminating in the scree skiers right about 25 feet away. The small size of the crown viewed did not prompt a strong mental response or an urgent reaction. Skier 1 tried to traverse into the scree field and was swept off their feet. Behind Skier 1 and to the left the crown was up to 12 inches deep and approximately 500 feet wide. Skier 1 lost the right (uphill) ski and was entrenched in the avalanche sliding ""baseball style"" on their right hip. Skier 1 fought to stay on top and tried unsuccessfully to release the downhill ski. Mid-slope Skier 1 went airborne over a steep rock band and landed in the same position. Skier 1 came to rest on top of the debris in the flats approximately 600 feet downslope. Skier 2 immediately started following Skier 1 on the bed surface of the avalanche. Skier 1 was able to signal OK when Skier 2 reached the rock band.  Skier 1 was lucky to suffer what appears to be a bruised knee and was able to collect all of their gear and ski out.  The skiers had begun before the CAIC report was released but did check CAIC-compiled weather reports noting high winds and moderate snow in the area. These in addition to high winds while out and snow available for transport were not properly accounted for given the terrain. Previous ski line on similar aspect had given a false sense of stability even though snow was obviously dense there too where exposed.

column20: We went and checked out a large Wet Slab avalanche that was previously reported on Wednesday April 25. As reported the avalanche released on a southwest-facing slope above treeline at 12400 feet. The avalanche was triggered remotely as the skier descended supportable refrozen surface snow. The avalanche released about 50 feet below the skier. The crown of the avalanche was about 150 feet wide and 2 feet deep. Although this was confirmed to be a Wet Slab avalanche the avalanche released in a similar fashion to some of our March avalanches entraining the entire snowpack and knocking over trees in the run out. The size of the avalanche was quite impressive for one with a crown of only 2 feet.---Although the skier was skiing on a supportable snow surface when he triggered the avalanche the entire snowpack was wet and saturated down to large depth hoar at the ground. As we bootpacked through soggy snow down to the avalanche we initiated more collapses. We talked about how we too could have been easily fooled by the supportable snow surface and how it is important to step out of your skis or off of your snowmobile to truly feel if the snowpack is wet beneath superficial melt-freeze crusts.

Our first cut into a north-facing couloir at approximately 13200' popped a small isolated wind pocket averaging 8"" deep and 200' wide (full width of the path).  This pocket stepped down another 4-6"" and ran to the valley floor.  The aforementioned pocket took a member of our party for a 50' ride where he self-arrested as the avalanche flushed around him.  It could be classified HS-R1-D1-ASc.  The avalanche gathered more snow as it flushed and would have certainly been D2 by mid path however this was not entirely visible to the party.

I skied into a safe zone in the rocks and the slab broke down to ground approximately 100' below me and ran down to 11200' taking out about 10 trees mid path. Size R3D3 possibly bigger wet slab

Our group of 2 triggered a lot of sluffing/ rollerballs as we skied the top 500 feet 1 at a time. The slope is north facing around 12000' at the top low 40s slope angle. We were both pulled off to a safe spot and watched as a slow wet loose pile slid on down entraining the new snow (~3 inches worth) as it went. It left a nice firm bed surface to continue our descent the rest of which went without incident. The underlying snow appeared to be solid with no wetness on the surface underneath. As we got lower to the exit below 10000' the snow got very wet. We carefully picked our way down and out of the exit.   In retrospect we started too late for the temperatures today and mistakenly assumed that north aspects would ski colder even that late in the day.  Another group of 2 in silver around the same time reported a similar avalanche and similar conditions.   The slide wasn't big but if you weren't paying attention it could have easily taken you for a ride.

One very small loose-wet as I descended from Royal Mountain summit to the gully entrance at around 10:45-11am.  There appeared to have been an earlier (much bigger) slide in recent days and I skied a mix of the bed surface and - when coverage was lacking - the trees at skier's right most of the way down without incident.  At 9.6K' I saw the choke and was concerned I couldn't manage any loose-wet consequence here so headed toward the trees.  I felt a collapse although nothing slid out from under me or otherwise appeared to slide (at least in the direction I was facing).  I continued to move slowly and cautiously toward the side and my route took me under the edge of a rock outcrop.  As I was under it the snow under my feet slid cohesively but I was able to keep from being pulled down with it.  The seemingly small contained slab (thought it was possible it was simply rotten snow on top of unseen rock) slid through some brush and over some rocks.   I took some observations/pictures of what I thought was maybe a small isolated 1' slab (and accidentally dropped a glove that joined the avy debris down below) and finished my exit to the side and bushwhacked down about 100' through the trees to retrieve my glove.  In taking a few more pictures from below where I retrieved my glove I realized that it's possible that the slab propagated behind me quite a bit further across the full choke point (maybe 20').  Either that or it slid prior to me skiing the gully and I somehow missed the crown on the left as I descended...don't think so though given the picture as I'm not sure how I could have missed seeing that up to 2' crown spanning the full choke point.  It's also possible that the first collapse I felt was that slide occurring and because I was facing away from it and focused on getting to the side of the gully I completely missed it.  Again doubt I could have missed that but given the direction I was facing maybe?  Regardless of when it happened that crown looks to be about 2' at it's deepest from the picture.  In hindsight despite the solid refreeze skiing something late-morning with such a steep tight rock-sided choke at a relatively low elevation was unwise given the quick warming today. column20: An avalanche was triggered by the first rider on the third lap. The avalanche (most likely a wind slab) was triggered (around 1 pm) at the top of a roll where the slope transitioned from <30 degrees to a roughly 32 degree slope on an east facing aspect. The crown of the slide was roughly 6 inches thick. The triggered slide moved the rider about 40 feet down with no partial burial. The toe of the slide ended roughly around 80 feet from the crown. (Figure 1 includes a picture with one of the riders for scale.) The rider who triggered the slide noticed the icy layer beneath the new snow. As the two riders started exiting the area they noticed several other slides in the same area. It is not clear if those slides were natural or triggered by other riders (Figure 3).

**This appears to have been already reported as a natural slide (https://avalanche.state.co.us/caic/obs/obs_report.php?obs_id=56346). The two crowns are actually a single skier-triggered release.**  The chute entry began as very hard packed snow and turned to very soft new snow upon entering the couloir. The crown broke ~10 feet above me almost immediately on entering the couloir burying me before I could shout out a warning. My left ski released but I was able to get an edge on my right ski get above the surface and ride out the last 1/3 of the couloir. I lost a pole but was able to retrieve the released ski and ski out.   My experience sounds startlingly similar to this report on the same day. (https://avalanche.state.co.us/caic/obs/obs_report.php?obs_id=56335) I agree with their closing statement.  ""It was hard to distinguish [between] nervousness about the ski route and a dispassionate analysis of conditions. We thought we were overcoming the fear of the line and suboptimal weather when in reality we were placing ourselves in danger of a wind slab. Additionally most of the couloir did appear sheltered from the wind as anticipated and had great stable snow. But it was the top 50 feet of the route that counted today and that's where the slab had developed.""

Group of 2 frequent partners.  The day started great with a sunny and somewhat windy skin through the valley. We had discussed potential issues mainly wind slab and the technical nature of the route. We were in this area last year around May so we knew exactly how we wanted to do the approach what we wanted to descend and a few plan B's.  We discussed and observed wind at the ridge throughout the approach. Lots of snow transport; we were guessing 30+ W winds. However we also believed the couloir we were aiming for would be mostly sheltered from this wind. We saw what appeared to be some sloughing in the couloir and considered this positive because the touchy layers had been naturally shedding (note: we were either wrong on this point or the sloughing hadn't helped enough).  The skies started darkening as we booted up to the saddle. We discussed visibility issues and how they would affect skiing. The forecast hadn't called for storming until later in the day so we assumed it was simply pockets of clouds. The saddle to the summit had sustained winds. When we got to the couloir the visibility was flipping between mediocre and poor. Winds were still relatively sustained and there was some blowing snow at our entrance. At first look it seemed like this wasn't the day for the route.  Because we were a bit nervous about the route in general we thought we should put our skis on before deciding whether to drop. For us a steep route is easier to gauge when actually on skis.  Our main concerns were a) wind b) low vis and c) a steep exposed entrance. We briefly mentioned stability/wind slab but dismissed this as a manageable risk.  The wind died down momentarily and I decided to start side-slippering into the couloir. At first the snow was hard pack / chalky and a good surface for a steep ski. About 15 feet in some soft snow started to show up at the surface. I started moving slowly. Saw a small shooting crack and had a plate about 5x5 feet and 4 inches deep released down the slope directly in front of me. I was pretty nervous at this point but going back up didn't seem to be an option. It felt too exposed of a location to do anything but continue. I tried to kick in front of me a bit to get some more to slide away but couldn't get much else to go. I decided to point it for the center of the couloir and get moving quick - in case something went wrong I did not want to be above the rocks/cliffs. I was hoping that if something did release it would be at my feet. I was wrong. As I started into the couloir a slab broke above me and I started accelerating down the couloir with a bunch of snow. This point of the couloir is easily high 40s might hit 50 degrees.  I yelled ""avalanche"" and then was concentrating on keeping my feet downhill. Neither of my skis released as I had my toes locked out. I had an axe in my hand and briefly attempted a self-arrest before realizing it was fruitless. I was in a river of snow. Next I tried some swimming motions and was luckily staying on top. The snow was still moving fast but had at least stopped accelerating. I was eventually able to dig my downhill edge into what I think was the bed surface and shoot off to the side of the slide.  In the end the wind slab had carried me about 500 feet downhill and I got lucky. I managed to avoid the rocks and the top of the couloir and didn't slam into the side walls.  I radioed to my partner that I was ok and we were both relieved. Having radios was a huge benefit this day. My partner asked if he should ski the couloir or find another route. I left it up to him but said that the bulk of the slab was probably gone. He dropped into the couloir and kicked off another small slab but wasn't caught. We met back up and made the exit which was slow because I had lost both my poles.  We made some mistakes this day and plan to regroup for a post-mortem in the coming days. There were a lot of human factors that came into play in this avalanche. In retrospect it's very easy for us to say that we should have gone to a plan B and that there were more than enough signs that we shouldn't have skied the line in those conditions. But in the moment it was not so obvious. It was hard to distinguish nervousness about the ski route and a dispassionate analysis of conditions. We thought we were overcoming the fear of the line and suboptimal weather when in reality we were placing ourselves in danger of a wind slab.  Additionally most of the couloir did appear sheltered from the wind as anticipated and had great stable snow. But it was the top 50 feet of the route that counted today and that's where the slab had developed.

The Mount Washington Observatory webcam on top of Wildcat aimed at the Cutler River Drainage showed that the avalanche occurred between 1200 and 1205.

We triggered two avalanches.  Slide #1 As we approached the summit of Peak 1 we discussed our options to get to the ridge safely and bypass a large cornice. Our options were to move to the N and gain the ridge by traversing the N face or to head to the S and skin/boot pack between two large cornice features. We chose to head S and skin to the open area between the two cornices. The slide was triggered by skier 1 after one switchback. It caught Skier 1 and moved him downhill. The slide also pushed Skier 2 onto his stomach head downhill and buried most of his body up to his waist. Skier 3 was able to grab Skier 2 by the arm as he slid by and bury his body into the bed surface and not move. The debris settled at the knee height of skier 3. This avalanche was skier triggered moved downhill apx. 35-50' and propagated out of sight of all members of the party.   After avalanche #1 we decided to boot pack the bed surface and get to the summit ridge to have a look into our objective. The winds on the summit at this point were sustained 30mph with gusts of 40+mph. It was a fairly miserable experience.  We moved down our N facing line on hard wind-scoured snow in hopes the wind would die down and the snow would get better as we descended the terrain.

The first was to the lookers right. HS was thin and about 80cm. Basal depth hoar was massive and estimated at 5mm. An ice lens capped these facets and they were also moist. The next quick crown profile was closer at about 20 ft to the looker right of where the track exited. Here HS was 180cm. The crown was 90cm. The basal facets where smaller also moist and again an ice lens capped these facets. The avalanche appeared to have failed at this ice lens or at the interface with the basal facets. Shortly after getting to that location water started running like a faucet out of the new/old snow interface and I quickly packed up and left. Slope angles were estimated to be near 40 degrees where the snowmobile track left the crown. Crown hight averaged an estimated 70cm. The crown appeared to propagate into a deeper snowpack area.

column20: The first rider dropped into the couloir with an avalung deployed but not in his mouth. He made it safely through the upper hard pack section where the couloir is steepest and most narrow. Then the snowboarder and made 2-3 turns in soft snow before the wind slab broke and began to slide. The snowboarder who was caught shouted ""SLIDE"" twice. All party members on top heard this and one skier was positioned directly above the mouth of the couloir and maintained a line of sight to the snowboarder in the avalanche as much as possible. The observing skiers only lost site of the snowboarder when he was underneath sliding snow. The snowboarder was caught and carried approximately 250-300 feet down the couloir before managing to self arrest and escaping on the skiers left side of the couloir. The rest of the snow ran straight down to the valley floor. The snowboarder quickly signaled up to group members that he was okay. He moved farther down the couloir and behind a cliff to a safe zone. Then the other three group members made careful turns down the slide path and reunited in a safe zone.   We estimated the crown of the avalanche to be 18-24 inches thick and 50-70 feet wide at the top. Staunch walls ran down the sides for at least 100 feet if not more.  In debriefing the incident we identified several major factors that contributed to the avalanche. The first was underestimating both wind and temperature. Though we had attempted to gather accurate wind data for representative slopes in RMNP on Friday and Saturday nights we were unable to find specific data for the Bear Lake weather station site. We used nearby sites as a reference which led to us vastly underestimating the amount of wind that the slope had experienced. We also underestimated how much the temperature would rise during the day. Though our party discussed warming and one group member even expressed concern at the base of the couloir and suggested the possibility of turning around other party members dismisses concerns of warming and we gained false confidence as we climbed the couloir and clouds came out.  We also identified the upper bowl as the most likely area for a wind slab or cornice to form and we neglected to properly assess stability in the main/middle part of the chute. We were not concerned with this area though this was the part of the chute that had indeed built up a heavy soft slab.  We also discussed heuristic traps. Three group members met up with a 4th solo skier in the couloir. Though we were concerned about the decision making of someone climbing this couloir alone we appeared knowledgable and reasonable in his assessment of the snow. He expressed confidence in the snowpack and even mentioned that he had spoken with some local Estes Park guides that were friends of his and they had told him they thought the elevator shaft couloir was safe and had been skied several days before. We all buoyed each others confidence as we boot packed up what we shoot have known was a dangerously deep soft slab of snow.

column20: On 23-Mar-19 at approximately 8:30 am one skier and one snowboarder were caught and carried in a wind slab avalanche (R2 D2) halfway up the Northeast Couloir of Hallett Peak (NNE aspect) while boot packing. The slab broke several feet above the leader when it failed. Both individuals were caught and carried in the avalanche (estimated 6-8"" crown not sure how wide). One rider was able to take a few steps to the left before getting carried 150 feet and coming to a stop on the left side of the couloir with no injuries or lost gear. The second rider was also caught carried 300 feet and lost two poles an ice axe and a snowboard during the slide. The second rider was carried off a small cliff at the top of the apron and sustained an injury from impact with a rock. The snowboard and one pole were recovered and both partners were able to safely exit to the parking lot under their own power.  Both individuals discussed the forecast the night before stating that wind and new snow in the forecast were a potential concern. In the morning it was verified that there were sustained winds through the night and in the parking lot unsure of how much new snow was on hand the team decided to head up Tyndall Gorge to see what conditions were like (and to keep options open) avoiding an ascent of Flattop Mountain due to high winds. Near the Bear Lake parking lot there was 1-2"" of new snow. Above Nymph Lake there was 3-4"" of new snow (likely wind deposited) and there were high winds on Dream Lake and above. As the team ascended toward the NE couloir up the south edge of the Gorge they skinned up a small slope where a small 4"" pocket of wind deposited snow released on a hard windboard base. The team noted the event but continued on aiming to examine conditions in their intended line. On the apron a mix of windboard and shallow new snow was found (likely wind deposited). The team felt comfortable transitioning to boot pack near the top of the apron. They ascended the left side of the couloir finding old edge-able/boot-able snow and a previously set boot pack with the steps slightly filled in with new snow. While boot packing above the apron they noticed a couple of small sluffs coming down the couloir to their right. About one-quarter of the way up the team switched places at a small rock band. After the rock band the snow consistency changed (in hindsight it was a newly deposited soft wind slab). The team was heading for a rock island in the middle of the couloir (at roughly 11000 ft) to reassess conditions when the slab released below a small convexity on the left side of the slope.  Both riders are trained to the level of AIARE 1 (one having taken a refresher in December) were carrying active avalanche rescue gear (beacon shovel probe) and consider themselves experienced in the backcountry and familiar with the terrain that was on hand.  Warning signs: - Forecast new snow - Forecast winds - Verified winds in the parking lot - Increasing snow deposition with elevation - High winds on the ascent with lots of snow transport in the air! - Small test slope release - Medium hard base when booting with new snow deposition - Sluffing in the couloir - Boot pack steps filled in - Change in snow consistency to wind slab after switching leaders.

The avalanche occurred in and above the three main chutes that loom above the lake at the end of the Takshanuk Mountain Trail road (See maps above and below). This area including the chutes is easily accessed via state land and is commonly skied. We have multiple reports of people skiing these chutes this year without incident.

column20: On the morning of Friday March 15 my ski partner and I skied from the Hermit Lake Trailhead on I-70 into Watrous Gulch via the Watrous Gulch trail . As we turned the corner into the Gulch itself we observed the aftermath of a large slide that originated near the top of the wide gully on the SW side of Mt. Parnassus. (See map) The crown was at an elevation of 12400 feet. The slide ran a surprisingly long distance along the Watrous Gulch creek down to an elevation of around 10800 feet. We guessed that the slide ran the day before some time after the snow storm of Wednesday March 13. No new snow had been deposited on top of the debris.  Several things surprised us about this slide: First was the volume of snow which upon deposition formed a large moraine-like structure at the base of the gully. Second was the distance estimated around 200 yards that it travelled along the creek bottom. Third was the way the flowing snow had split discretely into two separate areas: one being the aforementioned creek bed and the second being an apron of snow that ran across the creek at a right angle covering the summer trail. This debris field surpassed the summer trail a distance of 150 feet. Interestingly an undisturbed glade separated these two areas.  There is little doubt in our minds that the slide released naturally as it is inconceivable that anyone would have attempted to ski this line. Finally a couple other fresh slides were observed within the basin bounded by Point 12396 (aka Machebouef) Woods Mtn and Mt. Parnassus but none was as dramatic as the one just described.

CNFAIC staff visited the site on Tuesday March 12th with the two survivors during a break in the weather. The crown was completely blown in by the time of the site visit. Due to continued avalanche hazard traveling to the top of the slope was determined to be unsafe. Snowpack and likely weak layer information was gathered from a snowpit dug adjacent to the avalanche path at a lower elevation (~1800’). Many dimensions are estimated from the description of the group involved and Google Earth imagery. 

Avalanche Danger

This area does not have an avalanche advisory. Geographically it is closest to Summit Lake an area that the CNFAIC gathers snowpack observations and often includes in the Bottom Line portion of the Turnagain Area Advisory.  The CNFAIC staff visiting the accident site found the snowpack structure to be very similar to what has been observed in the Summit Lake area this season. All three members of the group read the Friday March 8th CNFAIC Turnagain Area Advisory prior to going into the cabin. There is no cell service near the cabin so they were not able to get the forecast for Saturday March 9th (day of accident) but were all aware that the weather was generally deteriorating with an incoming storm over the weekend.   

Friday March 8th 2019:

The avalanche danger has risen to CONSIDERABLE for Turnagain Pass Girdwood Placer Valley and the Seward zone due to strong winds and a mix of rain and snow. Above 1000’ triggering storm slabs up to 1’ thick is likely on slopes steeper than 35 degrees today.  Below 1000’ loose-wet avalanches are possible. Careful snowpack evaluation conservative decision-making and cautious route-finding are essential.

PORTAGE VALLEY: Natural avalanches are possible today in steep channeled terrain and could entrain wet snow in the lower elevations. Avoid places with significant avalanche terrain above like Byron Glacier Trail. In addition Portage Lake could be pretty dangerous this weekend due to thin ice above freezing temperatures and rain.

JOHNSON PASS/SUMMIT LAKE ZONE: There is a shallow snowpack with a generally poor structure. Strong winds and new snow will be adding stress to the snowpack. In addition to storm slabs more uncertainty exists for triggering a deeper avalanche in an older layer of the snowpack.

From the Storm Slab Primary Concern: 

South of Turnagain in the Summit Lake and Silvertip zones: Similar surface conditions to Turnagain Pass exist and any new snow that falls today is not expected to bond well. In addition a variety of old weak layers (facets and buried surface hoar) sit in the mid and base of the snowpack and wind loading and new snow will be adding more stress to these layers. Although less snow is expected to fall in this zone today keep in mind uncertainty exists for triggering a deeper more dangerous avalanche. 

Advisory link

Saturday March 9th 2019:

The avalanche danger is CONSIDERABLE this morning due to 1-2 feet of new snow in the past 24-hours. The danger is expected to rise to HIGH this evening as another round of snow and wind moves in. Human triggered slab avalanches up to 2+ feet thick will be likely. Natural avalanches will be possible. The new snow is falling on a very weak base and expected to slide easily on steep slopes. We are entering spring break with a dangerous avalanche situation and restraint will be required as travel in avalanche terrain is not recommended. 

PORTAGE VALLEY: Natural avalanches are possible today that could send debris to valley floors. Areas with steep slopes and avalanche terrain above you such as the Byron Glacier Trail should be avoided.

SUMMIT LAKE:  Despite little new snow this area has a very shallow snowpack with multiple weak layers. Strong winds and the potential for a few inches of new snow today could overload buried weak layers producing an unexpected slab avalanche. Caution is advised if heading to this area.

LOST LAKE:  Dangerous avalanche conditions are expected in the Lost Lake and Seward regions as well due to 1-2 feet of new snow and strong winds.

column20:
This was a hard slab avalanche that released naturally close to the largest avalanche possible in this path capable of destroying a substantial amount of forest and broke at the ground (HS-N-R5-D4-G). The crown face was around 12000 feet in elevation and extended approximately 3200 feet along west to northwest-facing slopes near treeline. The avalanche ran about 2200 vertical feet and 5400 horizontal feet. The avalanche crossed the valley floor and covered about 600 feet of US Highway 91 in debris. There were no records of this avalanche path previously reaching the highway. The angle from the highway to the high point of the crown  was about 21 degrees.

 Aerial imagery (Cloud-free Landsat imagery Oct 9 2015 available from Google Earth or USGS) of the Y Chute before this event shows a distinct toe of the avalanche path 1100 feet horizontally from the highway. Imagery also shows a change in the vegetation 580 feet from the highway which could indicate the extent of previous avalanche damage. The avalanche in March of 2019 ran through about 750 feet of dense forest with mature trees. It tore through the forest uprooting mature trees and across Tenmile Creek before hitting the roadway.

The Y Chute is part of a group of avalanche paths known as the SKY Chutes. Three adjacent avalanche paths to the north the S and both arms of the K chutes ran simultaneously or in close proximity to the Y Chute. The avalanche in the K Chute was also near the largest avalanche possible relative to the avalanche path and capable of destroying a substantial amount of forest (HS-N-R5-D4-G). Debris from the northern K Chute stopped within two feet of the Copper East parking lot. Debris from the southern track of the K Chute stopped within six feet of the highway. A power line near the valley bottom suffered extensive damage from these avalanches. The avalanche in the S Chute was slightly smaller and less destructive (HS-N-R4-D3.5-G) than the other three.

The avalanche occurred in a large complex group of avalanche paths. Multiple starting zones likely released at the same time after a large cornice collapse near the top of the slope. The avalanche initiated on an east northeast-facing slope at around 12000 feet but it propagated across multiple terrain features. Starting zone aspects ranged from north-northeast to east-southeast. The wall left by the cornice collapse was over 15 feet tall. The resulting avalanche broke to the north and south of the initial collapse. There were a mix of hard and soft slabs that broke on persistent weak layers. Portions of the slide released below recent wind-drifted snow other sections released on near-surface faceted crystals about four feet below the snow surface and some released on depth hoar at the ground (up to 6.5 feet below the snow surface). The avalanche broke about 2000 feet wide and ran about 1000 vertical feet. The alpha angle was 22 degrees which is close to the maximum distance an avalanche in this path can run. The avalanche was large relative to the path and had a destructive force large enough to break mature trees and create a powder cloud that reached 15 to 20 feet into the air (HS-NC-R4-D3.5-G).

There were two avalanches that ran on the same slope on March 3. Avalanche A that caught Skier 1 was a soft slab avalanche unintentionally triggered by a skier. It was small relative to the path and large enough to bury injure or kill a person. It broke at the interface between the new and old snow (SS-ASu-R1-D2-I). The avalanche broke approximately one foot deep 100 feet wide and ran 520 vertical feet. It was a storm slab avalanche.

The avalanche ran to a small flat terrain feature where the majority of debris stopped. Some debris continued downslope and Skier 1 was caught about 100 feet downslope of the terrain feature. Observers noted that the avalanche path ran several times previously in the winter and the terrain features could be previous avalanche debris.

Avalanche B occurred about 160 feet to the south. Investigators could not determine a trigger. It was larger in size relative to the path and large enough to bury injure or kill a person and also broke at the interface of new and old snow (SS-U-R2-D2-I). Debris from the second avalanche did not overlap with Avalanche A.

The largest pocket on north was 25'x10'x1' and ran 50' and also propagated/remotely triggered two small pockets 30' away. Did not ski steep north slopes with larger slabs. The largest slide on south was 100'x50'x1.5' and ran 200-300' - storm snow on top of a crust - skier triggered it intentionally and it took the skier for a small ride. Very small failures on small rolls.

There were two naturally triggered slides: one very small R1/D1 storm slab (not pictured) that sat below this bigger slide (attached images) which was a deep persistent slab R4/D2. Slope angle for the persistent slab slide was the usual sweet spot: 37 degree angle. East aspect. We assessed it as a D2 due to the bank which halted it as well as the low angle (~22 deg slope just below/around it). Area in which we were touring was pretty low risk given the low angle terrain but we spotted this slide after we passed the smaller storm slab slide â€” found the persistent slab just behind/above it. We believe the slide occurred earlier that morning (we departed the hut around 9am Sat for our day touring).

A small avalanche was triggered in a recently windloaded portion of the bed surface of a previous avalache. The prrevious avalanche was intentionally released to prepare for a local skimo race. A racer fell near the old crown and triggered the avalanche which also released a small portion of the hangfire.

Approximately 2/3 up or 100â€™ below the ridge Skier 1 noticed splinter propagation running in front of him. He turned downhill and saw Skier 2 & Skier 3 approximately 50â€™ below when the avalanche broke. Skier 2 & 3 immediately turned into the fall line. Skier 3 successfully deployed his airbag while Skier 2 did not.   The avalanche carried both skiers to the end of the slope. They were visible to Skier 1 nearly the duration of the slide. Both skiers were not buried and confirmed â€œOKâ€ on the radios. Concerned Skier 1 might trigger a secondary event waited for his friends to clear the debris field. The avalanche was medium sized relative to the path and had the destructive force to bury injure or kill a person (HS-ASu-R2-D2-O). The crown face was 32 inches deep at its maximum and averaged 24 inches deep. The width of the avalanche was estimated at 450 feet with a vertical fall of about 300 feet. The avalanche released on a south-facing slope above treeline. Although the crown broke on a part of the slope where the slope angle was 30 degrees the slope was convex with a maximum slope angle of 36 degrees.

Backcountry Avalanche Forecast

On January 30 the Colorado Avalanche Information Center’s (CAIC) Gunnison zone forecast rated the avalanche danger as Moderate (Level 2) at all elevations. Persistent Slab avalanches were listed as the only avalanche problem. The aspect/elevation diagram identified the most likely areas to encounter this problem as all aspects above treeline west to north to southeast aspects near treeline and northwest to northeast to east aspects below treeline. There was a Possible Likelihood and the avalanche size was Large to Very Large. The Summary read:

Avalanche danger is easing but it's not gone. Avalanche mitigation at Irwin continues to produce a few avalanches each day. With recently formed slabs resting on widespread weak layers many slopes lie waiting for a human trigger to avalanche. The danger is higher in shallower the eastern half of the Gunnison zone where the snowpack is still only three to five feet deep.

Recent avalanches broke two to four feet deep most commonly on slopes where northwest winds drifted snow. Look for these dangerous drifted features below cornices on steep slopes with a smooth pillowed snow surface. If you feel the snow stiffening and becoming more consolidated underfoot you're approaching a drift. To not over-emphasize drifted terrain alone keep in mind CBMR has triggered large avalanches this week in closed terrain that faces west to northwest. Slopes less than about 30 degrees are your safest options.

HS-NC-R2-D2.5-O  The avalanche was not witnessed. We were sent out to survey the area and document the slide. It would appear that a piece of the cornice had released and fell onto the slopes below triggering the avalanche. There was documentation of another slide adjacent to this one earlier this week. The initial crown fracture stepped out to the right side as it moved down slope triggering more of the slope. The debris ran over a bench at the bottom and continued into the trees near Olsen Lake.

The avalanche occurred on a steep south facing slope at an elevation of 9050 feet. Due to dangerous conditions and challenging terrain that could be only accessed by elite riders avalanche specialist from the Bridger-Teton National Forest Avalanche Center did not visit the accident site. Information about the terrain and avalanche attributes were obtained from a Bonneville County Search & Rescue volunteer who was on site during the body recovery efforts on January 26.

The avalanche was reported to have had a two foot deep crown. Two skiers ascended a southern ridge of peak 12271 from Prospect Gulch. We confined our uphill and downhill travel to the lower angle ridgetop/rib deliberately avoiding the steeper south and southwest facing gullies on either side of the ridge. As the skier #1 descended a moderate SW slope from the ridgetop he immediately remotely triggered a large slab avalanche approximately 500 feet to the west of the skier on a steeper SW slope at the head of a gully. The avalanche was far enough away to not be immediately visible to the skiers but the sound of moving snow and snapping branches/trees was audible soon followed by a visible plume of snow. We estimated that the avalanche crown extended at least 800 feet across the slope propagating across two different gullies. Large avalanche debris extended out of sight down the gullies but did not run all the way to the Prospect Gulch road. Due to safety concerns the skiers did not approach the avalanche site or crown to investigate the bed surface but the crown appeared to be 3 - 5 feet deep and at an elevation of 12100 feet. No other skiers or tracks were seen in the immediate vicinity that would have indicated that other parties were below the slope and could have been affected by the the avalanche.

Three skiers all AIARE L1 approached a roller that was wind swept to ground at the top Skier 3 approached on skis and determined top part of slope to be too steep for safe descending. Party circled around roller avoiding dangerous open and steep slopes to both sides. Party attempted to cross below roller on more shallow angle portion of lower slope to bench below. Two skiers approached the west side of Battleship crossing the middle fork of Mineral Creek from Ophir Pass Road.  We skinned up new avalanche debris that had come from the first major path on the west side of Battleship presumably part of the natural avalanche cycle a few days prior.  They chose this aspect because the forecasted winds would be out of the west and loading east aspects.  Halfway up the slope skinning up 25 degree hard avalanche debris they were struck by what appears to have been a natural avalanche and were caught and carried approximately 600-700 feet.  Skier 1 was buried to her waist.  Skier 2 was totally buried face down head downhill.  Skier 1 dug herself out switched her beacon to search and immediately found a signal and pinpointed Skier 2 approximately 50 feet below. She dug quickly removing about a meter of soft storm snow before revealing Skier 2.  Skier 2 was unconscious and not breathing but had a pulse.  Skier 1 stimulated breathing and continued to dig out Skier 2.  Skier 2 began spontaneous breaths slowly coming around until he could stand up.  Skier 1 retrieved her equipment and she and Skier 2 self rescued.  Miraculously no injuries were sustained by either skier   Of note was the sudden shift in wind direction about halfway up their skin track.  They had stopped to survey the slope and quickly discuss cutting their tour short due to conditions.  The plan was to continue a few hundred feet to the bottom of a large tree island to plan their descent.  At that time Skier 2 noticed that winds had shifted and were blowing directly downhill from east to west.  Having skied the terrain several times in the past month and presuming that the overhead hazard of the open slopes towards the ridge above had already slid naturally in the last cycle there was less concern for danger from above.  Furthermore the fact that they were on hard avalanche debris meant that they would probably not remote trigger terrain adjacent.  Finally Skier 2 had hunted extensively in this basin over the past several autumn seasons and was intimate with slope angles and terrain despite the obscured weather conditions.  It appears that the slope that slid and struck the skiers had a southwest aspect and the start zone was TL.  The new debris from this avalanche ran over 300 meters before hitting the skiers and then continued another 500 meters to the bottom of the drainage.

We observed recent avalanche activity on all aspects including buried debris from the previous storm and activity from the current storm. On northerly aspects slabs were breaking in the top 40-60 cm of snow and in the higher elevations it appeared wind slabs were contributing to slope failure. We encountered slide debris from the previous storm cycle buried under the most recent storm snow that was 10-15 feet deep. The debris slide in a northerly aspect in relatively dense trees and was R2D2 only breaking small trees.    We observed natural slope failures on convexities on north-north east aspects. These failures were cracking and collapsing under the weight of storm snow (old cracks) or fresh cracking under the weight of a skier jumping. These cracks were 40-60 cm deep failing underneath the storm slab. It seems the warm wet snow was heavy but also bonding well to old layers and thus slopes that were failing and collapsing were not sliding however the weight of wind effected snow or a skier could likely cause slopes to slide.

column20: Avalanche remotely triggered by a party of 2 skiers who traversed above the main skin track to the east.  The failure zone was a heavily cross-loaded convex southeast-facing slope.  We encountered a fresh debris pile partially covering the skin track below.  After talking to other groups who were ahead of us on the skin track the slide was remotely triggered just before we passed by two skiers we could still see above us on top of the convexity.  They appeared oblivious to the fact that they remotely triggered an avalanche onto the skin track below.  The crown looked to be ~75 cm deep which corresponds to the firm layer observed in our test pit.  There may have been a sympathetic release around the corner to the East.  We estimated the slope to be 38 degrees.  The avalanche occurred at approximately 10:45 am at 10750 ft right at tree line.  East Portal was extremely busy this morning and we encountered at least three other parties on the same skin track the avalanche partially covered.  People were everywhere and it was very difficult to keep track of the movements of other parties.

We observed a collection of debris piles from several R4D3+ naturally triggered avalanches. These slides appeared to have run down each major gully feature along the Star Peak massif. Most of these slide paths or gullies are by-and-large east facing but their sides are steeper and lean to the north ans south. As we climbed higher onto the riblets separating each gully we could see crown lines ranging in depth from 2-4 feet. These seemed to have failed on a crust/facet combo just above the October/November depth hoar layers. These long-running crowns lined the northeast sides of each sub-ridge from 9K all the way to their summits at 11.5K.  Most of these crown lines were in the trees and had cracked on every slope nearing 32-35 degrees in steepness.  The fascinating part of this natural event can be seen in attached photos- where the debris piles showed evidence of multiple avalanches coming down simultaneously or in close succession.  Although no one will ever know for sure our group surmounted that the upper more east facing loading zones came down first after the strong westerly winds overloaded the leeward sides of each peak.  Although we did not see these upper crowns up close we could see them from a distance and they were some 100 feet below the ridgetops. We theorized that these initial avalanches then triggered the steeper northeast sides of each gully; filling in the gullies with fresh debris as the upper slides then rumbled down through them. We observed trenches some 20-30 feet deep and as we walked up the paths the debris piles resembled a glacier- with medial and terminal moraines. The end result was that each major path had run full track leaving piles of snow at their bottoms that were some 40-50 feet high!

I believe this same event was documented on Friday 1/18 with vague location details so I'm providing these details and a photo to complete the report. (location description and travel pattern in 1/18 report generally match what we observed). To skinner's right of the main skin track that ascends directly S to the Butler Gulch saddle immediately above treeline there is a steep slope (descending from knob on ridge to the right/W) with rock bands and shallow gullies. Below this is a (very) low-angle treeless zone that is commonly skid. We observed an avalanche crown ~300 ft up the knob's slope where a crown had broken and snow had slid off to the ground surface revealing grass and small rocks. The avalanche debris stopped in the first ~50 ft of very-low angle terrain. New ski tracks from saturday went under the same slope through this debris (!!) and since Friday's tracks were likely buried/erased we could not corroborate the Friday report's narrative but it is easy to imagine that it played out as described. The start zone for this avalanche was on a very wind-loaded aspect (N just E of a micro-ridge that was heavily drifted on the lee (E) side) and was up an increasingly steep convex slope from the low-angle area with tracks. We did not ascend to the start zone to get an accurate measurement of the crown; we estimate it to be < 2' and > 1'.  I'm including this with details because this low-angle slope where the debrid ended (and the avalanche could have been remotely triggered from) appears very safe and is frequently skid by parties that are not considering themselves in avalanche terrain. A good heads-up to the possibilities of remote triggering and paying attention to ""hangfire"" above.

First slide observed from top of Benchmark looking across to West Marvins in the West Wall area.       1st Slide: Appeared natural and a day or two old likely running sometime late Friday 1/18 due to the few inches of new snow covering the debris.  West Wall slide was approximately 300' wide and ran to the valley floor approx 600 vertical feet.  Slide appeared to have started above the prominent cliff band.  Crown estimated at 1 foot deep and only included the new storm snow.  No ski tracks observed around this slide.  Slide was easily big enough to carry and bury a skier.  This was enough evidence for us to stick with original plan of a more conservative ski route.    Skied down west ridgeline on Mill Creek Rd above West Marvins stopped and looked back south at Abrahams and Old Man's/CDC.    2nd Slide: Observed a prior skier-triggered avalanche starting from the top of Benchmark encompassing about two-thirds of the Abrahams slide path from Tweeners over to start of trees on west side of Abrahams.  Observed 10+ ski tracks at top of and on either side of slide and exiting from bottom of the path.  Crown depth was again about 12-20"" of recent storm snow.  Slide was approximately 200' wide at top and ran approximately 400 vertical feet to the first bench.  Slide was big enough to have swept a rider through the trees and cliffband around Mushroom rock and bury them on the bench.  Slide must have occurred that morning and likely started from observed ski cuts at the top of the path.  We observed what looked to be evidence of either a recovery or people investigating the debris pile based on ski tracks foot prints and disturbances in the toe of the slide.  3rd Slide -  Smaller skier-triggered avalanche observed in the Old Man's path from this vantage as well.  Saw approximately 3 tracks heading from east entrance of Old Man's dropping straight into the gut.  Slide began mid-path from a ski cut where the slope first rolls over steeply from first bench .  Slide was approx 50-100 feet wide with 12-20"" crown running 100-200 vertical feet to next bench.  Saw original ski tracks exiting slide from the bottom.  Other ski tracks stayed to east side of slide path.  Slide was from that morning as well.    We counted tracks in and out of the areas as best we could and looked closely for any skiers or riders remaining in the area but saw none and departed.  Other parties we saw on the way up were headed for watertank area and were accounted for at the bus stop upon exit.    Fortunately none of the slides stepped down into older snow.    These events heighten my concern for increased avalanche activity in the area this week as loading from last night's storm and additional forecasted snow this week could push the snowpack past it's tipping point to produce some large full-path slides particularly in the paths that haven't seen recent activity.  I expect to see poor bonding of new snow with the surface hoar we saw on Sunday morning as well.  Stay frosty out there.

column20: In the basin south of the Sangree Froelicher hut there was a large avalanche that broke in old snow and at the ground in places. This terrain feature was only 100 vertical feet but the avalanche piled up deep debris as the crown was estimated at 500 feet wide and broke 3 feet deep with a portion breaking 6 feet deep. The weak layer was mid pack facets except in the deeper section where it was depth hoar. The avalanche was impressive for a small terrain feature but what was even more impressive was the extensive cracking to the south of this avalanche and cracking towards smaller avalanches thousands of feet away. The collapse of the weak layer in this basin must have been massive. Widespread weak layer is obvious. Places where the slab is thickest from previous wind loading are highly suspect. Other places are just waiting for more of a slab. The other interesting thing about the large avalanche was the 8 inches of new snow was evenly distributed at the top of the crown from end to end. This shows there wasn't much wind loading and the weight of the new snow was enough to cause this natural avalanche.

The avalanche occurred on a steep east-northeast facing slope at an elevation of 9500 feet.  It was a soft slab avalanche that failed on a layer of coarse grained faceted snow.  A crown face profile was conducted above the location of the buried rider on January 10.  At that location the total snow depth was 40 inches.  The crown depth was 24 inches.  The crown fracture propagated into adjacent terrain features.  Although the slab was generally two feet deep there were portions of the crown fracture that were up to three feet deep.  The slope angle at the location of the crown face profile was measured to be 36 degrees.  

There was an abrupt transition in steepness at the base of the slope where the rider was buried.  It is believed that the rider was at or near this change in slope when the avalanche was triggered.  The avalanche debris was deepest at this slope transition and did not flow very far past that slope change.  This avalanche was classified as relative size 2 and a destructive size 2 event.

This was a hard slab avalanche triggered unintentionally by a snowmobile large relative to the path which had the destructive force to bury a car damage a wood frame house or break trees. The avalanche failed on an old snow layer of well-developed faceted snow and depth hoar near the ground (HS-AMu-R4-D3-O). These facets sat above a thin decomposing crust at the location of a crown profile conducted Jan. 6 2019. The avalanche crown ranged from 12 to 60 inches thick (estimated) and spanned 1750 feet across (estimated). The avalanche released on an east-facing slope with flanks wrapping into southeast and northeast aspects. Two snowmobilers were below the fracture when it released one near the crown and one lower in the path.

This accident involved two avalanches. The first was a hard slab avalanche unintentionally triggered by the group of skiers medium sized relative to the path and had the destructive force to bury injure or kill a person (HS-ASu-R2-D2-O). The group triggered the avalanche near a shallow rocky outcrop. It likely broke on a buried layer of near-surface facets that developed between storms during the first few days of the year. The avalanche stepped down to deeper weak layers near the ground entraining the entire season’s snowpack. The face of the crown ranged from 12 inches to 54 inches deep. The avalanche released on a south-southeast facing slope around 32 degrees in steepness. 

A crack from the first avalanche ran through the snow releasing a second avalanche (remote trigger) on a connected east-facing slope. The second avalanche was a hard slab medium sized relative to path and had the destructive force to bury injure or kill a person (HS-ASr-R2-D2-O). Investigators estimated that the average depth of the crown face was 36 inches. The avalanche released on a slope around 35 degrees in steepness. 

The debris from both slides overlapped at the bottom of the slope.

column20: <TL SS ASu-R4-D2-G On a NNE aspect at ~11500' occurred on the second ski slope on the standard Midnight ski path.  Triggered by second skier as the skier reached the 1/2 point in the slope fracturing at the top of the path (slow crack) which then released the entire slope running on the bed surface of large facets on the ground. Full depth of snowpack released with an average depth of ~100cm across the entire path (~20m wide) and ran into the dense trees below for a total distance of debris at ~90m). Skier 2 was able to ski out of the slide to the west when they heard a call from Skier 3 who noticed the growing crack at the top of the slope (slow release no noticable collapse). Skier 2 was able to nearly exit the path and post behind a larger tree at the far west end of the path and was minorly impacted by the flank of the debris flow.  Skier 1 was further below at a safe location.    Party felt that the agreed upon ski/spotting plan and exit routes helped avoid injury or serious incident.  All realized prior to skiing that the slope had potential to slide but matched the upper slopes in characteristics investigated prior to skiing. No noticeable layers were found with quick pole penetration tests slope appeared to be mostly facets and 30-35 deg. Slope had been skied by a party of 2 skiers prior to the recent storm loads (Tuesday) without incident and old tracks were still visible prior to skiing.  Because of concern with the new snow load the party proceeded cautiously.    Inspection after the slide revealed a slightly steeper rollover with on the ground under skier 2's line than the first skiers (<2ft to the east of skier 2's line) due to a rocky spot on the ground.  This feature was not evident prior to the avalanche with the snow cover however which was uniform across the slope at that location.  Slope angle was not measured but estimated between 35-37deg at the rollover itself.

The avalanche occurred on a short steep slope at an elevation of 8950 feet.  This steep slope was in a small concave terrain feature.  It was on a northeast aspect.  The slide was estimated to be 150 feet wide.  The distance from the crown to the toe of the debris was also estimated to be 150 feet.  

The crown of the avalanche was measured to be 22 inches deep.  It was a hard slab avalanche.  Due to the shape of the terrain feature (quick flattening of the slope) this hard slab avalanche did not flow very far past the avalanche stauchwall.  Due to the short run out distance and an abrupt slope change the avalanche debris primarily experienced laminar flow and for that reason was mostly intact but fractured.  This slide was classified as a 1.5 on the destructive size scale.  The avalanche debris was several feet deep.  Without the complication of being pinned beneath a snowmachine it is unlikely that the debris would have fully buried a person. The slab failed on a persistent weak layer of faceted snow.  Figure 3 is a photograph of the slide that was taken on December 23.

We triggered an avalanche on an east facing slope of about 38 degrees at 11000ft in lightly gladed terrain outside the ski area boundary on Aspen mountain. Time of day was approximately 4pm. That avalanche in turn remote triggered the slope to our right which is a much steeper and more prone slope in general. With the heavy rate of snowfall we couldn't see the adjacent slide too well but assumed it was similar to what we just witnessed. The slide we witnessed certainly had the power and speed to smash a victim through the trees and rocks below and could have caused serious harm or death had someone been caught. We failed to capture any photos of the path.

column20: I was traversing across an approximately 30 degree east facing slope at 11700 on the east side of Ophir Pass approximately 1/2 miles southwest of the Opus Hut and 1000' northeast of Crystal Lake. Avalanche on NE slope. I was standing still thinking about how I was probably in a bad spot with a 33 degree rollover above me. There was also a significant rocky and wind loaded slope adjacent to me with large cornice. A kite could be seen above on the McMillan/Red Mountain side. I was standing still for 15 seconds or so coming to the conclusion I should turn around when the avalanche went. It seemed to trigger about 100-150 yards away. I played a roll in it but it is possible the kite skier did as well as the sun/wind on the cornice. My wife was well below the runout and I skied out via the debris path which was surprisingly soft. 5 years and my first trigger. I am the guy who plays it safe but had an early season lapse of reason that was compounded by not skiing much last year and general foolishness. Luckily we skied away safely and with the biggest lesson yet here in the San Juan's. In the photos you can see my skin track got burried. The last turn to the right is where I stopped and the avalanche triggered the turn to the right going into the debris path was me exiting after avalanche.

Skier 2 was downhill below the bench in the slope where the avalanche stopped. Skier 2 was able to maintain sight of skier 1. The debris accumulated on the bench and stopped. column20: Grizzly Couloir Grizzly Peak. N/NE aspect. 12750'.  The avalanche occurred in a N/NE facing couloir above tree line. Due to the large cornice blocking our entrance to the couloir we decided to dig our way through the cornice and cut away as much as possible with shovels and skis. After attempting to cut a large section of overhanging cornice (10 ft. long 5 ft. wide 7 ft. deep) a member of our party Skier 1 set up a rappel with a backup to more safely manage the cornice hazard. After a few attempts Skier 1 was able to successfully kick off the large block of cornice. However this then triggered a much larger cornice fall. The subsequent cornice fall was approximately 40 ft. long 15 ft. wide and 5-15 ft. deep. The cornice fall then triggered an additional avalanche within the slide path. Due to the damage done to the couloir's snow surface by the cornice fall it was difficult to determine specifics about the triggered avalanche. However based on our observations the avalanche most likely broke just below the cornice and entrained snow as it traveled down hill (SS-AS-R2-D2.5-O). The avalanche broke approximately 40 feet wide and ran 1500 vertical feet. It was difficult to determine the depth of the slide due to the cornice damage.

Loose avalanches (likely the new snow) starting below cliff bands within couloirs and in open bowls. I went to check out the previously reported snowmobile triggered persistent slab avalanche from 3/25/18 on the northern flank of Treasurevault Mountain. NNW aspect NTL. Due to a variety of hazards I was only able to check out the crown in the shallowest rockiest part of the flank. HS in this area ranged from 60-100cm. I found a 20-30cm slab up to 1F hardness sandwiching a weak layer of F hard facets with a 1F hard bed surface. The weak layer was 40-50cm from the ground and large depth hoar made up at least the bottom 30cm of the snowpack. The avalanche appeared to have stepped down to the depth hoar/ground in many other spots. In loaded areas where the crown was up to 3 feet deep the slab was clearly thicker and I suspect harder. Point 7054 is approximately 1 mile southeast of Setting Sun Mountain drains into Weenan Creek which feeds into Lost River and is located roughly 6.5 miles to the northwest of Mazama and 16 miles northeast of Washington Pass.

The avalanche on Point 7054 initiated on a west-northwest aspect at 6900 ft on a 34 degree sparsely treed convex slope. The starting zone was surrounded by thicker stands of trees and the terrain rolled over and steepened to 41 degrees through a gully feature with small trees.

This was a human triggered (splitboarder) hard slab avalanche that was large in relation to the path and had the destructive force to bury injure or kill a person. The crown face was 12 to 55 inches (30 cm to 140 cm) deep averaging 28 inches (71 cm) and was approximately 230 ft wide. The avalanche ran approximately 800 vertical ft and broke a number of trees up to 6” in diameter banking a left turn onto the opposite side of the drainage. The avalanche likely failed within a layer of faceted snow and immediately stepped down to and slid on a thin crust believed to be the 2/8 rain crust.

column20: Positive feedback on the avalanche problem for once. No obvious signs to instability yet again traveling through the terrain. On our second run we were skiing a line with the intention to trend left for an easier exit. When the first skier kept trending skiers right I had a WTF moment as that was not the direction we wanted to go. The remaining group had a quick chat as to whether we wanted to follow them and of course the double date ski stayed together. Upon regrouping we realized he was trending skiers right to avoid a big terrain trap face thing that wasn't obvious before. We chatted about whether we wanted to descend the steeper slope that ended in a gully feature and was in the direction that we wanted to head. However it was fairly quick for the group to rule that out as a not so sweet looking slope and setup. So we kept skiing in the safer terrain heading in the wrong direction. Near the bottom of the terrain the 3rd skier trended more in the fall line as the total slope size decreased. The 4th skier followed suit and triggered a Persistent Slab avalanche breaking at the ground. 1 to 3ft deep crown breaking at the ground. The avalanche was relatively small giving the smaller scale of the slope. However it could have been large and deadly had we skied the larger slope that was in the path of our intended decent. This was a windward exposed slope from down valley winds. You definitely couldn't tell that just by looking at the terrain given all the recent fresh snow in February. However the HS was shallower then average on that terrain feature.

column20: Avalanche Crown / Trigger Point - Taylor Hill (39.3860 -106.2884) - Elevation: 11693 - Aspect: 40 deg TN - Slope Angle: 35-37deg (measured after the fact and for the starting zone / trigger point). - Crown Width: 10 - 12 meters - Crown Height: 1 - 2 meters - Distance: 30 - 25 meters  While discussing whether to ski this line or traverse all the way around the East / South East ridge up towards Chicago Ridge I volunteered that we could practice the ski rappel and inspect the slope so we built a dead man anchor roughly 10 meters from the edge of the convex roll over. The dead man anchor was around 1.25 meters deep and while building it no obvious hard slab layers or worrisome weak layers were encountered.   I rappelled (backed up with tail knots and a third hand) into the line unfortunately a bit past the trigger point (~10ft past it) got my skis perpendicular to the fall line and jumped 6 -7 times on the slope with no response at all. At this point I radioed to the group that I was going to dig a quick hand pit because the slope seemed stable initially. I quickly discovered that the newly drifted snow (4-6in) hadn't bonded at all to the second layer and that the second layer was 6-8in of pencil hard wind slab. After getting through the second layer I found it was ""supported"" by non-cohesive medium-grain facets.   I quickly radioed to the group that we won't be skiing this line and told them I'd be climbing back up immediately. I struggled to make progress due to punching through into the weak layer so I un-clipped my skis to use them as a pull-up bar and began ascending pausing to pull slack through my belay device as I climbed. On the 3rd overhead placement of my skis I felt the skis punch through the top layers easily and all the snow under me washed away I looked over my shoulder and saw everything to my right had let loose.  My spotter saw the slide happen and called it out on the radio I then responded that I was fine and that I was standing on the bed layer of facets.   At this point I was right in front of the crown which was roughly 2 meters tall. It looked and felt like a step down avalanche triggered by my skis punching through the identified wind slab which appears to have thinned to around 1 - 3 in at the trigger point. I took some pictures while contemplating climbing over the crown / hang fire ( I don't know if it was but it was spooky looking). At this point my spotter radioed to me that there was a 1 - 2 in wide crack running along the edge of the roll over and we agreed that the best course of action was to ski down the bed surface and into the trees. As I descended through the trees I kept finding that wind slab layer in the un-sheltered openings so I stuck to tight trees and skied a lot of downhill kick turns.  In the mean time half of our group decided to return to Vance's while the other half started to traverse the ridge to find a low angle entry into the area I was in. The dead man anchor was around 1.25 meters deep and while building it no obvious hard slab layers or worrisome weak layers were encountered.   I rappelled (backed up with tail knots and a third hand) into the line unfortunately a bit past the trigger point (~10ft past it) got my skis perpendicular to the fall line and jumped 6 -7 times on the slope with no response at all. At this point I radioed to the group that I was going to dig a quick hand pit because the slope seemed stable initially. I quickly discovered that the newly drifted snow (4-6in) hadn't bonded at all to the second layer and that the second layer was 6-8in of pencil hard wind slab. After getting through the second layer I found it was ""supported"" by non-cohesive medium-grain facets.   I quickly radioed to the group that we won't be skiing this line and told them I'd be climbing back up immediately. I struggled to make progress due to punching through into the weak layer so I un-clipped my skis to use them as a pull-up bar and began ascending pausing to pull slack through my belay device as I climbed. On the 3rd overhead placement of my skis I felt the skis punch through the top layers easily and all the snow under me washed away I looked over my shoulder and saw everything to my right had let loose.  My spotter saw the slide happen and called it out on the radio I then responded that I was fine and that I was standing on the bed layer of facets. The avalanche occurred on a steep east-northeast facing slope at an elevation of 9130 feet.  The slope was treed however the slide released from a convex open area in the upper portion of the slope.  The slide was characterized as a relative size 3 destructive size 2 hard slab avalanche.  It ran a distance of 600 feet.   It was 190 feet across at it widest point which was up near the crown.  The estimated vertical fall of this avalanche from the crown to the toe of the avalanche debris is about 280 feet.  Figure 2 depicts the extent of the slide the location of the partially buried snowmachine the burial location of the rider and the location of a crown profile.  

A crown profile was conducted on February 22.  The slope angle at the location of the profile was 38 degrees.   The depth of the crown at the location of the profile was 34 inches.  This slide failed on a persistent weak layer of faceted snow that formed during a dry period in early December.

column20:
The Ralph’s Slide avalanche path has a history of avalanche and non-avalanche accidents including 3 past avalanche fatalities (one in 2001 and two in 2016). Due to the terrain being easily accessed from the Upper Rock Springs backcountry access gate the dangerous area has a tendency to attract people who leave the resort regardless of warning signs at the gate identifying the hazardous terrain below as well as other backcountry travel warnings including the daily backcountry advisory and the need for proper knowledge and equipment. 

The path itself is in complex high consequence terrain as the slabs that form there are directly above a wide cliff and are therefore unsupported. The avalanche was recorded as SS-ASu-R2-D2-I indicating it was a soft slab avalanche and unintentionally skier triggered.  It had a relative size of 2 out of 5 a destructive size of 2 and it released on the interface below recently fallen snow and the previous snow surface. The crown height averaged two feet and width of the crown was approximately 80 feet. The slope faces to the southeast and has a slope angle in the starting zone of approximately 38 degrees at elevation of 9900 feet.

The Bridger-Teton National Forest Avalanche Center had rated the high elevations of the Tetons as Considerable during the day of the accident.

SS - ASc - R1/D1.5 - O. Failed on 4mm DH on a slick old bed surface. SS - ASu - R2/D2 - O. Same structure propagated wider and ran 800' vertical. Went looking to see if the Jan 20th interface would reactivate under the weight of a new load. Turns out the Jan 20th interface wouldn't be our concern. Found radically different structures between slopes that had and had not avalanched. We dug in 2 slopes that had not avalanched which gave us information that we misapplied the slopes below which it turns out had avalanched previously and had much different structure. First went to look for 1/20 interface in a deep spot with light drifting near treeline. Northeast aspect 11200'. HS 240cm. ECTX with slab fractures within in the new snow. No concern at the 1/20 interface down 50cm. Second went to look for changes to 1/20 interface within 10 or 15' of a skier triggered avalanche from last week. Northeast aspect 11100'. HS 140cm. ECTX with slab fractures within the new snow. No concern at the 1/20 interface down 50cm. Third dropped into a slope that we believed had not avalanched this season expecting to trigger a shallow storm slab in the new snow. A little ways down the slope at the first significant roll-over one skier placed a hard cut and triggered D1.5 slide about 50cm deep. The hitch was the total HS was only 80cm. This slope had slid before leaving a dramatically different 1/20 interface with much much much weaker snow. There was no visual indication that the slope had previously avalanched and only a change in feel underfoot right at the point of the avalanche.Â  After the first skier moved to safe ground a second skier came down near the first track and remotely triggered (15' away) a much broader avalanche in steeper adjacent terrain. Same structure the slope had slid previously. At that point both skiers skinned back to the ridge opting toÂ avoid this unexpected change in conditions and revert to the great snow on the lower angles sunny slopes. Big lesson learned - thinking we were digging and looking for one problem we found another problem that was far touchier and broader propagating than expected. We were trying to figure out and find the weak layer responsible for the avalanches triggered a week before which had been described as ""wickedly touchy.""Â  Our evidence in profiles very close to the prior avalanches didn't match what we expected to find nor the prior reports.Â  Turns out we were in a completely different snowpack because they were several feet outside of previous avalanches.Â  When the evidence doesn't match the report (of touchy conditions recently) consider the weirdness as a sign of uncertainty - proceed with caution.Â  Fortunately our habits of skiing the less exposed lines payed dividents though it was too close for comfort.
