column20: SS - ASc - R1/D1.5 - O. Failed on 4mm DH on a slick old bed surface. SS - ASu - R2/D2 - O. Same structure propagated wider and ran 800' vertical. Went looking to see if the Jan 20th interface would reactivate under the weight of a new load. Turns out the Jan 20th interface wouldn't be our concern. Found radically different structures between slopes that had and had not avalanched. We dug in 2 slopes that had not avalanched which gave us information that we misapplied the slopes below which it turns out had avalanched previously and had much different structure. First went to look for 1/20 interface in a deep spot with light drifting near treeline. Northeast aspect 11200'. HS 240cm. ECTX with slab fractures within in the new snow. No concern at the 1/20 interface down 50cm. Second went to look for changes to 1/20 interface within 10 or 15' of a skier triggered avalanche from last week. Northeast aspect 11100'. HS 140cm. ECTX with slab fractures within the new snow. No concern at the 1/20 interface down 50cm. Third dropped into a slope that we believed had not avalanched this season expecting to trigger a shallow storm slab in the new snow. A little ways down the slope at the first significant roll-over one skier placed a hard cut and triggered D1.5 slide about 50cm deep. The hitch was the total HS was only 80cm. This slope had slid before leaving a dramatically different 1/20 interface with much much much weaker snow. There was no visual indication that the slope had previously avalanched and only a change in feel underfoot right at the point of the avalanche.Â  After the first skier moved to safe ground a second skier came down near the first track and remotely triggered (15' away) a much broader avalanche in steeper adjacent terrain. Same structure the slope had slid previously. At that point both skiers skinned back to the ridge opting toÂ avoid this unexpected change in conditions and revert to the great snow on the lower angles sunny slopes. Big lesson learned - thinking we were digging and looking for one problem we found another problem that was far touchier and broader propagating than expected. We were trying to figure out and find the weak layer responsible for the avalanches triggered a week before which had been described as ""wickedly touchy.""Â  Our evidence in profiles very close to the prior avalanches didn't match what we expected to find nor the prior reports.Â  Turns out we were in a completely different snowpack because they were several feet outside of previous avalanches.Â  When the evidence doesn't match the report (of touchy conditions recently) consider the weirdness as a sign of uncertainty - proceed with caution.Â  Fortunately our habits of skiing the less exposed lines payed dividents though it was too close for comfort. Bottom lineÂ - head's up the slopes that avalanched in the Holiday cycle or the early January cycle have reloaded in the deeper snow zones around Paradise Divide and they may react much differently than the adjacent terrain with an intact full-season's snowpack.

column20: We skier triggered this R2D1 on a NE aspect at around 10800â€™ today. I thought we were making the right call by heading to terrain that had already slid in the last storm cycle but though there isnâ€™t much new snow the new slab hasnâ€™t bonded to the bed surface and had just enough energy to potentially take you off your feet and into hazards. So I underestimated the hazard dropping into the zone but once we were committed we recognized the danger and negotiated the terrain as best we could. We had stopped just above this convexity and my partner (unintentionally) triggered it with his first turn and was able to quickly cut back to the safety zone from which I shot the second photo before the failure further propagated. It ran slowly about 250 ft(?) into trees below. Hard to say how consequential it would have been if heâ€™d been caught in it - definitely not enough to get buried probably enough to take you off your feet possibly enough to break bones hitting trees definitely enough to scare you - so both of us feel fortunate that we were already on guard and ready to make the quick move to safety. Avalanche problem was on the smaller side due to the thin snowpack where it had already slid but magnified by the consequence of the terrain with trees below and continued exposure as we navigated our way out of the zone. Feeling sheepish that I pushed to ski this zone incorrectly assessing the dangers versus benefits of skiing the slide path. But we learn way more when things go wrong - after all we never really know if things went right in the backcountry the danger of the positive feedback loop. Thanks to my partner shif for an educative and ultimately safe day and to other tourers who also successfully picked their way through the tender zone.

A group of 3 snowmobilers on rental mountain sleds attempted to summit Ptarmigan Hill up the eastern ridgeline route from Ptarmigan Pass.  One of the party members successfully summited Ptarmigan Hill and turned back around to help another party member who had a sled stuck in a very precarious location roughly 30 feet below the summit.  The rider was able to turn the sled around and the rider began descending the eastern ridgeline however was unable to steer the sled and descended directly down the fall line. My group of 7 were in a field below and out of harms way we all attempted to direct the rider to his right to avoid dropping into a wind-loaded cornice however he was completely unable to maneuver the sled.  As the rider dropped over the ridgeline into the NE aspect of Ptarmigan Hill he triggered a large (R3 D2)? slide from the SE flank of the crown.  The rider was ejected from his sled and tumbled ~20 feet to a small shelf.  The rider was not buried and his sled was partially buried.  Nobody else was in the path of the slide; the rider who triggered the avalanche was the only person caught.  Half of my group approached the scene of the accident prepared for a rescue and discovered that everyone was okay.  Not a single member of the rental group had beacons shovels or probes and the rider who caused the slide didn't even know what a beacon is.

This was a skier-triggered soft slab avalanche that was medium-sized relative to the path and had the destructive force to bury injure or kill a person (SS-AS-R3-D2-O/G). The avalanche failed on a layer of faceted early-season snow near the ground and released the entire season’s snowpack. The crown face was 18 to 22 inches deep and 240 feet across. The avalanche initiated on the steep north-facing slope that forms the skier’s right side of the gully the group was descending. The fracture crossed the slope and then continued down the ridgeline that formed the south side of the gully resulting in a large slide that entrained a significant amount of snow. The avalanche broke at a subtle mid-slope convexity leaving a significant amount of snow in the start zone and lingering hazard above the fracture line. A smaller avalanche was triggered sympathetically from the side of the gully as the debris ran by. The terrain in the track was open glades with some brush and aspen clumps. The force of the slide was insufficient to cause significant damage to the vegetation in the track.

column20: A 30 x 30 foot Slab was released by a patroller. The slab broke 10 feet above the patroller and carried him for at least fifteen feet before he was able to stop his movent.  The avalanche continued for at least another 100 ft.      Patroller returned to ski cut the area and released at least one more slide of similar size in the same area.       The slab was propagating and was running on the interface between the oldest (pre-christmas) facets and the storm which came in over Christmas.        Again as Patrol we normally don't comment on slides we create in our area as we are going out of our way to release them and they often ocurr in snow conditions that are only unique to our area. The the initial fracture entrained enough of the snow below the crown to bury a skier in the trees at the bottom of the slope. This slope was chosen for a ski cut after seeing the result of  an unknown trigger natural avalance on the same elevation location aspect and slope anchoring. The initial fracture was right where some unknowing snowshoers will wander across from time to time. Due to location of the fracture a crown profile was unable to be obtained but a close enough inspection revealed new windslab sitting on top of matured facets and waterice attached to the rockslab underneath. column20: At 1:45 PM I triggered a shallow but wide (70m+) slab avalanche while skiing alone on the NW aspect of Mt. Baldy. I was alone because I was really just out for a tour on the roads. But I had bootpacked up to Baldy's West ridge for the exercise in very shallow snow/talus and I was planning to sideslip back down a trough and then do a descending traverse back to the road. As I traversed out of the trough onto an open slope of about 25 degrees I heard the snow whumph then immediately saw cracks form above and all around me. Before I could do anything a wide swath of the slope cut loose and slid with me approximately in the middle. I was still on my feet so I skied with it heading down but slightly across it for about 20 meters before I reached stable snow. Luckily the slide was relatively slow and shallow (4-6"") with no trees rocks or obstacles in its path. It slid for about 50-60 meters before stopping.

column20: Our group of four ascended Point 12118 which sits opposite Vazquez Mountain to the west. Two of the group decided about half way up to turn around and ski what we climbed due to the appearance of some rollerballing occurring near our ascension path. Myself and my partner decided to summit and ride down a north eastern facing chute that had not been subject to the sun as much.  We had both ridden this area a few times in years past but had not done this particular chute before since it is steeper than some of the others sitting further up valley. My partner descended about 3/4 down and stopped in a safe zone so we could regroup and descend to the other two members of our party. He rode down the least steep portion of the chute and noticed a few rollerballs starting there as well.   I descended next and followed a fall line to drop in. This line had a convexity and became steeper. I did a few turns and was picking up speed when the slope to my left began to crack.   To my right were two large rocks poking out so i decided to go left so if I was swept off my feet I would not be dragged through them. I straight lined it hoping to escape but got swept off my feet.   We believe the slide carried me about 200 feet. I was able to keep my face skyward and as I came to a stop I didnt have any snow on my head so I threw a hand up so as the debris settled my partner would be able to see me quickly.   My left side ended up being buried under about a foot of wet snow while my right side was free. My partner reached me about 10 seconds after I stopped and checked me over and extricated me. I did not have any injuries and was able to snowboard out. We met the rest of our party who where not too far away and were attempting to skin up to meet us and we all left from there.  Looking at the slide afterwards it appears that only the new snow that fell after 5/19 slid out as the slide did not step down any further into older layers. The crown only looked like a few inches tall but that was enough to take me out.

After skiing my primary objective with only minor sluffing from the new snow (a north facing shot at higher elevation) I decided to traverse over and ski this gully. I dropped into this line skied about halfway down and got caught by a wave of my own sluff. It knocked me off my feet and carried me about 100 yards downslope. Luckily this line is low consequence with a huge apron below but still this was an eye-opener!

A similar small slide was triggered near the top of the slope while traversing in (not visible in the picture) and so this loose wet slough movement was expected. Please categorize it as unintentional as I was skiing and not ski cutting. With more snow tonight and Friday I hope that folks are alert and aware this weekend especially with the intense May sun. Thank you!

At around 11am our party of 3 began ascending the dragontail couloir in RMNP under stormy conditions. We were well aware of storm slab potential and saw fresh debris fields below west elk couloir and dragontail itself.  Based on reports from previous skiers who had finished skiing dragontail and stated it had already sluffed we ascended the couloir - trying to stay on the climbers left side near the rocks. The sun briefly shone through the clouds a handful of times which didn't seem to change the nature of the snow appreciably but was noticeably warm. During the ascent there were pockets of deep snow but much of the couloir had already run and seemed relatively safe. Things changed quickly once we passed a large rock on climbers left side of the couloir. I was out in front and soon was up to my thighs in deep snow as I was bootpacking. I began to get concerned and noticed that the fresh snow was upside down (heavier on top). I could see a safe zone not far above me where the couloir forms a Y. The distances were hard to appreciate from my vantage point and what seemed close was much further than it looked. I was ahead of my party and trying to quickly get in the safe zone so I could reassess things hopeful that I could reach the safe zone before they left the protective nature of the large rock on the climbers left.   I was probably 20 or 30 feet from the safe zone at about 1pm when I felt the snowpack settle and crack in a large slab about 6-8 feet above me. I was standing in thigh deep snow and it seemed like I was standing on the slab because I felt the whole thing moving with me on it - so I would guess the crown was at least 2-3 feet but possibly more. A split second later the snow hit my chest and I was drug underneath. The avalanche slammed into the other two in my party who had just left the safety of the climbers left rock. The avalanche carried us 800-1000 feet down the couloir and the entirety of the time we were under the snow fighting to swim to the surface. When it stopped we were all within 6 feet of one another and only buried up to our waists. It was easy to stand up and we didn't need shovels to extricate ourselves. We lost 2 skis off our backpacks when the straps ripped and I was the only person with two functional skis so I skinned up the debris field conducting a beacon search. The debris field was probably 600-800 feet in length. 3 skiers who were below us skied out after the slide and after we had conducted a thorough beacon search we skied out. Luckily we were all unscathed from the accident and walked away.   Postscript: This accident was completely avoidable and many factors contributed to it. I'm a former professional ski patroller and avid backcountry skier/climber who has been backcountry skiing for 15 years. In this situation my experience did not help me - but rather contributed to bad decision making. With the current stable snowpack I've been skiing in big terrain frequently and feeling very comfortable with the avalanche conditions. I incorrectly thought I could manage the storm snow and I inaccurately estimated the amount of snow that was actually loading. We were spread out as a group due to different fitness levels which limited our communication. Finally when things changed and the alarm bells started going off in the back of my head I didn't stop and think or turn around - I tried to move quickly to a safer place. Rushing is never a good idea and in my rush I failed to appreciate the magnitude of the terrain between me and the safe spot. Looking at the terrain from below after the avalanche - I was amazed at how much vertical terrain was between the climbers left rock and the cliffs below the middle of the Y. It looked deceivingly short but was in fact very far. Finally it's often hard to appreciate how much snow is actually loading during a snowstorm. Especially high above you.   Hindsight being 20/20 this all seems pretty predictable and straightforward from an avalanche perspective. This is an easy time of year to forecast avalanches and because of that the big terrain I'd recently skied and my years of experience in the backcountry I became overconfident in a dangerous situation. It was an extremely humbling experience for me. It doesn't matter how many times you are cautious and play it safe. All it takes is one day of carelessness and it could be your last. Avalanches are unpredictable and decision making is far from perfect for anyone. Good things to keep in mind every time you go out.

A partner and I were climbing up below the rocks in the picture on the right side. Once we hit the rocks we were wallowing in the facets so we headed left to try and continue climbing through the knee deep snow. We stopped climbing and were wondering if there were easier ways to climb up and over a very small but steep convexity instead of traversing climbers left and the wind slab broke. This was right at 9:20 am. We were both tumbled around by the slide and it pretty much had its way with us until it came to a rest. We definitely had to fight it by pushing down on the bed surface.  When the slide came to a rest we were both on top of he snow surface with maybe a couple inches of snow on top of us. Snow down the wind pipe lost sunglasses one ice axe one whip it and torn snow pants from crampons. The bed surface still seemed to be almost knee deep older snow as the avalanche did not step down.

Today we (grp of 5) witnessed three splitboarders skinning below and west of the Drainpipe on Parnassus today shortly before noon or so. Saw the slide but couldn't see if people were involved. We ripped skins and made our way down to assist. Three in our group headed down immediately (one is an EMT).By the time our three guys got there they had located and extracted their friend. column20: While approaching the steeper section of the run the snow turned soft threw me off balance and I fell.  After getting up and while standing the steeper face ripped out below me approximately 14-16"" of the more recent snow sliding on the persistent layer below which continues to exist after the long dry period and the more recent snow.  The avalanche was not major but did run out to the bottom of the run.  It was roughly 50 feet wide and ran 300 feet.  After this slide I skied the area to skier's right of the slide thinking that the loading of the face and aspect had subsided and that the remaining snow closer to trees and rock faces along the edge of the run would be relatively stable.  This was not the case however this triggered a similar slide which carried me down the slope 200 feet.  I was not buried and as the slide slowed down I was able to stand up and ski out.  Myself and my skiing partner both had beacons shovels and probes.  It was a good reminder that the new snow still has poor if any cohesion to the persistent slab beneath and to avoid areas prone to sliding and or avalanche exposure until it does.

column20: R2 - D1  soft slab Wind slab on top of surface hoar (?)   Started up from second creek trailhead about sunrise 6"" new snow in the parking lot and pretty windy. Had a north facing line that I'd skied two weeks before in mind. Skinned up the same aspect in sheltered and didn't see anything of concern. Got to the aqueduct and traverse to the top of the line and it looked great (purely skiing perspective). Hopped on a test slope right by it and saw only what would equate to sluffing but nothing slabby. We were running late and realistically only had time for one good lap so decided to go for it instead of taking a first lap in the trees next to it. Started to internally question the decision a bit right before dropping but just went for it.  We stopped at a safe zone about a third of the way down to regroup and so that we could keep eye's on for the second part. My partner dropped the second pitch (couple degrees steeper and a bit more exposed) and on his second turn it looked like he fell and slid out. I quickly realize that the entire slope was actually moving. At this point it hits me that we had just messed up. I watched as he took a ride down the last 150' of the chute through some small tree to the bottom. Luckily he ends up on the top a bit shaken up but otherwise alright. The crown was 2""-8"" deep and about 30' wide with a debris field 2' - 3' wide. Needless to say we called it a day after that..   LEARNING LESSONS Human Factor - This was in my mind the biggest mistake. I had really committed to ski this line and we passed up what would have been some perfectly fun and safer tree lines. It also allowed us to ignore the steepness which we both admitted afterwards we had thought was a bit steep but didn't say anything.  Little changes = Big differences  The slope after the first safety zone was a couple degrees steeper and a bit more exposed to the wind and this made all the difference. The bit of extra wind created enough of a slab and the extra degrees put us right below the sweet spot for slides.  Trust your gut - I was starting to have second thoughts right before we dropped but decided to go for it. If you have any hesitation in the backcountry you have to right to veto a line. I realized that that also means you can change your mind and veto your own line.

After deciding we were comfortable with the snow stability I proceeded to ski the first pitch of the chute. After 10 turns or so the snow became much deeper and I stopped to yell up to my partner to not venture any further than skier's left of my tracks in the chute. Another few turns and I paused again feeling very uncomfortable now in 18'' of new snow. At this point in time I was two turns away from our first safe zone and the entrance of the four skier's tracks just an hour or two prior of us. The chute ""Y's"" at the top and they had used the eastern entrance. It was during this next two turns where the slab released. I was then carried down the entirety of the couloir while my partner watched in horror. I came to rest sitting up as the debris slowed down after a brutally violent ride nearly 1500ft long. It is nothing short of a miracle that I sustained no major injuries. I lost both skis and poles in the slide. The debris however was only 2-3 feet deep at most not that much snow moved.   I would suspect the slab was around 75â€™ x 100â€™ and 18â€™â€™ deep. SS-ASu-R3-D2.   I should have been Coloradoâ€™s 1st fatality this season. Donâ€™t let this seasonâ€™s somewhat atypical Colorado snowpack lure you into terrain of high consequence without proper risk assessment and confidence in your decision making abilities. I was overly confident that the conditions I found while on the belay at the top of the chute would be the most suspect stability wise. After deeming the entrance safe I should have been more diligent in my ongoing observations of the snow.  I also should have trusted my intuition when I stopped for the second time due to the deeper snow farther down the couloir. Two turns away from a safe zone and 4 tracks from the same day also gave me a false sense of security and I proceeded without doing a thoughtful reassessment of the conditions. Do not underestimate the potential for unsuspecting large loads in couloirs such as this one a dusting at the car and I ended up triggering an 18â€™â€™ soft slab.   I plan to write a more in depth analysis of the day at some point once I have fully processed the situation. Be thankful for the beautiful mountains we get to plan in and live to ski another day.

column20: We triggered a small slide today up on Garret's which sounds like the type the CAIC has described. North facing slope at 10600' long and skinny slide path with good pitch for much of it but filled with many Christmas tree anchors a small rollover around 35Â° (guess) in an open pocket. Crown was maybe 30cm x 120' wide and ran into a narrow funnel below for 300'. Released with plane-like rush (not a high energy bang). Most of the run is filled with small trees except the slide zone which is open. There was a shallow gully to one side of the open feature and my partner skied that while i watched from above. She got to a safe zone below and suggested I follow her path rather than over the rollover which was good advice. While skiing in her tracks the slide began 50' below me and I managed to ski off to the side just below the crown. we didn't study the slide surface or crown in depth but it was a soft slab which broke up easily and the debris was soft to ski on. we still had quite a bit of skiing below without incident. we figured it would be good to put this information out there so people know that there are traps lurking in the snowpack.

column20: On 1/25 at approximately 10:30am a small avalanche was reported in the backcountry near the Beaver Creek Ski Area boundary in an area known as the Y chutes.  The reporting party was also the victim.  According to the report he described himself as being face down in/near a tree well with his snowboard/feet above him and he was unable to dislodge himself.  He stated that he started a small avalanche and it carried him to this position.  He was buried from his chest up and was apparently able to create some space around his face and head.  He was alone and without equipment. He was able to access his phone which was in his chest pocket and called rescuers. The rescue party instructed him to remain calm and that they were responding  to assist. The rescue team was able to instruct the victim on how to send them his GPS coordinates via his smart phone which allowed them to determine his location.   Before the rescuers reached the victim the reporting party called back and said a group of skiers/riders discovered him and freed him of his position. The victim stated that he was skiing a line that he skis often.  When he descended in to a small clearing the area broke around him and it began to carry him down the slope.  He stated that he was able to ""surf"" most of it until he contacted a small tree or something that pitched him forward resulting in him being somewhat upside down/face down and unable to free himself.  He described the slide being relatively small approximately 30 yards wide and 100 yards long.

After snow stopped the 2 skiers who were skiing the ridge appeared above this witness and discussed the sequence of events. It was determined that the 2 skiers had remotely triggered the slab approx 500ft below them that it initially broke on the original skier's track (possibly due to weakness created by that 1st ski track) then slabs released sequentially uphill as a series of soft slabs taking approx 5 seconds for the entire ridge edge to collapse. column20: A party of three skied an easterly slope with no signs of instability except a Storm Snow avalanche on a northerly slope nearby. They estimated this occurred the day before. They skinned east and ascended a low angle gully to the top of a northerly slope for their 2nd run. The slope avalanched on the first skier when he was midway down. The slab was 50 or so feet across but the debris moved quickly and the skier was unable to escape. He was carried several hundred feet down slope and stopped on the surface. Unfortunately he hit a small tree on the way down with left him with a serious lower leg injury. The party made a cell phone to request a rescue provided first aid and moved the victim several hundred feet to a landing zone. They had difficulties communicating with SAR and getting accurate coordinates for their location. Searchers located them just before dark and transported the victim to a hospital. The remaining two members of the group evacuated under their own power.

column20: The average slope angle of the starting zone was 35 degrees. The crown face depth ranged from 1 to almost 4 feet. The avalanche was approximately 270 feet wide and traveled downslope approximately 2300 vertical feet and a total of 4100 feet in length. The crown was located at approximately 7360 feet in elevation and the toe of the debris was estimated at 5100 feet. The avalanche is classified as SS-ASu-R2-D2-O. This means that it was a soft slab avalanche (SS) unintentionally triggered by a skier (ASu). It was small relative to the path and large enough to bury injure or kill a person (D2). The avalanche released within the old snow (O) on weak faceted snow above a firm wind scoured layer.

This was a Storm Slab avalanche. It was a soft slab unintentionally triggered by backcountry tourers was medium sized relative to the path capable of burying a person and broke at the interface between old and new snow (SS-ASu-R3D2-I). The avalanche started on a convex roll on a rocky knob. For about 40 to 60 vertical feet the slope below the knob is steeper than 30 degrees. The avalanche ran about 200 vertical feet.

The avalanche site was investigated by CAIC forecasters on 1/7.

column20: The avalanche occurred on a 30-35 degree north-facing slope at 11500 feet.  The crown was 2-4 inches deep on top of that 12/14 frozen bed surface (that was the ground in some places) from the previous large avalanche cycle.  It initiated and propagated to my right on my first left-hand turn.  Fully committed to the slope I took another right-hand turn before realizing that I had initialed an avalanche with my first turn.  If I hadn't made the second turn I might not have been swept off my feet but I still wouldn't have been able to exit the slope as I was blocked by a 2 ft frozen crown/flank wall.   There wasn't much snow involved but it was enough to push me harder than I could stick my edges into the frozen bed surface and approx 150 ft down the slope through several trees that I passed slow enough to think I could grab onto but with enough force pushing me that I couldn't hold on.  I stopped on the surface of a shallow pile of debris with one ski and one pole nearby.  The other ski was pinned against a tree a short way up the slope.  The pole is still missing.  It's a Black Diamond pole with yellow tape and an orange ski strap.  Please leave at Markley hut if found.

According to the skier's involved with the avalanche they passed the avalanche terrain warning signs at the base of the hike to the Knife Ridge. The group had discussed that they had forgotten their beacons.shovels and probes at home but decided to enter the terrain. They decided to ski off the Knife Ridge in to the Big Cornice/Gully 1 area. The first three skiers skied the path and waited for the fourth skier at the bottom. When the fourth skier was near the bottom of the slope it broke above him and the soft storm snow began pushing him downhill from behind.  He fell forward and was buried face down under 2' of snow. He lost a ski as he was being buried and came to rest below a small tree (see photo).  His friends were calling out to him and when he did not respond they began to make their way up hill to where they could see his ski sticking out of the snow. They called 911. Once there they dug the buried skier out with their hands. He was uncovered within 3-5 minutes. When they uncovered his face he was unconscious. They removed snow from his face and mouth and he regained consciousness.  Patrol arrived and assisted with further extrication and medical treatment.  The slide was 50' wide 50' long. The fracture occurred within the storm snow and did not step down into the old facet layer. The crown line was soft and 6-8"" deep.  Two additional slides were documented in the ski area the same day on very similar aspects.

column20: 8 riders in our group riding along 311 where 311 turns into a steep hill that the trail crosses a rider triggered avalanche occurred.  2 rear riders had paused to make sure front riders made it across the 'danger zone' just as the entire hill slid.  4' slab at deepest point.  2 riders buried 4' deep pinned on trees.  1 rider remained on top of slide.  Both buried riders were breathing with searchers only having radio confirmation of 1 breathing but pinned under sled.  Probe search and extraction took 10-14 minutes both buried riders were ok.  Both riders had Avy packs one deployed one did not grasp handle which appeared pretty high on shoulder.  Both lives were saved by people who had taken Avalanche courses taken control of the situation and did an efficient and effective search and rescue.

We observed another party of four involved in a natural D1.5 loose-snow avalanche at 10:20. Mouth of Dragontail where it opens onto the fan caught one skier and carried him while he was booting. He broke a ski lost a helmet but was unhurt. He came to a stop on the apron where the debris fanned out. The party said it was a natural avalanche from above--perhaps from the eastern entrance (skier's left) as we had skied and sluffed-out the right (western) entrance during our descent.   The incident occurred during the brief period of slightly more solar input during the ""muggy"" period mentioned above. We were climber's left of the couloir entrance skinning up for a lap on the apron when we heard someone yell looked up and saw the victim entrained in snow. He briefly went out of sight but then rode the avalanche to a stop sitting upright.   There was also loose dry debris at the bottom of the Dead Elk the ""S"" couloir and we had sluffed out the skier's right entrance of the Dragontail during our descent. We ski-cut the entrance to the Dragontail while on belay without significant result--just sluffing. Skied the whole feature while managing small sluffs but no slab avalanches observed. Sluffs were running without much energy and were pretty easy to avoid.

column20: Two parties (Party 1: three skiers / Party 2: four skiers) simultaneously made a bootpack ascent of the couloir. Party 1 reached a highpoint approximately 20m below the ridgeline (~12900') ~20m above the partially covered rockband and just above the steepest (~50degree) part of the couloir and began to transition for descent. Meanwhile three of four skiers from Party 2 began to ascend from the widest section of the couloir ('the torso') into the narrow upper section with the fourth skier of Party 2 (skier 2.4) below in the 'torso' section. At this point Party 1 indicated they would wait for everyone to ascend before skiing. Party 2 then communicated the offer to stand off to skier's right in the narrow upper couloir section below the partially covered rock band (20m below Party 1) to let Party 1 descend past them. Party 1 agreed. As Party 1 prepared to ski the fourth skier of Party 2 (skier 2.4) was still ascending the bootpack in the narrow upper couloir section (far climbers left) approx. 10m below the rest of Party 2. At this point Party 1 and probably Party 2 expected the possibility of loose dry sloughing in the middle of the narrow upper couloir feature. The lead skier from Party 1 (Skier 1.1) edged out slowly 1-2m from the couloir wall at which point a storm slab avalanche released nearly wall to wall from Skier 1 down to the top of the partially covered rock band where the first three members of Party 2 stood( Skiers 2.1 2.2 2.3). The initial slab released (Avalanche 1) had a 15cm crown 3-4m width and 20m length. This soft slab drained below the partially covered rock band bypassed skiers 2.1 2.2 and 2.3 but caught skier 2.4. Avalanche 1 began to build downslope entraining the upper (dustless) part of the storm slab in the central gut of the couloir but did not appear to entrain any snow outside of the runout path. Skier 2.4 was observed to come to rest on top of the thin deposit near the top of the apron (12150'). At this point Party 1 was wary of hangfire in the upper couloir and remained in place so the lower placed skier 2.1 quickly transitioned and began to descend. As soon as skier 2.1 entered the wider 'torso' part of the couloir (approx. 35-40 degrees) nearly all of the remaining upper (dustless) storm slab in the couloir released (Avalanche 2) in particular drawing crowns well up the eastern sidewalls (skiers left) of the couloir. Skier 2.1 immediately descended the scour surface to assist skier 2.4 below. The remaining 5 skiers from both parties then descended the couloir on the scour surface. All seven members of both parties were able to descend to the trailhead on ski from that point. Collectively the two avalanches ran 850' vertical and were estimated at D2R4 In the case of both avalanches the slip surface was the interface between the dusty and dustless parts of the storm slab and the slide did not seem to step below this interface aside from minor scouring.

column20: Two skiers approached the top of the Little Wasatch Face around noon. After transitioning skiers headed NW across the ridge toward the top of the Grandfather Couloir. They approached two snowboarders who were also planning to ski the Grandfather but entering from Oblivion Bowl. The snowboarders were still transitioning so they said the skiers could ski before them. The skiers had radios but snowboarders did not so skiers took phone numbers -knowing that there is cell service at the bottom- and told them that when they were in a safe zone out of the couloir they would call and tell the snowboarders to go to avoid getting skied on top of. Both parties understood and agreed with the plan so the skiers proceeded to the top of the Grandfather. The ski down consisted of mostly soft wintery snow. The areas in the sun had not yet warmed up and were still very firm. The two skiers got to the mandatory rappel and went one at a time skier 1 rappelled down while skier 2 stayed at the anchor at the top of the rappel. When skier 1 was nearing the end of the rappel about 5-10 feet from end of rope skier 2 notified skier 1 of avalanche by yelling. Skier 2 held on to rope and managed to not get taken down with the avalanche. Skier 1 held onto rope for as long as possible but was then taken down by the avalanche. When the slide stopped skier 1 was on top of the debris unburied. When skier 1 realized he/she was okay they took out beacon to switch to search mode when skier 2 skied out of the couloir uninjured. Both skiers made it to a safe zone.

I made it to skier's right and to my safe zone but my ski hit a rock under the fresh fallen snow and bounced me BACK into the path of the growing slide. The Central Couloir is a prominent NE-facing chute accessed via a ridgeline extending NW from the summit of Chief Joseph Mountain. The ridgeline is oriented normal to the prevailing winds and develops large cornices due to the relatively warm intermountain snow climate. As in most alpine terrain cornice size varied due to local terrain features. The cornice was largest near the center of the chute and tapered on the sides. The chute itself is generally planar ranging from 35-38 degrees in steepness except for a short steeper section at the very top. The cornice that failed was 50 feet wide 25 feet tall and 20 feet from the lip to the failure point. Using an estimated 33% density (333 kg/cubic meter) for the involved cornice this mass of snow weighed approximately 500000 pounds. This large block of snow did not trigger a slab avalanche when it struck the slope beneath it but it did entrain loose surface snow as it descended.

On 2/7/2016 visitors reported remotely triggering an avalanche on the trail between Calypso Cascades and Finch Lake trail. The visitors stated they observed shooting cracks and then saw an avalanche release in front of and above them. Rangers investigated the avalanche on 2/8/2016 and found a HS-ASr-R3-D2-S/I avalanche on a 39 degree slope at 9400 feet on a N aspect in a drainage. The crown and flanks had drifted in somewhat but appeared to average 18-22 inches. The avalanche was around 30-40 feet wide and ran approximately 600-700 feet. The path was being crossloaded by WNW winds. In some thinner areas the avalanche had stepped down to weak snow near the ground. Photos and pit profile attached. The avalanche did cross the established trail.
